item.title: 视频模型会画出「物理不对」的物体运动：MotionCore 干脆去学一个可微分的 PDE 求解器，只做刚体 ｜ MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics
item.description:
一句话：画面逼真但物理不成立，说明纯视觉建模给不出可迁移的动力学表示。

要点：

  • 作者从现象下手：视频生成模型能产出高度真实的画面，却经常生成物理上不一致的物体运动——这说明**只靠视觉建模无法提供可迁移的物理动力学表示**
  • MotionCore 的做法是学习一个**可学习的偏微分方程求解器**，把物理动力学作为表示来学，而不是从像素里间接推断
  • 论文聚焦刚体运动，并在 latent 空间里训练神经模拟器来预测运动演化

为什么值得看：「视频世界模型物理不对」是最常被诟病的问题，多数方案靠堆数据或加惩罚项。把动力学写成可学的 PDE 求解器，是把它变成结构约束——这也是「世界模型当引擎」需要的物理层。

中文摘要：视频生成模型能产出高度真实的画面，却常常生成物理上不一致的物体运动，这说明仅靠视觉建模可能无法提供可迁移的物理动力学表示。MotionCore 因此把物理动力学本身作为学习对象：它构建一个可学习的偏微分方程求解器，在 latent 空间里训练神经模拟器来预测刚体运动的演化。与在像素上间接推断物理、或仅用渲染一致性做监督的做法相比，这条路线试图让模型学到一个能跨场景迁移的动力学表示。对希望世界模型承担「物理层」职责的引擎来说，这是更根本的一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics

Abstract

Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulators learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. The latter setting measures obedience to a specified physical rollout, while the former evaluates broader physical and semantic consistency. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.

1 Introduction

Video generation models have made rapid progress in visual quality. They can synthesize detailed scenes, realistic appearances, and complex motions. Yet visual realism does not imply physical correctness. Generated objects may accelerate without a clear cause, pass through one another, or follow trajectories that conflict with collisions and gravity. This limitation is not restricted to older or small-scale models. Recent systems, including Seedance 2.0 [43] and MiniMax H3 [31], demonstrate advances in visual quality. Recent benchmarks, including VideoPhy, PhyGenBench, Physics-IQ, and VideoPhy-2, report a persistent gap between visual quality and physical consistency [3, 29, 33, 4]. These observations suggest that a strong visual prior alone is insufficient for reliable physical prediction. More broadly, improving visual modeling capacity does not automatically provide a transferable representation of object dynamics.

A physical model should predict how a system evolves when its initial state, object properties, or interactions change. Hand-designed simulators provide an explicit way to model such evolution. They require, however, detailed descriptions of object geometry, materials, and governing rules. These descriptions are effective for predefined systems, but they are costly to construct and difficult to extend to the diversity of real-world scenes. A learned physical model offers a complementary approach. It can extract regularities from observations without requiring a complete symbolic description of every object and interaction. Such models may still fall short of high-fidelity simulation in the wild. They nevertheless provide a practical route toward learning physical dynamics from large-scale visual observations.

Videos are a natural source of such observations. They contain object trajectories, interactions, and changes in motion under diverse conditions. Object-level representations can be inferred from video and used for learned dynamics prediction [48]. This suggests a modular view of video generation. AI Flow advocates intelligence emerging from coordinated models and their interactions [2], with device–edge–cloud inference as one concrete setting [41]. A physical dynamics learning modular learns how the observed system evolves. And a pretrained video diffusion model then acts as a visual tool that renders the predicted state with realistic appearance. In this setting, video generation works like a piloted mech: the dynamics-learning part is the pilot that decides how the scene moves next, and the diffusion model is the body that carries out that decision by rendering it into frames.

However, how to learn physcis dynamics beyond visual cues becomes a major obstacle. Physical dynamics can typically be described by differential equations with unknown parameters: rigid-body motion is governed by the Newton–Euler equations, and the propagation of light by Maxwell’s equations. This suggests that a solver tailored to a specific scene can serve as an abstract description of that real-world scene. We learn such a solver in latent space with a neural operator, and use it to build a path from physical space to visual space.

In this paper, we introduce MotionCore, a framework for video-grounded rigid-body dynamics learning. MotionCore uses a latent neural simulator to model the evolution of object-level physical states. The neural simulator predicts future object states from observed motion and produces intermediate latent features that describe the evolving physical system. And we use a controllable video generation model VACE [12] built on Wan2.1-1.3B [46] as the video generator. A lightweight adapter converts the predicted states into spatially aligned control maps on the latent video grid. The generator remains fixed and provides appearance, texture, and visual detail, while the dynamics model provides the physical trajectory.

2 Related Work

Neural operators in Latent Space.

Neural operators learn maps between function spaces and can therefore transfer across spatial discretizations. DeepONet represents nonlinear operators with branch and trunk networks [28], whereas the Fourier Neural Operator performs global kernel integration in the spectral domain [19]. Latent formulations reduce the cost of evolving high-dimensional physical fields by learning a compact solution manifold or an encoder–operator–decoder factorization. NOMAD uses a nonlinear decoder for finite-dimensional solution manifolds [39]. Latent Spectral Models and the Latent Neural Operator learn the principal transformation in a compact space [50, 47], while latent DeepONet compresses both input and output functions before operator learning [13]. Geometry-aware variants map irregular meshes or particles to latent grids or tokens [20, 1], and AROMA retains spatially organized latent sequences and learns their temporal evolution with a conditional Transformer and a diffusion objective [40]. More recent models use state-space dynamics for long-range propagation [45] or flow-matching autoregression for generative PDE evolution [14]. AROMA and ENMA are especially relevant because they combine compressed physical states with generative dynamics, but their outputs remain numerical PDE fields. MotionCore instead places a PDE-informed solution operator inside video latent denoising, using the operator state to guide the generation of detailed visual frames.

Simulator-based physical video generation.

One line of work obtains motion from an explicit simulator and transfers it to a generative visual model. MotionCraft warps diffusion noise latents with optical flow computed from a physical simulation [32]. PhysGen infers scene properties, simulates rigid-body motion, and renders the result with video diffusion [27], while PSIVG reconstructs a dynamic scene and places a simulator in the generation loop [6]. These pipelines provide interpretable control, but their behavior is coupled to reconstructed object states, simulator assumptions, or test-time optimization. A complementary line learns physical control or supervision from data. PISA combines simulated-video fine-tuning with reward-based post-training for free fall [15]. PointVid regularizes generation with 3D point trajectories [5], Force Prompting conditions videos on local or global force fields [7], and VLIPP converts vision-language reasoning into coarse motion plans [53]. VideoREPA instead distills pairwise spatiotemporal relations from a video representation model [59]. These methods inject useful motion variables, plans, or preferences, but do not learn the governing field evolution as a reusable solution operator.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Representation of Rigid-body Dynamics

A physical trajectory records one realization of a dynamical system, whereas its governing equation describes an entire family of realizations. The governing equations of rigid-body dynamics are usually in the forms of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). For example, in the case of motion without collisions and external constraints, the Newton-Euler equations are given by Eq. 1.

ṗ=v, mv̇=F,(1)
Ṙ=Rω̂, Iω̇+ω×(Iω)=τ.

where p,v,F,I,τ,R,ω specify the position , velocity, net external force, inertia tensor. net external torque, rotation matrix and angular velocity of the rigid body’s mass center. If F and τ are uniquely determined by current states and time, the govern equations could be reduced to one ODE which takes the form

ẋ=f(t,x;φ)

(2)

where φ includes settings mentioned in Eq. 1. Eq. 2 is a finite-dimensional ODE evolving on a physical-state manifold. However, not all rigid-body motion can be described by this smooth ODE such as impulsive dynamics in the scene of ideal rigid-body collision and externally constrained rigid-body system.

To address this limitation, we approximate rigid bodies as deformable elastic body with large but finite stiffness, and collisions through elastic-body’s contact laws [36, 37]. The observed instances are modeled as elastic continua, which means we could describe general rigid-body dynamics via partial differential equations (PDEs), unifying smooth and impulsive response. Our aim is to find an intermediate physical-state representation which can guide the video diffusion models generate plausible outputs.

3.2 Neural Operator

While treating the general rigid-body dynamics as a PDE, we should build a model reusing a single evolution rule as the initial state, physical parameters, or boundary conditions change. Neural Operator (NO) makes this precise by treating the quantities involved as functions [28, 19]. An operator maps a function in one space to a function in another. A neural operator composes layers that each act on functions.

NOs have following properties that enable it to effectively learn mappings between functions. (i)Initial conditions, coefficients, and boundary data enter as inputs rather than as fixed settings, so one set of parameters represents a whole family of solutions. (ii)The same parameters apply across compatible discretizations: inputs can be sampled on different grids, outputs can be queried at any resolution, and predictions converge as the discretization is refined. This transfer concerns different samplings of the same instance, and extrapolation to unseen physical regimes remains a separate question. (iii)A trained NO evaluates a new instance in one forward pass, amortizing the cost of a numerical solve.

Evolving a full-resolution field at every step can nevertheless be expensive. Latent neural operators [47] reduce this cost by factorizing the operator into three parts: an encoder that maps the input to a compact latent representation, an operator that evolves this representation, and a decoder that returns the result to physical space. Because the decoder can be queried at arbitrary points, the latent form keeps the resolution independence of the second property while moving the costly evolution into a smaller space. Section 4 adopts this factorization for structured physical states and analyzes what the latent representation must preserve for the approximation to hold.

4 Latent Neural Simulator

4.1 Problem Setting

We study rigid-body video generation with physical prediction separated from visual rendering. A semantic condition c, typically a text prompt with the first frame, specifies visual appearance and initial condition. A physical model receives the geometry and object states of the initial frame estimated from the observed frames, and predicts the future trajectory at the video timestamps t₁,…,t_K, and a video generator renders that trajectory. Motion is the responsibility of the physical model, and appearance that of the generator.

Following Section 3, a scene contains K bodies, and body k has state xₖ=(pₖ,Rₖ,vₖ,ωₖ), with Rₖ embedded in ℝ^3×3. Between contacts, xₖ follows the Eq. 1. At contact this description breaks down, so we adopt the compliant model of Section 3: each body is treated as an elastic body with large but finite stiffness, and contact follows elastic contact laws [36, 37]. The coefficients φ∈Φ collect mass, inertia, stiffness, and contact parameters. Under this model the trajectory remains continuous in time through collisions, and the impulsive rigid-body motion is recovered as the stiffness tends to infinity [36, 37]. With geometry and φ fixed over the horizon [0,Tₕ], the dynamics define the solution operator

S^†:X^K×Φ\longrightarrowC([0,T];X^(K)),(x(0),φ)\longmapstox(·)

(3)

where X is the state space of single rigid body. This is the coefficient-to-solution setting of operator learning in Section 3.2. Just as a permeability field determines the pressure of a Darcy flow [19], the coefficient field and the initial state determine a rigid-body trajectory, and one operator covers the entire family of scenes. Learning S^† therefore means learning the shared law of rigid-body motion rather than any single trajectory.

We learn this operator on an encoded state. The observed history provides the initial state. An encoder 𝔼 maps the history to latent codes ℤ, a neural operator T_N evolves the code, and a decoder D returns the predicted trajectory [50, 47]. Because the token has a fixed size independent of the number and shape of objects, one operator can serve environments that an explicit simulator would have to set up one by one. Theorem 4.1 makes this precise: the error is controlled by how well the token preserves the evolution and by how simple the induced latent operator is.

4.2 Theoretical Boundary

Inspired by the function-space analysis of latent nonlinear operators between Hilbert spaces [52], we formulate the upper boundary on the approximation error of latent neural operator approximation. We model the physical flow with a latent neural operator [47],

L_N=D∘T_N∘𝔼, L_N(u)=ŝ_1:T,

(4)

where 𝔼:U→ℤ encodes the observed history, T_N:ℤ→ℤ evolves the physics in a learned latent space, and D:ℤ→V decodes the predicted evolution. We assume U and V are separable real Hilbert spaces, which is usually plausible in physical scenes. Learning physics in this formulation means minimizing approximation error to the PDE-induced flow map over the distribution of physical systems. The error has two sources: how well a finite network represents one latent transition which we denote as εₐₚₚᵣₒₓ=∥S^†-D∘T_N∘𝔼∥_L_ρ^q(V)., and how one-step errors accumulate over the rollout which is derived in Appendix A.4.

We first consider a sufficient condition under which the ideal latent transition admits a quantitative finite-width approximation. Specifically, we assume that the ideal latent dynamics T^† belongs to a variation space by a family of bounded ridge features, whose norm quantifies the functional complexity of representing the target operators through these features and controls its finite-width approximation error. Importantly, the ridge representation serves as an auxiliary approximation class for the theoretical analysis. The definition of this variation space is shown in Appendix A.2.

Let ℤ̄:=ℝ⊕ℤ and z̄:=(1,z), and B_ℤ̄ be the closed unit ball of ℤ̄. A width-N latent ridge operator T_N(z)=∑ⱼ₌₁^Nbⱼ σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩) with h̄ⱼ∈B_ℤ̄ is a finite instance of an infinite-width operator class; writing h̄ⱼ=(αⱼ,aⱼ) recovers the biased feature bⱼ σ(αⱼ+⟨aⱼ,z⟩). Then we give the finite-width approximation boundary in Theorem A.2.

Theorem 4.1(Finite-width approximation of latent dynamics).

Let 2≤q<∞, let σ:ℝ→ℝ be L_σ-Lipschitz, and let μ be a probability measure on ℤ with ∫_ℤ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^q/2 \rmdμ(z)<∞. Define

Γ_σ,q(μ):=(∫_ℤ[|σ(0)|+L_σ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^1/2]^q \rmdμ(z))^1/q.

(5)

Γ_σ,q(μ) is the L^q average of the unit envelope over the encoded states. If T^†∈Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ), then for every N≥1 and ε>0 there is a width-N latent ridge operator T_N with ∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥bⱼ∥_ℤ≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε and

∥T^†-T_N∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)≤(C_q Γ_σ,q(μ) (∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε))/(√N),

(6)

where C_q>0 depends only on q. If the variation norm of T^† is attained by a representing measure, the bound holds with ε=0.

The bound decomposes the physical approximation error into a latent factorization error and a finite-width operator approximation error. The former quantifies how accurately the target physical evolution can be represented through the latent dynamics formulation, while the latter is controlled by the variation norm of the ideal latent transition and decays at a rate of O(N^-1/2) under the stated assumptions. This reveals a fundamental trade-off in latent compression: an effective representation should preserve the target physical evolution while reducing the complexity of the induced latent dynamics. Notably, the guarantee requires neither an injective encoder nor an inverse decoder, provided that the target evolution admits an accurate latent factorization. Furthermore, the bound contains no explicit dependence on the latent dimension, although such dependence may enter implicitly through its constants. This is a conditional approximation result: the ideal latent dynamics must admit a representation with a sufficiently small variation norm, and the finite-width guarantee applies to the specified auxiliary approximation class rather than arbitrary neural architectures. Detailed assumptions, proofs, and corollaries are provided in Appendix A.

5 Framework of MotionCore

5.1 Overview

MotionCore predicts a rigid-body scene frame by frame from one initial frame and renders the prediction with a video generator. The overall architecture is shown in Fig 1.

Scene encoder. The encoder turns a frame into the latent geometry state. It is an temporary-occupancy autoencoder in the style of 3DShape2VecSet [55] and Perceiver [10]. Its encoder embeds points (x,y,z,t) sampled inside the occupied volume with Fourier features [42]. The decoder returns an occupancy logit at any query point [30]. Applied to single frames, all points carry t=0, and the rollout starts from ẑ₀. The latent code orders an unordered point set into slots on which an operator can act rather than compressing it.

Latent neural operato r. The latent transition advances the geometry by one frame. The state adapter A_c first writes the object states into the latent: the 256 slots cross-attend to one token per object. The latent neural operator T_N[47] then aggregates the slots into latent modes by physics cross-attention, evolves the modes with attention blocks, and maps them back. Because the slots have no physical position, its trunk receives fixed coordinates ξ∈[-1,1]²⁵⁶.

Free-motion proposal. The proposal predicts where each object moves if no contact occurs. Each object token, formed from sⁱ and a Fourier embedding of tₖ₊₁, cross-attends to ẑₖ₊₁ and then to the other objects. A head outputs bounded residual corrections δ=c\tanh(·), and p̃ⁱ=pⁱ+vⁱ+δⁱₚ, ṽⁱ=vⁱ+δⁱᵥ, ω̃ⁱ=ωⁱ+δⁱ_ω,.

Collision operator. The collision operator ℂ_col corrects the proposal at contacts. For the proposed positions, gaps gᵢⱼ and unit normals nᵢⱼ (from j to i) are computed for every object pair. A pretrained surface operator, frozen here, adds gap and normal estimates from oriented surface samples as edge features. With uᵢⱼ=ṽⁱ-ṽʲ, its tangential part uᵗᵢⱼ, and m̄ᵢⱼ=(mᵢ⁻¹+mⱼ⁻¹)⁻¹,

\begingatheredJⁿᵢⱼ=(1+eᵢⱼ) m̄ᵢⱼ\max(0,-uᵢⱼ·nᵢⱼ), Jᵗᵢⱼ=\min(m̄ᵢⱼ∥uᵗᵢⱼ∥, fᵢⱼJⁿᵢⱼ), Jᵢⱼ=πᵢⱼ(Jⁿᵢⱼnᵢⱼ-Jᵗᵢⱼûᵗᵢⱼ), vⁱ=ṽⁱ+mᵢ⁻¹(∑_j≠iJᵢⱼ+Jᵢ₀),\endgathered

(7)

The normal impulse reverses the closing speed with restitution eᵢⱼ, the tangential impulse stays in the Coulomb cone of friction fᵢⱼ, and equal and opposite impulses conserve linear momentum between bodies for any mass ratio. Overlapping pairs are separated along nᵢⱼ, which resolves resting contacts without closing speed. An edge network predicts the contact probability πᵢⱼ=sigmoid((ε-gᵢⱼ)/τ_c+ρᵢⱼ), a geometric logit plus a learned residual ρᵢⱼ, and bounded corrections to eᵢⱼ and fᵢⱼ around priors from φ. Both are symmetrized over each pair, which keeps the exchange equal and opposite. The corrected state re-enters the latent through A_c at the next step, so a collision also changes the predicted geometry.

Video interface. The interface turns the predicted latents into a condition for the video generator. Our video generator is Wan 2.1-VACE [46, 12], whose control branch reads position from where a feature lies in a spatially aligned control video. The renderer decodes ẑₖ with the decoder of the latent neural operator, projects the occupied geometry with the calibrated camera, separates it into instances matched across frames, and draws each in its own label colour.

5.2 Training

The modules are trained in stage-wise pattern, each frozen before the next, and the simulator is never trained through the video objective: with the physical loss active the diffusion gradient leaves it unchanged, and without it the simulator drifts toward more motion and nearly doubles its short-horizon error (Appendix D.2).

Stage 1 pretrains the surface operator on exact gap and normal targets, and the occupancy autoencoder on space–time segments with the binary cross-entropy loss [30].

Stage 2 freezes both and trains A_c, T, ℙ_free, and ℂ_col jointly on free-running rollouts of K frames from a single initial frame, with

L=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^K(λ_zL_lat,k+λₒL_occ,k+λₛL_state,k+λ_cL_con,k).

(8)

The latent term Lₗₐₜ is a smooth-L₁ loss between ẑₖ and the posterior mean μₖ of the ground-truth frame. The occupancy term L_occ is a binary cross-entropy on query points [30]. The state term Lₛₜₐₜₑ applies the smooth-L₁ loss to the normalized position, velocity, and angular velocity, including the collision response. The contact term L_con is a focal loss [25] on per-object, pairwise, and floor contact labels, which supervises πᵢⱼ. Because no step is teacher-forced, L scores the accumulated error described by Theorem A.4, not only single-step error.

Stage 3 needs no training for the rendered interface. The learned adapter A_θ (6.7×10⁴ parameters), designed for states without renderable geometry, splats object attributes and operator features at the projected centres and is trained with the flow-matching loss of the frozen generator on ground-truth states. Loss weights and optimization settings are in Appendix B.

6 Experiments

6.1 Setup

Data. The simulator is trained on rigid-body trajectories from MOVi-Spheres [8, 49] and Billiards [58]. Appendix B lists the production splits; Section 6.3 specifies the separate small-scale ablation protocol. For video generation we use two benchmarks: a subset of Physics-IQ-Verified [38], a general benchmark of physical reasoning, from which we select the scenes whose prompts describe rigid-body motion such as collision, rolling, sliding, and free fall and finally get 81 five-second videos; and RigidBench [11], a public benchmark built for rigid-body dynamics, which provides 100 two-second videos.

Metrics. Both benchmarks compare the generated video with a reference recording of the same scene. Physics-IQ [33, 38] uses binary motion masks for ST-IoU, measuring whether motion occurs at the right place and time. MSE compares temporally aligned RGB frames after resizing and pixel normalization to [0,1]. The Physics-IQ score aggregates these with the spatial and weighted spatial IoU, normalized so that the variation between two real recordings of a scene scores 100. RigidBench [11] recovers object masks, point tracks, and depth from the generated video and scores them against the simulator ground truth. We report per-object mask IoU, the mask-centroid error (L2) and the bidirectional Chamfer distance, both normalized by image height [15]. We also report the 2D trajectory error of tracked points (ATE), the 3D error of the reconstructed object positions (ATE-3D), and the scale-invariant depth error (SI-MSE).

Baselines. We choose general-purpose models of comparable scale CogVideoX-5B-I2V [54], HunyuanVideo-1.5-480P-I2V [44], MiniMax-H3 [31], Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [46], Cosmos-Predict-2.5 2B [35] to complete the quality axis. Baseline numbers are copied from the cited papers where benchmark, split, and backbone match, and re-run otherwise.

Implementation. Our generator is Wan 2.1-VACE-1.3B [46, 12] with base weights. Sampling uses 30 steps at 832×480 with classifier-free guidance 5.0 on the text and none on the physical condition; clips have 81 frames at 16 fps on Physics-IQ and 21 frames on MOVi-Spheres. The simulator is frozen after Stage 2, advances one block per step, and is decoded at every video timestamp. All experiments are conducted on 8 Nvidia H100 GPUs. Remaining details are in Appendix B.

6.2 Main Results

On the strict81 Physics-IQ-Verified subset of 27 scenes and three views, the R2 sphere model obtains an IQ score of 28.14±0.41, a raw ST-IoU of 0.3734±0.0117, and a raw RGB MSE of 0.008633±0.000268 (Table 1). Values are the mean and sample standard deviation over four diffusion-seed rounds, not independent training runs. All 81 scene-view samples are retained in each round, including the 20 native-VACE fallbacks. Known contact and support failures in the control cache limit the physical interpretation of these aggregate scores; they do not isolate a causal benefit of the simulator.

Qualitative comparison.

Figure 2 compares three selected collision, falling, and rolling scenes using the same switch-frame input and prompt across methods. MotionCore additionally uses an initial state estimated from the permitted observation history; the baseline models use the first frame and text only. Future reference frames are used for comparison, not generation. The sequences allow object persistence, motion, and interaction timing to be examined separately. For example, the falling scene shows that retaining the basketball and crate appearance does not ensure the reference descent or contact. The examples were selected post hoc for visualization and do not establish benchmark-wide rankings or equal-information simulator ablations.

6.3 Ablations

The small-scale study separates the learned dynamics from the analytic prior and compares LNO with Transolver [51] and GNOT-CGPT [9] processors adapted to a shared latent-slot interface. Only the processor is replaced for the learned variants. The pretrained occupancy encoder 𝔼 is shared and kept frozen (Appendix D.1); the state-head architecture, integrator, and contact rules are also shared. The analytic variant retains the same physical priors with all learned corrections zeroed. All three learned models start from matched shared-head weights and use the same 50 windows from a 32-scene training pool (23 actually observed), with 8 validation and 16 test scenes. They use dataset initial states, static geometry, state-only loss, and causal rollouts; no production checkpoint is substituted for the pilot Full.

All four rows are complete. Errors are close: Full has slightly lower test ADE and FDE than the alternatives at this budget, while the rollout curves nearly coincide (Appendix D.1). A single seed and 50 updates do not establish convergence, statistical significance, a production-model ranking, or video-control gains. These state-domain measurements are separate from production Physics-IQ and partial RigidBench results.

7 Conclusion

MotionCore separates rigid-body state prediction from visual synthesis. A latent neural simulator produces object-state rollouts, and a spatial adapter with control-branch LoRA conveys them to a video generator whose main backbone remains frozen. We evaluate video agreement on the strict81 Physics-IQ subset and report single-round RigidBench diagnostics and a controlled short-horizon processor pilot. These results characterize the current pipeline without establishing a causal simulator benefit. State-estimation uncertainty, contact and support failures, and imperfect object persistence remain limitations; stable long-horizon physical control is an open goal.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A More Proof

A.1 Setting

Let U and ℤ be separable real Hilbert spaces. U holds the state of one block, so that V=U in Eq. equation 4. ℤ is the latent space. The encoder 𝔼:U→ℤ is measurable, and the decoder D:ℤ→U is L_D-Lipschitz. Throughout, 2≤q<∞. A trajectory x₀,…,x_K is drawn from the data distribution, so its encoded states zₖ:=𝔼(xₖ) are random with laws μₖ:=Law(zₖ). For a random variable Y with values in a Hilbert space H we write ∥Y∥_L^q:=(𝔼∥Y∥_H^q)^1/q, and for an operator T:ℤ→ℤ and a probability measure μ on ℤ we write ∥T∥_L^q_μ(ℤ):=(∫_ℤ∥T(z)∥_ℤ^q \rmdμ(z))^1/q. The two notations agree along the trajectory: ∥T(zₖ)∥_L^q=∥T∥_L^q_μₖ(ℤ).

A.2 Latent Variation Space

Let σ:ℝ→ℝ be L_σ-Lipschitz. Write ℤ̄:=ℝ⊕ℤ and z̄:=(1,z), so that ∥z̄∥_ℤ̄=(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^1/2, and let B_ℤ̄ be the closed unit ball of ℤ̄.

Definition A.1(Latent variation space).

An operator T:ℤ→ℤ belongs to Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ) if

T(z)=∫_B_ℤ̄σ(⟨z̄,h̄⟩) \rmdΛ(h̄)

(9)

for a ℤ-valued Borel measure Λ of bounded variation. Its variation norm is

∥T∥_Vₗₐₜ:=\inf_Λ|Λ|(B_ℤ̄),

(10)

the infimum being over all measures that represent T in equation 9.

The representation equation 9 is a one-hidden-layer network of unbounded width. Each point h̄=(α,a)∈B_ℤ̄ is a hidden unit z↦σ(α+⟨a,z⟩), and \rmdΛ(h̄) is its output weight, a vector in ℤ. The total variation |Λ|(B_ℤ̄) is then the total size of the output weights, and the variation norm is the smallest such total over all networks that compute T. It measures how simple T is for this model class rather than how many parameters represent it: the constraint ∥h̄∥_ℤ̄≤1 fixes the scale of the hidden units, so the norm cannot be lowered by shrinking output weights while enlarging input weights. A finite network belongs to the space. For N≥1, a width-N latent ridge operator is

T_N(z)=∑ⱼ₌₁^Nbⱼ σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩), h̄ⱼ∈B_ℤ̄, bⱼ∈ℤ,

(11)

which is represented by the atomic measure Λ=∑ⱼbⱼδ_h̄ⱼ and therefore has ∥T_N∥_Vₗₐₜ≤∑ⱼ∥bⱼ∥_ℤ. Writing h̄ⱼ=(αⱼ,aⱼ) recovers the biased feature bⱼ σ(αⱼ+⟨aⱼ,z⟩). The space is the latent-to-latent case of the variation spaces for encoder–decoder operators of [Yang and Shi [52]].

The second quantity describes the distribution μ of the encoded states. If ∫_ℤ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^q/2 \rmdμ(z)<∞, set

Γ_σ,q(μ):=(∫_ℤ[|σ(0)|+L_σ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^1/2]^q \rmdμ(z))^1/q.

(12)

The bracket bounds the output of a single hidden unit at z, since |⟨z̄,h̄⟩|≤∥z̄∥_ℤ̄ for h̄∈B_ℤ̄, and Γ_σ,q(μ) is its L^q average over the encoded states. Minkowski’s inequality gives

\begingatheredΓ_σ,q(μ)≤|σ(0)|+L_σ M̄_q(μ), M̄_q(μ):=(∫_ℤ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^q/2 \rmdμ(z))^1/q.\endgathered

(13)

and for ReLU, where σ(0)=0 and L_σ=1, Γ_σ,q(μ)≤M̄_q(μ). The quantity therefore grows with how far the encoded states spread from the origin, and it is finite exactly when this q-th moment is.

A.3 Finite-width Approximation

Theorem A.2(Finite-width approximation of latent dynamics).

Let μ be a probability measure on ℤ with M̄_q(μ)<∞, and let T^†∈Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ). For every N≥1 and ε>0 there is a width-N latent ridge operator T_N with ∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥bⱼ∥_ℤ≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε and

∥T^†-T_N∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)≤(C_q Γ_σ,q(μ) (∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε))/(√N),

(14)

where C_q>0 depends only on q. If the infimum in equation 10 is attained, the bound holds with ε=0.

The proof uses the Marcinkiewicz–Zygmund inequality in Hilbert space: for independent, mean-zero, ℤ-valued random variables Y₁,…,Y_N with finite q-th moments,

𝔼∥∑ⱼ₌₁^NYⱼ∥_ℤ^q≤B_q 𝔼(∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥Yⱼ∥_ℤ²)^q/2,

(15)

where B_q depends only on q. Because the inequality holds in every Hilbert space with the same constant, no dimension of ℤ enters C_q.

Proof.

Fix ε>0 and choose a measure Λ representing T^† with V:=|Λ|(B_ℤ̄)≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε. If V=0, then T^†=0 and T_N=0 satisfies the claim, so assume V>0. Because Hilbert spaces have the Radon–Nikodym property, Λ admits a polar decomposition \rmdΛ(h̄)=λ(h̄) \rmd|Λ|(h̄) with ∥λ(h̄)∥_ℤ=1 for |Λ|-almost every h̄. With the probability measure ν:=|Λ|/V,

T^†(z)=V 𝔼_h̄∼ν[λ(h̄) σ(⟨z̄,h̄⟩)].

(16)

Draw h̄₁,…,h̄_N independently from ν and set

T_N(z):=V/N∑ⱼ₌₁^Nλ(h̄ⱼ) σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩).

(17)

This is a width-N latent ridge operator with bⱼ=Vλ(h̄ⱼ)/N, so ∑ⱼ∥bⱼ∥_ℤ=V.

Fix z∈ℤ. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the Lipschitz continuity of σ,

|σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩)|≤g(z):=|σ(0)|+L_σ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^1/2.

(18)

The variables Yⱼ(z):=Vλ(h̄ⱼ)σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩)-T^†(z) are independent and have mean zero. By equation 18, the first term of Yⱼ(z) has norm at most Vg(z), and so does its expectation T^†(z); hence ∥Yⱼ(z)∥_ℤ≤2Vg(z). Since T_N(z)-T^†(z)=N⁻¹∑ⱼYⱼ(z), equation 15 yields

𝔼∥T_N(z)-T^†(z)∥_ℤ^q(19)
≤(B_q)/(N^q)(N (2Vg(z))²)^q/2
=(C_q^q V^q g(z)^q)/(N^q/2), C_q:=2B_q^1/q.

The integrand is jointly measurable in (z,h̄₁,…,h̄_N), so integrating over z∼μ and applying Fubini’s theorem gives

𝔼 ∥T_N-T^†∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)^q≤(C_q^q V^q Γ_σ,q(μ)^q)/(N^q/2).

(20)

At least one realization of h̄₁,…,h̄_N therefore satisfies ∥T_N-T^†∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)≤C_qVΓ_σ,q(μ)/√N, and V≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε proves equation 14. If the norm is attained, the same argument applies with V=∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ. ∎

A.4 Rollout Bound

The rollout applies a learned transition T̂:ℤ→ℤ to its own output. To compare it with the data, fix any reference transition T^†:ℤ→ℤ.

Definition A.3(Rollout quantities).

For 0≤k≤K, the closure defect, one-step error, and reconstruction error are

\begingatheredηₖ:=∥zₖ₊₁-T^†(zₖ)∥_L^q, δₖ:=∥T^†-T̂∥_L^q_μₖ(ℤ), rₖ:=∥xₖ-D(zₖ)∥_L^q.\endgathered

(21)

where ηₖ is defined for k

Each quantity isolates one component of the simulator. The closure defect depends only on the data, the encoder, and T^†. It vanishes exactly when zₖ₊₁=T^†(zₖ) almost surely, that is, when the encoded states evolve as a closed system under one latent map. It is positive whenever the code omits information on which the next block depends, such as velocity when a block is a single frame. The one-step error compares T^† with the learned transition on the distribution of encoded states at step k; these distributions change with k because the scene evolves. The reconstruction error depends only on the autoencoder.

Theorem A.4(Long-horizon latent rollout bound).

Let ẑ₀ be any initial latent state and let ẑₖ₊₁=T̂(ẑₖ) and x̂ₖ=D(ẑₖ). Suppose that T̂ is L_T-Lipschitz on a set containing every zₖ and every ẑₖ. Then for every 1≤k≤K,

∥zₖ-ẑₖ∥_L^q≤L_Tᵏ ∥z₀-ẑ₀∥_L^q+∑ₛ₌₀ᵏ⁻¹L_Tᵏ⁻¹⁻ˢ (ηₛ+δₛ),(22)
∥xₖ-x̂ₖ∥_L^q≤rₖ+L_D ∥zₖ-ẑₖ∥_L^q.(23)

Proof.

Let eₖ:=∥zₖ-ẑₖ∥_L^q. Inserting T^†(zₖ) and T̂(zₖ) gives, pointwise,

∥zₖ₊₁-ẑₖ₊₁∥_ℤ≤∥zₖ₊₁-T^†(zₖ)∥_ℤ(24)
+∥T^†(zₖ)-T̂(zₖ)∥_ℤ
+∥T̂(zₖ)-T̂(ẑₖ)∥_ℤ.

Both zₖ and ẑₖ lie in the set on which T̂ is L_T-Lipschitz, so the last term is at most L_T∥zₖ-ẑₖ∥_ℤ. Taking L^q norms, applying Minkowski’s inequality, and using ∥T^†(zₖ)-T̂(zₖ)∥_L^q=δₖ (Appendix A.1) gives

eₖ₊₁≤ηₖ+δₖ+L_T eₖ.

(25)

Iterating equation 25 from k=0 proves equation 22. For the decoded prediction,

∥xₖ-x̂ₖ∥_X≤∥xₖ-D(zₖ)∥_X(26)
+∥D(zₖ)-D(ẑₖ)∥_X
≤∥xₖ-D(zₖ)∥_X
+L_D∥zₖ-ẑₖ∥_ℤ.

and taking L^q norms proves equation 23. ∎

Substituting equation 22 into equation 23 gives

∥xₖ-x̂ₖ∥_L^q≤rₖ+L_DL_Tᵏ ∥z₀-ẑ₀∥_L^q+L_D∑ₛ₌₀ᵏ⁻¹L_Tᵏ⁻¹⁻ˢ(ηₛ+δₛ).

(27)

The rollout starts from ẑ₀=𝔼(x₀)=z₀, so the middle term vanishes and equation 27 reduces to Theorem A.4. The bound holds for every T^†. With T^†=T̂, every δₖ is zero and ηₖ is the one-step error of the learned transition on encoded ground truth.

A.5 Corollaries used in Section 4.2

The first corollary shows that one sampled operator controls the one-step error at every step of the rollout and satisfies the Lipschitz assumption of Theorem A.4 with an explicit constant.

Corollary A.5(One operator for the whole rollout).

Let T^†∈Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ), let each μₖ satisfy M̄_q(μₖ)<∞, and let μ̄:=K⁻¹∑ₖ₌₀^K-1μₖ. For every N≥1 and ε>0 there is a width-N latent ridge operator T_N such that, for every 0≤k≤K-1,

∥T^†-T_N∥_L^q_μₖ(ℤ)≤(K^1/q C_q Γ_σ,q(μ̄) (∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε))/(√N),

(28)

and T_N is Lipschitz on ℤ with Lip(T_N)≤L_σ(∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε).

Proof.

The average μ̄ satisfies M̄_q(μ̄)<∞, so Theorem A.2 applied to μ̄ gives T_N satisfying equation 14 in L^q_μ̄(ℤ). For each k,

∫_ℤ∥T^†-T_N∥_ℤ^q \rmdμₖ(29)
≤∑ⱼ₌₀^K-1∫_ℤ∥T^†-T_N∥_ℤ^q \rmdμⱼ
=K ∥T^†-T_N∥_L^q_μ̄(ℤ)^q.

which gives equation 28. For the Lipschitz bound, write h̄ⱼ=(αⱼ,aⱼ) with ∥aⱼ∥_ℤ≤1. Then

∥T_N(z)-T_N(z^′)∥_ℤ(30)
≤∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥bⱼ∥_ℤ L_σ |⟨aⱼ,z-z^′⟩|
≤L_σ(∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥bⱼ∥_ℤ)∥z-z^′∥_ℤ.

and ∑ⱼ∥bⱼ∥_ℤ≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε. ∎

The second corollary describes the residual parameterization, in which the network represents only the change between consecutive blocks.

Corollary A.6(Residual transition).

Let ℝ^†:=T^†-I belong to Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ), and let μ satisfy M̄_q(μ)<∞. For every N≥1 and ε>0 there is a width-N latent ridge operator T_N such that T̂:=I+T_N satisfies

\begingathered∥T^†-T̂∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)≤(C_q Γ_σ,q(μ) (∥ℝ^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε))/(√N), Lip(T̂)≤1+L_σ(∥ℝ^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε).\endgathered

(31)

Proof.

Apply Theorem A.2 to ℝ^† and note that T^†-T̂=ℝ^†-T_N. The Lipschitz bound of Corollary A.5, applied to T_N, gives Lip(T_N)≤L_σ(∥ℝ^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε), and Lip(I+T_N)≤1+Lip(T_N). ∎

The same quantity, ∥ℝ^†∥_Vₗₐₜ, thus controls both the one-step error and the amplification factor L_T of Theorem A.4. When consecutive blocks differ little in the latent coordinates, a residual transition is accurate at small width and amplifies errors only slightly.

Appendix B Implementation Details

B.1 Data and Preprocessing

Data.

MOVi-Spheres [49, 8] contains 1200 Kubric scenes with 3 to 10 spheres of varying radius, mass, restitution, and friction, simulated at 1200 Hz under gravity 10 m/s² and stored at 240 Hz for 2 s. Scenes are split 80/10/10 into training, validation, and test sets with a fixed seed. We subsample the trajectories to 60 Hz and cut them into non-overlapping windows of 21 frames: the simulator receives the first frame and predicts the next K=20, matching the 21-frame clip of the generator. A pair or floor contact label is positive for a transition when the minimum gap over the 240 Hz frames between the two sampled frames is at most 0.02. Coordinates are mapped from the scene box [-5,5]²×[0,5] to [-1,1]³. Each object state sⁱ=(pⁱ,vⁱ,ωⁱ,rⁱ)∈ℝ¹⁰ stores the normalized position, the velocity as a normalized displacement per frame, the angular velocity multiplied by the frame interval, and the radius normalized by the mean box extent. Mass, restitution, and friction are read from the scene metadata and enter only the collision operator.

Point sampling.

The encoder input P contains Nₚ=2048 points drawn uniformly inside the spheres, with the same number of points for every object regardless of its size. The query set Q contains N_q=2048 points. Half are uniform over the scene box. The other half lie near objects: half of these inside the object volume and half on its surface, perturbed by isotropic Gaussian noise with standard deviation σₛ=0.05. Each frame is sampled independently. The autoencoder is pretrained on space–time segments of 16 frames with the time coordinate normalized to [-1,1]; for a single frame, all points carry t=0.

B.2 Simulator Architecture

Occupancy autoencoder.

Fourier features with eight octaves map each four-dimensional point to width 256. The encoder uses one cross-attention block from 256 learned query tokens to the points, followed by eight pre-norm self-attention blocks with eight heads and feed-forward ratio 4. Two linear heads produce μ and \logσ² of size 256×32. The decoder projects the tokens to width 256, applies eight self-attention blocks, and lets each query cross-attend to the result before an MLP predicts its occupancy logit. The reported autoencoder is trained with KL weight β_KL=0.001.

Latent neural operator.

Two-layer GELU MLPs project the reference coordinates ξ, evenly spaced in [-1,1], and the layer-normalized slot features to width 128. The physics cross-attention computes W∈ℝ^256×128 from the projected coordinates. A softmax over slots aggregates the 256 slots into 128 modes, eight attention blocks with four heads act on the modes, and a softmax over modes distributes the result back to the slots, where a two-layer MLP with a zero-initialized output layer returns the latent update. Since ξ is shared by all samples, W does not depend on the input.

State adapter and free-motion proposal.

The adapter A_c projects each object state with a two-layer MLP and the latent slots with a linear layer to width 128, applies one four-head cross-attention from slots to objects with absent objects masked, and maps the normalized sum back to the latent width as a residual. The proposal head ℙ_free adds an eight-band Fourier embedding of the target time to each object token and applies cross-attention to ẑₖ₊₁, masked self-attention among objects, and a feed-forward block, each followed by a residual connection and layer normalization, all at width 128 with four heads. Its zero-initialized linear output gives the corrections of free-motion proposal, bounded by 0.05 for position and 0.25 for linear and angular velocity in normalized units. The radius is copied from the initial state. The collision operator does not change ω, so spin changes from friction are learned only by this head.

Surface operator.

Each object is represented by 128 oriented surface samples placed on a Fibonacci lattice. For every object, the eight nearest samples of the other objects give a geometric gap and normal. Their relative positions and normals, scaled by the object radius, are encoded by a shared MLP of width 128, pooled by learned attention weights, and mapped to a gap correction bounded by 0.25 and a normal correction bounded by 0.5; both output layers are initialized to zero. The operator is pretrained on exact gap and normal targets with a smooth-L₁ gap loss weighted towards near and contacting queries and a cosine normal loss, reaching contact F1 0.934 against 0.840 for the uncorrected estimate on validation windows. It is frozen during Stage 2.

Collision operator.

Contact gaps and normals for the proposed positions are computed in closed form for sphere pairs and against the floor plane; the surface-operator estimates enter as features. Each contact edge is described by 21 features: the gap, the normal, the relative velocity and its normal and tangential speeds, both radii, both inverse masses and the reduced mass, the restitution and friction priors, the surface-operator gaps and their alignment with the contact normal, and an indicator for the static floor. A two-layer GELU edge network of width 128, shared by all edges, encodes them, and zero-initialized linear heads give ρᵢⱼ and the coefficient corrections, so the operator starts as exact geometry with the material priors of the data. The contact probability uses tolerance ε=0.02 and temperature τ_c=0.02. The restitution and friction priors are the geometric means of the per-object values for body pairs and the object’s own value against the floor; the learned corrections enter through 0.5\tanh(·), restitution is clipped to [0,1], and friction to [0,2]. The velocity correction of each object is clipped to norm 50, which leaves momentum conservation exact whenever the clip is inactive. Overlaps are removed by moving each body along the normal by half of the penetration depth, weighted by its share of the inverse mass, and positions additionally follow half of the velocity correction over one frame.

B.3 Video Interface

Learned adapter.

The adapter embeds object attributes and the operator features M_1:T, splats them at the projected object centres on the latent video grid, and applies a zero-initialized 1×1 projection to the control channels [57]. The video VAE compresses frames in groups {0},{1,…,4},{5,…,8},…, and the adapter concatenates the four sub-frame maps of each group along the channel axis before the projection. A 1×1 convolution on the pre-projection feature map produces one heat map per object and sub-frame, and a soft-argmax decodes a position p̂_t,i supervised by

Lₚₒₛ=(1)/(|I|)∑_(t,i)∈ISmoothL1(p̂_t,i,π(c_t,i))

(32)

over valid frame–object pairs I. With the video VAE latent z, flow time s∈[0,1], zₛ=(1-s)z+sε, and the frozen velocity network Gᵥ, only θ is optimized with

L_vid(θ)=∥Gᵥ(zₛ,s,c)-(ε-z)∥₂²+λₚₒₛLₚₒₛ,λₚₒₛ=0.1.

(33)

The adapter receives the ground-truth states of each paired sample, and the position head is discarded after training.

B.4 Training

Loss weights.

The occupancy temperature is τₒ=0.02, and the state losses use smooth-L₁ with threshold β_SL1=0.02. The weights of Eq. 8 are λ_z=λₒ=1, λₛ=1 with equal weights on position, velocity, and angular velocity, and λ_c=0.2 for the averaged object and pair contact terms and, separately, for the floor contact term. All contact terms use focal parameters α=0.75 and γ=2.

Optimization.

All stages use AdamW with weight decay 10⁻⁴ and gradient clipping at norm 1. The autoencoder is trained for 200 epochs with learning rate 4×10⁻⁵ and batch size 64. The surface operator is trained with learning rate 3×10⁻⁴, batch size 64, and a cosine schedule on 6000 training windows, with early stopping after at least 8 epochs. The dynamics stage uses learning rate 10⁻⁴ with a cosine schedule and a total batch size of 128 for 100 epochs, and the checkpoint with the best validation occupancy IoU is kept. Training runs with data parallelism on eight GPUs.

Appendix C Empirical Analysis of the Latent Neural Simulator

We evaluate on held-out MOVi-Spheres [49] scenes, none of which appear in training. Each episode is a 20-step free-running rollout in which the true state enters at the first frame only. Scenes hold 3 to 10 spheres of radius 0.35 to 0.70, and errors are distances between predicted and true object centres in scene units, where the mean radius is 0.54.

C.1 Accuracy Against Explicit Solvers

The analytic solver of Table 3 integrates gravity and resolves sphere–sphere and sphere–floor impulses with the restitution and friction the dataset records, and it beats the ballistic arm by 3.5×. The simulator cuts its 20-step error by 46%, from 0.1669 to 0.0908. The one column it loses is contact F1, 0.508 against 0.651. Its own contact head scores 0.691 on the same validation split, so the learned classifier recovers what the predicted geometry misses rather than the geometry being right in the first place. The solver applies one impulse per frame while the reference engine resolves contact over sub-steps, so it marks the weaker end of the classical range rather than its best.

C.2 Measuring the Rollout Bound

The rollout bound has two factors, and they can be measured separately.

Taking T^†=T̂ in Definition A.3 sets every δₖ to zero and leaves ηₖ, the one-step error of the learned transition from the encoded true state, so equation 27 reduces to ∥uₖ-ûₖ∥≤∑_s3a shows the bound against the measured accumulation at epoch 50, which it holds with a factor of 3.5 to spare.

Training buys contraction rather than per-step accuracy.

Over 50 epochs the two factors move in opposite directions (Figure 3b). The mean per-step defect η̄ falls to 0.0030 by epoch 6 and then rises fivefold to 0.0148, while L^⋆ falls from 1.095 at epoch 4 to 0.848 at epoch 50, crossing one between epochs 16 and 20. The rollout error follows their combination rather than either factor alone, e₂₀ falling from 0.124 to 0.090 across exactly the span in which the per-step defect is getting worse, so a single-step validation loss would report that half of training as a regression. The local rate explains none of this: L_loc sits between 1.0042 and 1.0075 at every epoch, and used in the bound it is violated early (2.57 times the bound at epoch 4) and slack late (0.287 at epoch 50), as a local linearisation must be when it stands in for a constant the theorem requires to hold uniformly on a set containing both trajectories.

C.3 Which Stream Accumulates

Only one of the two coupled streams accumulates. The latent state is a product of an occupancy code and an explicit object state, so substituting the encoded truth into one factor at every step isolates the other (Figure 3c). Re-encoding the occupancy latent from ground truth moves the 20-step error from 0.0903 to 0.0899. Resetting the object state instead collapses the rollout to its per-step defect regardless of what the latent does, so accumulation runs through the object-state factor alone. The occupancy latent is nonetheless read: a latent taken from a different scene costs 17% at k=20 and a zero latent costs 93%. It also drifts, to 0.80 of its own norm by step 20, and correcting that drift buys almost nothing. Sensitivity to the latent is therefore strongly anisotropic, which is one concrete reason a single L_D over the whole latent space leaves the bound conservative.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：画面逼真但物理不成立，说明纯视觉建模给不出可迁移的动力学表示。

要点：

  • 作者从现象下手：视频生成模型能产出高度真实的画面，却经常生成物理上不一致的物体运动——这说明**只靠视觉建模无法提供可迁移的物理动力学表示**
  • MotionCore 的做法是学习一个**可学习的偏微分方程求解器**，把物理动力学作为表示来学，而不是从像素里间接推断
  • 论文聚焦刚体运动，并在 latent 空间里训练神经模拟器来预测运动演化

为什么值得看：「视频世界模型物理不对」是最常被诟病的问题，多数方案靠堆数据或加惩罚项。把动力学写成可学的 PDE 求解器，是把它变成结构约束——这也是「世界模型当引擎」需要的物理层。

中文摘要：视频生成模型能产出高度真实的画面，却常常生成物理上不一致的物体运动，这说明仅靠视觉建模可能无法提供可迁移的物理动力学表示。MotionCore 因此把物理动力学本身作为学习对象：它构建一个可学习的偏微分方程求解器，在 latent 空间里训练神经模拟器来预测刚体运动的演化。与在像素上间接推断物理、或仅用渲染一致性做监督的做法相比，这条路线试图让模型学到一个能跨场景迁移的动力学表示。对希望世界模型承担「物理层」职责的引擎来说，这是更根本的一步。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

MotionCore: A Latent Neural Simulator for Video Generation with Rigid-Body Dynamics

Abstract

Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulators learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. The latter setting measures obedience to a specified physical rollout, while the former evaluates broader physical and semantic consistency. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.

1 Introduction

Video generation models have made rapid progress in visual quality. They can synthesize detailed scenes, realistic appearances, and complex motions. Yet visual realism does not imply physical correctness. Generated objects may accelerate without a clear cause, pass through one another, or follow trajectories that conflict with collisions and gravity. This limitation is not restricted to older or small-scale models. Recent systems, including Seedance 2.0 [43] and MiniMax H3 [31], demonstrate advances in visual quality. Recent benchmarks, including VideoPhy, PhyGenBench, Physics-IQ, and VideoPhy-2, report a persistent gap between visual quality and physical consistency [3, 29, 33, 4]. These observations suggest that a strong visual prior alone is insufficient for reliable physical prediction. More broadly, improving visual modeling capacity does not automatically provide a transferable representation of object dynamics.

A physical model should predict how a system evolves when its initial state, object properties, or interactions change. Hand-designed simulators provide an explicit way to model such evolution. They require, however, detailed descriptions of object geometry, materials, and governing rules. These descriptions are effective for predefined systems, but they are costly to construct and difficult to extend to the diversity of real-world scenes. A learned physical model offers a complementary approach. It can extract regularities from observations without requiring a complete symbolic description of every object and interaction. Such models may still fall short of high-fidelity simulation in the wild. They nevertheless provide a practical route toward learning physical dynamics from large-scale visual observations.

Videos are a natural source of such observations. They contain object trajectories, interactions, and changes in motion under diverse conditions. Object-level representations can be inferred from video and used for learned dynamics prediction [48]. This suggests a modular view of video generation. AI Flow advocates intelligence emerging from coordinated models and their interactions [2], with device–edge–cloud inference as one concrete setting [41]. A physical dynamics learning modular learns how the observed system evolves. And a pretrained video diffusion model then acts as a visual tool that renders the predicted state with realistic appearance. In this setting, video generation works like a piloted mech: the dynamics-learning part is the pilot that decides how the scene moves next, and the diffusion model is the body that carries out that decision by rendering it into frames.

However, how to learn physcis dynamics beyond visual cues becomes a major obstacle. Physical dynamics can typically be described by differential equations with unknown parameters: rigid-body motion is governed by the Newton–Euler equations, and the propagation of light by Maxwell’s equations. This suggests that a solver tailored to a specific scene can serve as an abstract description of that real-world scene. We learn such a solver in latent space with a neural operator, and use it to build a path from physical space to visual space.

In this paper, we introduce MotionCore, a framework for video-grounded rigid-body dynamics learning. MotionCore uses a latent neural simulator to model the evolution of object-level physical states. The neural simulator predicts future object states from observed motion and produces intermediate latent features that describe the evolving physical system. And we use a controllable video generation model VACE [12] built on Wan2.1-1.3B [46] as the video generator. A lightweight adapter converts the predicted states into spatially aligned control maps on the latent video grid. The generator remains fixed and provides appearance, texture, and visual detail, while the dynamics model provides the physical trajectory.

2 Related Work

Neural operators in Latent Space.

Neural operators learn maps between function spaces and can therefore transfer across spatial discretizations. DeepONet represents nonlinear operators with branch and trunk networks [28], whereas the Fourier Neural Operator performs global kernel integration in the spectral domain [19]. Latent formulations reduce the cost of evolving high-dimensional physical fields by learning a compact solution manifold or an encoder–operator–decoder factorization. NOMAD uses a nonlinear decoder for finite-dimensional solution manifolds [39]. Latent Spectral Models and the Latent Neural Operator learn the principal transformation in a compact space [50, 47], while latent DeepONet compresses both input and output functions before operator learning [13]. Geometry-aware variants map irregular meshes or particles to latent grids or tokens [20, 1], and AROMA retains spatially organized latent sequences and learns their temporal evolution with a conditional Transformer and a diffusion objective [40]. More recent models use state-space dynamics for long-range propagation [45] or flow-matching autoregression for generative PDE evolution [14]. AROMA and ENMA are especially relevant because they combine compressed physical states with generative dynamics, but their outputs remain numerical PDE fields. MotionCore instead places a PDE-informed solution operator inside video latent denoising, using the operator state to guide the generation of detailed visual frames.

Simulator-based physical video generation.

One line of work obtains motion from an explicit simulator and transfers it to a generative visual model. MotionCraft warps diffusion noise latents with optical flow computed from a physical simulation [32]. PhysGen infers scene properties, simulates rigid-body motion, and renders the result with video diffusion [27], while PSIVG reconstructs a dynamic scene and places a simulator in the generation loop [6]. These pipelines provide interpretable control, but their behavior is coupled to reconstructed object states, simulator assumptions, or test-time optimization. A complementary line learns physical control or supervision from data. PISA combines simulated-video fine-tuning with reward-based post-training for free fall [15]. PointVid regularizes generation with 3D point trajectories [5], Force Prompting conditions videos on local or global force fields [7], and VLIPP converts vision-language reasoning into coarse motion plans [53]. VideoREPA instead distills pairwise spatiotemporal relations from a video representation model [59]. These methods inject useful motion variables, plans, or preferences, but do not learn the governing field evolution as a reusable solution operator.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Representation of Rigid-body Dynamics

A physical trajectory records one realization of a dynamical system, whereas its governing equation describes an entire family of realizations. The governing equations of rigid-body dynamics are usually in the forms of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). For example, in the case of motion without collisions and external constraints, the Newton-Euler equations are given by Eq. 1.

ṗ=v, mv̇=F,(1)
Ṙ=Rω̂, Iω̇+ω×(Iω)=τ.

where p,v,F,I,τ,R,ω specify the position , velocity, net external force, inertia tensor. net external torque, rotation matrix and angular velocity of the rigid body’s mass center. If F and τ are uniquely determined by current states and time, the govern equations could be reduced to one ODE which takes the form

ẋ=f(t,x;φ)

(2)

where φ includes settings mentioned in Eq. 1. Eq. 2 is a finite-dimensional ODE evolving on a physical-state manifold. However, not all rigid-body motion can be described by this smooth ODE such as impulsive dynamics in the scene of ideal rigid-body collision and externally constrained rigid-body system.

To address this limitation, we approximate rigid bodies as deformable elastic body with large but finite stiffness, and collisions through elastic-body’s contact laws [36, 37]. The observed instances are modeled as elastic continua, which means we could describe general rigid-body dynamics via partial differential equations (PDEs), unifying smooth and impulsive response. Our aim is to find an intermediate physical-state representation which can guide the video diffusion models generate plausible outputs.

3.2 Neural Operator

While treating the general rigid-body dynamics as a PDE, we should build a model reusing a single evolution rule as the initial state, physical parameters, or boundary conditions change. Neural Operator (NO) makes this precise by treating the quantities involved as functions [28, 19]. An operator maps a function in one space to a function in another. A neural operator composes layers that each act on functions.

NOs have following properties that enable it to effectively learn mappings between functions. (i)Initial conditions, coefficients, and boundary data enter as inputs rather than as fixed settings, so one set of parameters represents a whole family of solutions. (ii)The same parameters apply across compatible discretizations: inputs can be sampled on different grids, outputs can be queried at any resolution, and predictions converge as the discretization is refined. This transfer concerns different samplings of the same instance, and extrapolation to unseen physical regimes remains a separate question. (iii)A trained NO evaluates a new instance in one forward pass, amortizing the cost of a numerical solve.

Evolving a full-resolution field at every step can nevertheless be expensive. Latent neural operators [47] reduce this cost by factorizing the operator into three parts: an encoder that maps the input to a compact latent representation, an operator that evolves this representation, and a decoder that returns the result to physical space. Because the decoder can be queried at arbitrary points, the latent form keeps the resolution independence of the second property while moving the costly evolution into a smaller space. Section 4 adopts this factorization for structured physical states and analyzes what the latent representation must preserve for the approximation to hold.

4 Latent Neural Simulator

4.1 Problem Setting

We study rigid-body video generation with physical prediction separated from visual rendering. A semantic condition c, typically a text prompt with the first frame, specifies visual appearance and initial condition. A physical model receives the geometry and object states of the initial frame estimated from the observed frames, and predicts the future trajectory at the video timestamps t₁,…,t_K, and a video generator renders that trajectory. Motion is the responsibility of the physical model, and appearance that of the generator.

Following Section 3, a scene contains K bodies, and body k has state xₖ=(pₖ,Rₖ,vₖ,ωₖ), with Rₖ embedded in ℝ^3×3. Between contacts, xₖ follows the Eq. 1. At contact this description breaks down, so we adopt the compliant model of Section 3: each body is treated as an elastic body with large but finite stiffness, and contact follows elastic contact laws [36, 37]. The coefficients φ∈Φ collect mass, inertia, stiffness, and contact parameters. Under this model the trajectory remains continuous in time through collisions, and the impulsive rigid-body motion is recovered as the stiffness tends to infinity [36, 37]. With geometry and φ fixed over the horizon [0,Tₕ], the dynamics define the solution operator

S^†:X^K×Φ\longrightarrowC([0,T];X^(K)),(x(0),φ)\longmapstox(·)

(3)

where X is the state space of single rigid body. This is the coefficient-to-solution setting of operator learning in Section 3.2. Just as a permeability field determines the pressure of a Darcy flow [19], the coefficient field and the initial state determine a rigid-body trajectory, and one operator covers the entire family of scenes. Learning S^† therefore means learning the shared law of rigid-body motion rather than any single trajectory.

We learn this operator on an encoded state. The observed history provides the initial state. An encoder 𝔼 maps the history to latent codes ℤ, a neural operator T_N evolves the code, and a decoder D returns the predicted trajectory [50, 47]. Because the token has a fixed size independent of the number and shape of objects, one operator can serve environments that an explicit simulator would have to set up one by one. Theorem 4.1 makes this precise: the error is controlled by how well the token preserves the evolution and by how simple the induced latent operator is.

4.2 Theoretical Boundary

Inspired by the function-space analysis of latent nonlinear operators between Hilbert spaces [52], we formulate the upper boundary on the approximation error of latent neural operator approximation. We model the physical flow with a latent neural operator [47],

L_N=D∘T_N∘𝔼, L_N(u)=ŝ_1:T,

(4)

where 𝔼:U→ℤ encodes the observed history, T_N:ℤ→ℤ evolves the physics in a learned latent space, and D:ℤ→V decodes the predicted evolution. We assume U and V are separable real Hilbert spaces, which is usually plausible in physical scenes. Learning physics in this formulation means minimizing approximation error to the PDE-induced flow map over the distribution of physical systems. The error has two sources: how well a finite network represents one latent transition which we denote as εₐₚₚᵣₒₓ=∥S^†-D∘T_N∘𝔼∥_L_ρ^q(V)., and how one-step errors accumulate over the rollout which is derived in Appendix A.4.

We first consider a sufficient condition under which the ideal latent transition admits a quantitative finite-width approximation. Specifically, we assume that the ideal latent dynamics T^† belongs to a variation space by a family of bounded ridge features, whose norm quantifies the functional complexity of representing the target operators through these features and controls its finite-width approximation error. Importantly, the ridge representation serves as an auxiliary approximation class for the theoretical analysis. The definition of this variation space is shown in Appendix A.2.

Let ℤ̄:=ℝ⊕ℤ and z̄:=(1,z), and B_ℤ̄ be the closed unit ball of ℤ̄. A width-N latent ridge operator T_N(z)=∑ⱼ₌₁^Nbⱼ σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩) with h̄ⱼ∈B_ℤ̄ is a finite instance of an infinite-width operator class; writing h̄ⱼ=(αⱼ,aⱼ) recovers the biased feature bⱼ σ(αⱼ+⟨aⱼ,z⟩). Then we give the finite-width approximation boundary in Theorem A.2.

Theorem 4.1(Finite-width approximation of latent dynamics).

Let 2≤q<∞, let σ:ℝ→ℝ be L_σ-Lipschitz, and let μ be a probability measure on ℤ with ∫_ℤ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^q/2 \rmdμ(z)<∞. Define

Γ_σ,q(μ):=(∫_ℤ[|σ(0)|+L_σ(1+∥z∥_ℤ²)^1/2]^q \rmdμ(z))^1/q.

(5)

Γ_σ,q(μ) is the L^q average of the unit envelope over the encoded states. If T^†∈Vₗₐₜ(ℤ;ℤ), then for every N≥1 and ε>0 there is a width-N latent ridge operator T_N with ∑ⱼ₌₁^N∥bⱼ∥_ℤ≤∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε and

∥T^†-T_N∥_L^q_μ(ℤ)≤(C_q Γ_σ,q(μ) (∥T^†∥_Vₗₐₜ+ε))/(√N),

(6)

where C_q>0 depends only on q. If the variation norm of T^† is attained by a representing measure, the bound holds with ε=0.

The bound decomposes the physical approximation error into a latent factorization error and a finite-width operator approximation error. The former quantifies how accurately the target physical evolution can be represented through the latent dynamics formulation, while the latter is controlled by the variation norm of the ideal latent transition and decays at a rate of O(N^-1/2) under the stated assumptions. This reveals a fundamental trade-off in latent compression: an effective representation should preserve the target physical evolution while reducing the complexity of the induced latent dynamics. Notably, the guarantee requires neither an injective encoder nor an inverse decoder, provided that the target evolution admits an accurate latent factorization. Furthermore, the bound contains no explicit dependence on the latent dimension, although such dependence may enter implicitly through its constants. This is a conditional approximation result: the ideal latent dynamics must admit a representation with a sufficiently small variation norm, and the finite-width guarantee applies to the specified auxiliary approximation class rather than arbitrary neural architectures. Detailed assumptions, proofs, and corollaries are provided in Appendix A.

5 Framework of MotionCore

5.1 Overview

MotionCore predicts a rigid-body scene frame by frame from one initial frame and renders the prediction with a video generator. The overall architecture is shown in Fig 1.

Scene encoder. The encoder turns a frame into the latent geometry state. It is an temporary-occupancy autoencoder in the style of 3DShape2VecSet [55] and Perceiver [10]. Its encoder embeds points (x,y,z,t) sampled inside the occupied volume with Fourier features [42]. The decoder returns an occupancy logit at any query point [30]. Applied to single frames, all points carry t=0, and the rollout starts from ẑ₀. The latent code orders an unordered point set into slots on which an operator can act rather than compressing it.

Latent neural operato r. The latent transition advances the geometry by one frame. The state adapter A_c first writes the object states into the latent: the 256 slots cross-attend to one token per object. The latent neural operator T_N[47] then aggregates the slots into latent modes by physics cross-attention, evolves the modes with attention blocks, and maps them back. Because the slots have no physical position, its trunk receives fixed coordinates ξ∈[-1,1]²⁵⁶.

Free-motion proposal. The proposal predicts where each object moves if no contact occurs. Each object token, formed from sⁱ and a Fourier embedding of tₖ₊₁, cross-attends to ẑₖ₊₁ and then to the other objects. A head outputs bounded residual corrections δ=c\tanh(·), and p̃ⁱ=pⁱ+vⁱ+δⁱₚ, ṽⁱ=vⁱ+δⁱᵥ, ω̃ⁱ=ωⁱ+δⁱ_ω,.

Collision operator. The collision operator ℂ_col corrects the proposal at contacts. For the proposed positions, gaps gᵢⱼ and unit normals nᵢⱼ (from j to i) are computed for every object pair. A pretrained surface operator, frozen here, adds gap and normal estimates from oriented surface samples as edge features. With uᵢⱼ=ṽⁱ-ṽʲ, its tangential part uᵗᵢⱼ, and m̄ᵢⱼ=(mᵢ⁻¹+mⱼ⁻¹)⁻¹,

\begingatheredJⁿᵢⱼ=(1+eᵢⱼ) m̄ᵢⱼ\max(0,-uᵢⱼ·nᵢⱼ), Jᵗᵢⱼ=\min(m̄ᵢⱼ∥uᵗᵢⱼ∥, fᵢⱼJⁿᵢⱼ), Jᵢⱼ=πᵢⱼ(Jⁿᵢⱼnᵢⱼ-Jᵗᵢⱼûᵗᵢⱼ), vⁱ=ṽⁱ+mᵢ⁻¹(∑_j≠iJᵢⱼ+Jᵢ₀),\endgathered

(7)

The normal impulse reverses the closing speed with restitution eᵢⱼ, the tangential impulse stays in the Coulomb cone of friction fᵢⱼ, and equal and opposite impulses conserve linear momentum between bodies for any mass ratio. Overlapping pairs are separated along nᵢⱼ, which resolves resting contacts without closing speed. An edge network predicts the contact probability πᵢⱼ=sigmoid((ε-gᵢⱼ)/τ_c+ρᵢⱼ), a geometric logit plus a learned residual ρᵢⱼ, and bounded corrections to eᵢⱼ and fᵢⱼ around priors from φ. Both are symmetrized over each pair, which keeps the exchange equal and opposite. The corrected state re-enters the latent through A_c at the next step, so a collision also changes the predicted geometry.

Video interface. The interface turns the predicted latents into a condition for the video generator. Our video generator is Wan 2.1-VACE [46, 12], whose control branch reads position from where a feature lies in a spatially aligned control video. The renderer decodes ẑₖ with the decoder of the latent neural operator, projects the occupied geometry with the calibrated camera, separates it into instances matched across frames, and draws each in its own label colour.

5.2 Training

The modules are trained in stage-wise pattern, each frozen before the next, and the simulator is never trained through the video objective: with the physical loss active the diffusion gradient leaves it unchanged, and without it the simulator drifts toward more motion and nearly doubles its short-horizon error (Appendix D.2).

Stage 1 pretrains the surface operator on exact gap and normal targets, and the occupancy autoencoder on space–time segments with the binary cross-entropy loss [30].

Stage 2 freezes both and trains A_c, T, ℙ_free, and ℂ_col jointly on free-running rollouts of K frames from a single initial frame, with

L=1/K∑ₖ₌₁^K(λ_zL_lat,k+λₒL_occ,k+λₛL_state,k+λ_cL_con,k).

(8)

The latent term Lₗₐₜ is a smooth-L₁ loss between ẑₖ and the posterior mean μₖ of the ground-truth frame. The occupancy term L_occ is a binary cross-entropy on query points [30]. The state term Lₛₜₐₜₑ applies the smooth-L₁ loss to the normalized position, velocity, and angular velocity, including the collision response. The contact term L_con is a focal loss [25] on per-object, pairwise, and floor contact labels, which supervises πᵢⱼ. Because no step is teacher-forced, L scores the accumulated error described by Theorem A.4, not only single-step error.

Stage 3 needs no training for the rendered interface. The learned adapter A_θ (6.7×10⁴ parameters), designed for states without renderable geometry, splats object attributes and operator features at the projected centres and is trained with the flow-matching loss of the frozen generator on ground-truth states. Loss weights and optimization settings are in Appendix B.

6 Experiments

6.1 Setup

Data. The simulator is trained on rigid-body trajectories from MOVi-Spheres [8, 49] and Billiards [58]. Appendix B lists the production splits; Section 6.3 specifies the separate small-scale ablation protocol. For video generation we use two benchmarks: a subset of Physics-IQ-Verified [38], a general benchmark of physical reasoning, from which we select the scenes whose prompts describe rigid-body motion such as collision, rolling, sliding, and free fall and finally get 81 five-second videos; and RigidBench [11], a public benchmark built for rigid-body dynamics, which provides 100 two-second videos.

Metrics. Both benchmarks compare the generated video with a reference recording of the same scene. Physics-IQ [33, 38] uses binary motion masks for ST-IoU, measuring whether motion occurs at the right place and time. MSE compares temporally aligned RGB frames after resizing and pixel normalization to [0,1]. The Physics-IQ score aggregates these with the spatial and weighted spatial IoU, normalized so that the variation between two real recordings of a scene scores 100. RigidBench [11] recovers object masks, point tracks, and depth from the generated video and scores them against the simulator ground truth. We report per-object mask IoU, the mask-centroid error (L2) and the bidirectional Chamfer distance, both normalized by image height [15]. We also report the 2D trajectory error of tracked points (ATE), the 3D error of the reconstructed object positions (ATE-3D), and the scale-invariant depth error (SI-MSE).

Baselines. We choose general-purpose models of comparable scale CogVideoX-5B-I2V [54], HunyuanVideo-1.5-480P-I2V [44], MiniMax-H3 [31], Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [46], Cosmos-Predict-2.5 2B [35] to complete the quality axis. Baseline numbers are copied from the cited papers where benchmark, split, and backbone match, and re-run otherwise.

Implementation. Our generator is Wan 2.1-VACE-1.3B [46, 12] with base weights. Sampling uses 30 steps at 832×480 with classifier-free guidance 5.0 on the text and none on the physical condition; clips have 81 frames at 16 fps on Physics-IQ and 21 frames on MOVi-Spheres. The simulator is frozen after Stage 2, advances one block per step, and is decoded at every video timestamp. All experiments are conducted on 8 Nvidia H100 GPUs. Remaining details are in Appendix B.

6.2 Main Results

On the strict81 Physics-IQ-Verified subset of 27 scenes and three views, the R2 sphere model obtains an IQ score of 28.14±0.41, a raw ST-IoU of 0.3734±0.0117, and a raw RGB MSE of 0.008633±0.000268 (Table 1). Values are the mean and sample standard deviation over four diffusion-seed rounds, not independent training runs. All 81 scene-view samples are retained in each round, including the 20 native-VACE fallbacks. Known contact and support failures in the control cache limit the physical interpretation of these aggregate scores; they do not isolate a causal benefit of the simulator.

Qualitative comparison.

Figure 2 compares three selected collision, falling, and rolling scenes using the same switch-frame input and prompt across methods. MotionCore additionally uses an initial state estimated from the permitted observation history; the baseline models use the first frame and text only. Future reference frames are used for comparison, not generation. The sequences allow object persistence, motion, and interaction timing to be examined separately. For example, the falling scene shows that retaining the basketball and crate appearance does not ensure the reference descent or contact. The examples were selected post hoc for visualization and do not establish benchmark-wide rankings or equal-information simulator ablations.

6.3 Ablations

The small-scale study separates the learned dynamics from the analytic prior and compares LNO with Transolver [51] and GNOT-CGPT [9] processors adapted to a shared latent-slot interface. Only the processor is replaced for the learned variants. The pretrained occupancy encoder 𝔼 is shared and kept frozen (Appendix D.1); the state-head architecture, integrator, and contact rules are also shared. The analytic variant retains the same physical priors with all learned corrections zeroed. All three learned models start from matched shared-head weights and use the same 50 windows from a 32-scene training pool (23 actually observed), with 8 validation and 16 test scenes. They use dataset initial states, static geometry, state-only loss, and causal rollouts; no production checkpoint is substituted for the pilot Full.

All four rows are complete. Errors are close: Full has slightly lower test ADE and FDE than the alternatives at this budget, while the rollout curves nearly coincide (Appendix D.1). A single seed and 50 updates do not establish convergence, statistical significance, a production-model ranking, or video-control gains. These state-domain measurements are separate from production Physics-IQ and partial RigidBench results.

7 Conclusion

MotionCore separates rigid-body state prediction from visual synthesis. A latent neural simulator produces object-state rollouts, and a spatial adapter with control-branch LoRA conveys them to a video generator whose main backbone remains frozen. We evaluate video agreement on the strict81 Physics-IQ subset and report single-round RigidBench diagnostics and a controlled short-horizon processor pilot. These results characterize the current pipeline without establishing a causal simulator benefit. State-estimation uncertainty, contact and support failures, and imperfect object persistence remain limitations; stable long-horizon physical control is an open goal.

(10)

the infimum being over all measures that represent T in equation 9.

The representation equation 9 is a one-hidden-layer network of unbounded width. Each point h̄=(α,a)∈B_ℤ̄ is a hidden unit z↦σ(α+⟨a,z⟩), and \rmdΛ(h̄) is its output weight, a vector in ℤ. The total variation |Λ|(B_ℤ̄) is then the total size of the output weights, and the variation norm is the smallest such total over all networks that compute T. It measures how simple T is for this model class rather than how many parameters represent it: the constraint ∥h̄∥_ℤ̄≤1 fixes the scale of the hidden units, so the norm cannot be lowered by shrinking output weights while enlarging input weights. A finite network belongs to the space. For N≥1, a width-N latent ridge operator is

T_N(z)=∑ⱼ₌₁^Nbⱼ σ(⟨z̄,h̄ⱼ⟩), h̄ⱼ∈B_ℤ̄, bⱼ∈ℤ,

(11)
