    qₜᵣₐᵢₙ=\begincases(qᵣₒₗₗ+q_LLM)/2,&valid LLM ranking, qᵣₒₗₗ,&otherwise.\endcases

    This blend retains information about travel, capacity, and contention from the rollouts while shifting probability toward actions that better follow the instruction. Both distributions follow the same candidate order, so their average cannot introduce an unavailable action.

    Table 2 shows an abridged instruction-related training record. The LLM call contains the candidate lists for all agents in the world, but only one agent is shown here for clarity. Candidate indices are created by the simulator before the LLM is queried. The table shows the LLM component numerically; the final training target also includes the rollout component as defined in Equation 2.

    Training corpus and optimization.

    We generate the training worlds procedurally, varying the layout, the number of agents, and the instruction that arrives. They cover ordinary behaviour, where agents simply satisfy their own needs, and the instruction types used in evaluation, such as a broken machine, an evacuation, and a gathering. The corpus holds 2,776 worlds and 73,606 agent decisions in total: 2,148 worlds train the policy, 258 select the final checkpoint, and 370 are held out to test combinations of instructions the policy never saw during training. An LLM ranking is available for 61,439 of the decisions (Table 3).

    Training minimizes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the policy’s distribution over an agent’s candidates and the training target. KL divergence measures how far one probability distribution is from another, so minimizing it makes the policy’s choices match the target. Additional ranking terms encourage the policy to prefer actions that relieve a need, respond to an active instruction, choose a working alternative when the usual one is unavailable, or continue an activity the agent has already started. We use Adam with batch size 64 and an initial learning rate of 3×10⁻³, and keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation KL under early stopping.

    3.6. Executing the Selected Actions in Unity

    The policy decides what an agent should attempt; the Unity runtime determines how that decision is executed. Our implementation splits this across two processes. A Python process holds the symbolic state, meaning agent needs, active directives, and the crowd graph, and runs the trained policy. A Unity 2D client holds the scene geometry and executes each selected action. The two exchange messages over a WebSocket: Unity reports what has happened in the scene, and Python replies with the action each agent should attempt next.

    After a level is instantiated, Unity reports which objects and zones actually exist, where each object can be used from, and which of them can be reached. The policy draws its targets from that report, so an object that was never placed, or that cannot be reached, is never offered as an action. Unity then handles path planning and collision avoidance, object interactions, and animation transitions.

    An agent keeps its selected action until that action finishes, fails, or the directive changes, so the policy runs less often than the animation and agents do not stop and restart on the spot. The interface summarizes the nine needs as five bars, labelled hunger, thirst, rest, comfort, and social, so that an observer can read an agent’s state at a glance. This grouping affects the display only.

    4. Evaluation

    We organize the evaluation around three questions. E1 asks whether the system correctly identifies instructions that the current scene can execute. E2 asks whether the graph policy selects the intended agents and responses. E3 measures runtime cost and scaling relative to handwritten rules and per-tick LLM control.

    Each question is reported in three parts: how the measurement was made, what the result shows, and what it implies for the design.

    4.1. Evaluation Setup and Comparison Methods

    Participant reference.

    Fifteen volunteers (11 male and 4 female; age 18–50+) completed an anonymous, approximately 15-minute web form. A 5×4 pool covered five instruction categories across four venues; each participant received a stratified random sample of 10 scenarios. Q1 assessed scene feasibility, Q2 identified the affected agents, and Q3 selected the preferred response from four executable, scene-specific candidate actions. Answer order was randomized. Scenarios overlapped across participants, so confidence intervals use a cluster bootstrap over scenarios.

    Behavioural benchmark.

    We use a frozen benchmark of 100 scenarios, each run under 10 initializations. It is generated once and reused unchanged, so every method is measured on identical situations. Each scenario states in advance which agents should respond, and which of the actions open to them the instruction permits. An agent that takes a permitted action gives an acceptable response, and one that takes an action the user ruled out gives a prohibited response, even though both are physically executable in the scene. The agents that actually changed behaviour are compared against the intended set by precision, recall, and F1, so disturbing a bystander and missing an intended agent are counted separately. Learned variants are averaged over three seeds.

    We compare CrowdDirector, which interprets an instruction once and then decides locally, with two alternatives. A handwritten rule set never uses language at runtime, and a temperature-zero LLM decides every update from one batched call covering the whole crowd. E2 uses the matched subset in which all three faced the same situation, 760 of the 840 cached calls. Fifteen LLM outputs in that subset could not be parsed, leaving 745 valid rows; where the LLM validly assigned no agent, default behaviour is retained.

    4.2. E1: Can the Instruction Be Executed?

    Method.

    For each instruction–scene pair we collect two independent feasibility judgements and compare both against people. The LLM judges first: while interpreting the instruction, it also states whether it believes the scene can execute it. The scene validator then checks the same instruction against the live scene and returns its five-state verdict, which we reduce to a binary decision by treating executable and partially executable as supported, and unsupported, ambiguous, and invalid reference as unsupported. The reference is the majority Q1 judgement of the participants, and agreement is the proportion of scenarios on which an assessor matches that reference.

    Results.

    Table 5 reports the agreement. The scene validator agrees more closely with participant judgements than the LLM’s self-assessment. The intervals overlap, so the margin alone is not conclusive, but the direction is consistent: where the two disagree, the validator is usually the one people side with. The LLM’s errors are not random. It tends to accept instructions that read sensibly but name something the scene does not contain, which is exactly the case its own confidence cannot detect.

    Why separate interpretation from validation.

    These results support separating language interpretation from scene validation. An LLM can infer the likely meaning of an instruction, but its own confidence does not establish that the referenced object, affordance, or group exists, because that is a fact about the scene rather than about the sentence. Checking the interpretation against the explicit contents of the scene also produces a clear failure state before an invalid instruction reaches the graph policy, which is what allows the system to tell the user that part of a request cannot be carried out rather than silently doing something else.

    4.3. E2: Do Agents Respond to the Instruction?

    Method.

    E2 asks two separate questions about a response: whether the right agents reacted, and whether they did the right thing. Q2 scores the affected scope as the Jaccard overlap between the agents an approach moves and the agents participants identified, so both missing an affected agent and moving an unaffected one are penalized. Q3 scores the chosen response as the proportion of cases matching the participants’ preferred candidate. The benchmark additionally reports the acceptable and prohibited rates defined above, and precision, recall, and F1 over the affected agents. Panel A compares the three approaches on the matched subset. Panel B removes one component of CrowdDirector at a time, holding the data, candidates, masks, labels, and optimization identical, so a change can be attributed to that component.

    Results: comparison with rules and per-tick LLM.

    Panel A of Table 4 compares the three approaches. The ordering is the same on every behavioural measure. Per-tick LLM control is strongest, CrowdDirector is close behind, and the handwritten rules are far below both. CrowdDirector roughly doubles the rule set on both scope and response agreement, and it recovers most of the gap between the rules and an LLM that reasons at every update. On prohibited responses the two are effectively level, so the remaining gap is one of coverage rather than safety: CrowdDirector sometimes fails to find the intended response, but it is no more likely to choose one the instruction ruled out. These results match the intended operating point: CrowdDirector does not reproduce the full flexibility of recurrent LLM reasoning, but transfers substantially more instruction sensitivity into local control than a fixed rule set.

    Why store an instruction.

    This comparison is the case for storing the instruction rather than regenerating it. The handwritten rules show what is lost without language at runtime: they are efficient, but they only cover responses someone anticipated, and varied instructions fall outside them. Per-tick LLM control shows what continuous language buys, and it is real but modest relative to its cost, since it repeats the same inference even when the user’s intent has not changed. Keeping the validated instruction as state captures most of that benefit once, and leaves the repeated work to a component that can run locally.

    Results: component ablations.

    Panel B isolates two design choices. Removing the directive-target marker leaves scope agreement untouched but roughly halves response agreement. The two are therefore decided separately: the marker tells an already-affected agent which destination the directive assigned, and contributes nothing to deciding whether that agent is affected at all. Removing message passing behaves differently. Response agreement falls less sharply, but affected-agent recall and F1 both drop and the prohibited rate rises by more than half, which is the clearest single degradation anywhere in the table.

    What the graph policy contributes.

    The two components address complementary failures. A policy cannot follow an assigned destination unless that assignment is visible in its candidate representation, which is what the directive-target marker supplies and why its removal affects only the response. Relational context does something the marker cannot: it connects an agent’s decision to the surrounding event, object, and group structure, and without it the policy more often selects a response the instruction ruled out. One ablation is worth noting against us. Removing the directive-target marker lowers the prohibited rate slightly, because a policy that less often pursues the assigned destination also less often reaches the situation where a prohibited alternative is attractive. The marker improves instruction following, and that is what it is for, but it does not by itself make responses safer.

    4.4. E3: Runtime Cost and Scaling

    Method.

    E3 tests the central runtime premise of CrowdDirector: language is used when the scene or director’s intent changes, while repeated crowd-control updates are performed locally. Let N denote the number of user instructions and T the number of decision updates in a session. Including one initial scene-generation call, the API-call counts are

    (3)

    A_CD=1+N, A_LLM=1+N+T.

    Both configurations retain language-based authoring. CrowdDirector removes the recurrent T calls from the crowd-control loop. The difference is small symbolically and large in practice, because T is the length of the session while N is only the number of times the user speaks: for five instructions over 600 updates, six calls against 606. We measure latency per complete decision update on identical 20-agent worlds, and price each call at the provider’s published rate. Panel B then raises the crowd size at approximately constant density to separate the cost of the graph policy from the cost of language. Panel C reports how often the whole-crowd LLM returned a parseable assignment for every agent, over 15 calls at each crowd size.

    Results.

    Table 6 reports runtime and scaling. Removing language from the control loop reduces per-update latency by 189×, and over a session of five instructions and 600 updates it reduces estimated cost by nearly two orders of magnitude. Both configurations pay the same price to author an instruction; the difference is entirely in what recurs.

    Local runtime grows close to linearly with crowd size and adds no further API calls, staying interactive well past the range the policy was trained on. The whole-crowd LLM interface fails for a different reason: because it enumerates one assignment per agent, its output grows with the crowd and it stops returning complete responses shortly above the smallest size tested. Its limit is the response format, not the reasoning. Multiple calls or a grouped representation would move it, and CrowdDirector takes the compressed route by naming the event, scope, and target once and expanding it locally.

    The policy was trained on crowds of 8–40 agents. The large-crowd experiment therefore demonstrates computational scaling, not behavioural generalization. It shows that the crowd graph and graph policy can be evaluated beyond the training range without language cost; it does not establish that response quality is unchanged for thousands of agents.

    Connecting decisions to Unity execution.

    These savings depend on the boundary the method draws. The Unity implementation is not a separate decision maker but the execution side of the same pipeline: the graph policy selects an action and target, and the engine plans movement, carries the action out, and reports completion or failure. Keeping that boundary explicit is what makes the recurrent loop cheap, since the learned component never has to produce physically valid trajectories, and established navigation and animation systems continue to do the work they already do well.

    5. Conclusion and Future Work

    We presented CrowdDirector, a framework for directing a running crowd simulation with natural language. An LLM converts a new instruction into a structured instruction, the scene validator checks it against the current scene, the accepted directive remains active, and the graph policy selects a candidate action for each agent. Unity then executes those choices with its navigation and interaction systems. The evaluation shows that explicit scene validation improves agreement with participant judgements and that the graph policy follows instructions more closely than handwritten rules without requiring language inference at every update. Per-tick LLM control achieves higher response agreement in our benchmark, but with substantially higher recurrent latency and API cost. CrowdDirector therefore provides a practical middle ground between flexible instruction following and efficient runtime crowd control.

    However, we identify several limitations of the present study as follows: (1) the current implementation supports only the actions and interactions defined in its operation library and has been evaluated in 2D environments; (2) the participant study involved 15 volunteers and a limited set of instruction scenarios; and (3) the policy was trained with crowds of 8–40 agents, so the larger-crowd experiment evaluates computational scaling rather than behavioral generalization beyond the training range. Future work will extend CrowdDirector to richer environments and interactions, evaluate a broader range of participants and instructions, and improve large-crowd efficiency.

    Acknowledgements.

    This work was conducted with the financial support of the Research Ireland Centre for Research Training in Digitally-Enhanced Reality (d-real) under Grant No. 18/CRT/6224. For the purpose of Open Access, the author has applied a CC BY public copyright licence to any Author Accepted Manuscript version arising from this submission.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 世界模型的记忆不该只靠架构：把长期记忆搬进「测试时基于模型的强化学习」 ｜ Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
一句话：MBRL 的世界模型在需要长期记忆与规划的任务上仍难超人类；解法是换范式而不是换网络。

要点：

  • 现状：基于模型的强化学习（MBRL）能从轨迹里学出准确世界模型，但在需要**长期记忆与长程规划**的任务上仍难以超过人类
  • 作者把问题定位在「记忆的编码方式」上，并指出常见做法局限在架构侧（加记忆模块、拉长上下文）
  • 论文提出在**测试时**用基于模型的方法编码记忆，从而在部署阶段继续适应，而不是把记忆一次性固化进权重

为什么值得看：长时程是世界模型的老大难。把记忆放到测试时继续更新，等于允许系统在运行时「记住这次发生了什么」——这条思路对游戏里的持续世界状态尤其合适。

中文摘要：近年来基于模型的强化学习（MBRL）能从智能体的交互轨迹中学到较准确的世界模型，但在需要长期记忆与长程规划的任务上，现有方法仍难以超越人类水平。作者认为问题不只是模型容量，而在于「记忆如何被编码」：常见做法把注意力放在架构侧（增加记忆模块、拉长上下文）。这篇因此把记忆编码移到**测试时**——用基于模型的强化学习在部署阶段继续更新记忆，而不是把它一次性固化进权重。对需要持续维护世界状态的游戏与仿真系统，这意味着运行时仍能继续「记住」发生了什么。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

Encoding Memory in World Models with Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

Abstract

Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) approaches have demonstrated strong performance across diverse domains in recent years, learning accurate world models from agent trajectories. However, despite this progress, current approaches still struggle to surpass human performance on tasks that require long-term memory and planning. In this work, we address the problem of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. We introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode observations into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark. Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k. We will release our code at https://github.com/burchim/TT-MBRL.

1 Introduction

Model-based reinforcement learning has gained increasing research attention in recent years [(Kaiser et al., 2020; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2023; Hafner et al., 2025; Hansen et al., 2022; Hansen et al., 2024; Hansen et al., 2026; Micheli et al., 2024; Alonso et al., 2024)], driven in part by advances in hardware computing capabilities. These improvements have enabled the training of world models from high-dimensional observations using deep neural networks as function approximators [(Hafner et al., 2019)]. World models [(Sutton, 1991; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018)] capture an agent’s experience into a predictive function that can be used in place of the real environment to learn complex behaviors. By leveraging a model of the environment, agents can simulate multiple possible future trajectories in parallel, leading to improved generalization, greater sample efficiency, and more effective decision-making via planning.

Among these approaches, the Dreamer algorithm [(Hafner et al., 2020; Hafner et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2023)] has demonstrated strong performance across diverse environments by learning a world model capable of generating accurate trajectories in latent space. However, despite making realistic predictions for fully observable settings, Dreamer struggles to maintain temporal coherence in partially observable environments like Memory Maze (Figure 2). World model prediction error accumulates over time, leading to long-horizon trajectories that become increasingly inconsistent with past observations.

To remedy this problem, recent approaches have proposed architectural improvements to better handle past context information and enhance the memory capabilities of world models. [Pašukonis et al. (2023)] proposed to augment Dreamer with Truncated Backpropagation Through Time (TBTT), conditioning training sequences on previous context representations. TransDreamer [(Chen et al., 2021)] proposed a Transformer-based world model to bypass the limitations of recurrent neural networks and process long context with self-attention [(Vaswani et al., 2017)]. Building on this direction, TWISTER [(Burchi and Timofte, 2025)] further improved Transformer-based world models by incorporating a contrastive predictive coding objective to enhance temporal representation learning. Following the success of State Space Models (SSMs) in capturing dependencies across long sequences [(Gu et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2022; Smith et al., 2023)], several works have also explored SSM-based world models. Recall to Imagine (R2I) [(Samsami et al., 2024)] improved training efficiency and long-term memory using a modification of the S4 model [(Gu et al., 2022)], outperforming previous approaches on the Memory Maze benchmark [(Pašukonis et al., 2023)]. Concurrently, [Deng et al. (2023)] proposed S4WM, further demonstrating that SSM-based architectures outperform Transformer-based world models in terms of long-term memory.

However, despite this progress, existing approaches still encounter difficulties surpassing human performance on tasks requiring long-term memory and planning [(Samsami et al., 2024)]. Most prior works focus on architecture design, assuming that improved world model architectures can effectively exploit past context to capture long-term dependencies. These approaches rely on learning a single world model that generalizes across episodes, requiring it to extract common patterns and adapt to the unique structure of each new episode through contextual representations. While shared patterns can be learned effectively, modeling episode-specific information through context alone remains challenging, particularly in partially observable settings like Memory Maze. In contrast, biological systems are believed to encode long-term memory through persistent modifications of synaptic strengths, a process often associated with Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) in neural circuits [(Bliss and Collingridge, 1993)]. Motivated by this perspective, and by the observation that Test-Time Training (TTT) can improve predictive models when training and test data come from different distributions [(Sun et al., 2020)], we propose a learning strategy that encodes episode-specific memory directly into the model parameters via gradient-based updates at test time. This approach enables the agent to capture episode-specific information by adapting its world model online, rather than relying solely on contextual memory.

In this work, we address the challenge of long-term memory in MBRL by moving beyond the commonly studied paradigm of architecture design. Inspired by test-time training methods that adapt model parameters at inference time [(Sun et al., 2020; Gandelsman et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2025)], we introduce Test-Time Model-Based Reinforcement Learning (TT-MBRL), using gradient descent at test time to encode the memory of episode-specific information into world model parameters. This enables the agent to learn a distinct world model for each episode, improving memory capabilities compared to traditional approaches that solely rely on contextual memory. We first establish a proof of concept on a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark [(Pašukonis et al., 2023)]. We find that the effectiveness of TT-MBRL scales proportionally to the number of environment steps collected at test-time, increasing the amount of rewards obtained per step by 53.7% for R2I after 4000 environment steps on Memory Maze 15×15 (Figure 5(c)). Finally, we show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as DeepMind Control and Atari 100k. Figure 1 summarizes the results obtained on memory benchmarks.

2 Background

We evaluate the impact of TT-MBRL within the Dreamer family of world model architectures. The Dreamer algorithm was originally introduced in [Hafner et al. (2020)] and later refined in subsequent works [(Hafner et al., 2021; Hafner et al., 2023)] to master diverse environments with fixed hyperparameters. It has since become a prominent baseline in MBRL, demonstrating strong performance across a wide range of tasks from high-dimensional visual observations. The agent consists of three main components: The world model that learns to simulate the environment to generate imaginary trajectories, the critic network that estimates state values, and the actor network that learns to select optimal actions.

2.1 World Model Learning

Dreamer learns a world model of the environment in latent space using a sequential autoencoder architecture [(Hinton and Salakhutdinov, 2006; Kingma and Welling, 2014; Chung et al., 2015)]. Specifically, the world model encodes observations oₜ into compact stochastic representations zₜ learned via a reconstruction objective, while a Recurrent State-Space Model (RSSM) [(Hafner et al., 2019)] predicts future states zₜ₊₁ given actions aₜ. In addition, the world model includes multi-layer perceptron (MLP) heads for predicting rewards rₜ and episode continuation cₜ signals from model states sₜ={hₜ,zₜ}. The trainable subcomponents of the world model are the following:

RSSM \begincases \endcasesSequential Network:hₜ=f_φ(hₜ₋₁,zₜ₋₁,aₜ₋₁)
Encoder Network:zₜ∼q_φ(zₜ | hₜ,oₜ)
Dynamics Predictor:ẑₜ∼p_φ(ẑₜ | hₜ)
Reward Predictor:r̂ₜ∼p_φ(r̂ₜ | sₜ)
Continue Predictor:ĉₜ∼p_φ(ĉₜ | sₜ)
Decoder Network:ôₜ∼p_φ(ôₜ | sₜ)
(1)

While the original Dreamer algorithm uses a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) [(Cho et al., 2014)] for the sequential network, other variants have been proposed using Transformer-based world models with self-attention [(Vaswani et al., 2017)] and Structured State Space Sequence models (S4) [(Gu et al., 2022)]. These variants allow computing deterministic states h_1:T in parallel using a non-recurrent encoder network zₜ∼q_φ(zₜ | oₜ) and a parallelizable sequential network h_1:T,x_1:T=f_φ(z_0:T-1,a_0:T-1,x₀), where xₜ are SSM hidden states. In this paper, we experiment with three recently proposed world model designs based on the Dreamer algorithm: DreamerV3 [(Hafner et al., 2023)], which uses an RNN-based world model; TWISTER [(Burchi and Timofte, 2025)], which uses a Transformer-based world model with self-attention; and R2I [(Samsami et al., 2024)], which introduced the Structured State-Space Model (S3M), a modification of S4 to handle temporal dependencies.

The world model is trained on trajectories sampled from a replay buffer. Trajectories are collected during the exploration phase, where the current policy interacts with the environment. Given an input batch containing B sequences of T image observations o_1:T, actions a_1:T , rewards r_1:T, and episode continuation flags c_1:T, the world model parameters (φ) are optimized to minimize the following loss function:

L(φ)=1/BT∑_b=1^B∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ[β_predL_pred(φ)+β_dynL_dyn(φ)+βᵣₑₚLᵣₑₚ(φ)]

(2)

The prediction loss L_pred learns hidden representations with a reconstruction loss and predicts environment quantities such as rewards and continuation flags:

L_pred(φ)=\underbracket-\logp_φ(oₜ | sₜ)_reconstruction loss\underbracket-\logp_φ(rₜ | sₜ)_reward predictor loss \underbracket-\logp_φ(cₜ | sₜ)_continue predictor loss

(3)

The dynamics loss L_dyn trains the dynamics predictor to predict the next state representation by minimizing the KL divergence between the predictor p_φ(ẑₜ | hₜ) and the next stochastic representation q_φ(zₜ | hₜ,oₜ). The representation loss trains the representations to become more predictable if the dynamics predictor cannot predict their distribution. Both loss terms use the stop gradient operator sg(·) to prevent the gradients of targets from being backpropagated and are scaled by the corresponding loss weights β_dyn and βᵣₑₚ, respectively:

(4)

2.2 Actor-Critic Learning

The agent’s policy and value functions are learned by imagining trajectories using the world model. Learning takes place entirely in latent space, which allows the agent to process large batch sizes and increase generalization. To do so, the model states of the sampled sequence are flattened along batch and time dimensions to generate B_img=B×T sample trajectories. The world model imagines H=15 steps into the future using the sequential network and dynamics predictor, selecting actions by sampling from the actor network. Analogously to world model predictor networks, actor and critic networks are designed as simple MLPs with parameter vectors (θ) and (ψ), respectively. We describe the actor-critic learning process of the agent in more detail in Appendix A.3.

3 Method

We introduce TT-MBRL, a novel learning framework for MBRL that takes advantage of test-time observations to learn episode-specific patterns and acquire long-term memory. TT-MBRL learns a unique world model and policy for each evaluation episode. In contrast to training time, where model parameters are shared across all episodes in the replay buffer, this allows the agent to fine-tune its parameters to each individual episode. An overview of the proposed method is provided in Figure 3.

3.1 Test-Time Optimization

At test time, the agent initializes test-time network parameters (φ^′, θ^′, ψ^′) with the set of weights learned during the training phase (φ, θ, ψ) at the beginning of each episode. A dedicated test-time replay buffer is also created to store observations collected within the current evaluation episode. Analogous to the training procedure, the agent samples mini-batches of trajectories to update its parameters. We find it beneficial to draw half of the trajectories from the training replay buffer and the other half from the test-time buffer. This strategy acts as a form of regularization, mitigating overfitting to the limited test-time observations, which could otherwise degrade performance. When the number of test-time samples is smaller than the required world model sequence length, mini-batches are concatenated with trajectories from the training buffer. We also freeze the encoder and decoder parameters and drop the reconstruction loss at test time to improve TT-MBRL efficiency, preserving the representation space learned during training. Unlike the sequential and dynamics networks, which must adapt to the specific layout and structure of each new episode, the encoder and decoder learn general visual representations that are independent of their temporal ordering. Freezing these parameters significantly reduces evaluation time without impacting performance. We provide an empirical analysis of these design choices in Section 4.3. For each new policy step, the world model loss optimizes the test-time parameters φ^′ as follows:

L(φ^′)=1/BT∑_b=1^B∑ₜ₌₁ᵀ[β_predL_pred(φ^′)+β_dynL_dyn(φ^′)+βᵣₑₚLᵣₑₚ(φ^′)]

(5)

With the test-time prediction loss L_pred(φ^′) omitting the reconstruction objective:

L_pred(φ^′)=\underbracket-\logp_φ^′(rₜ | sₜ)_reward predictor loss \underbracket-\logp_φ^′(cₜ | sₜ)_continue predictor loss

(6)

The agent’s behavior at test time is optimized using the adapted world model to learn an improved policy. By reducing world model prediction errors, TT-MBRL enables more accurate estimation of imagined returns, which in turn allows the actor and critic to be more effectively optimized.

4 Experiments

In this work, we investigate the potential of TT-MBRL to learn long-term memory via gradient descent. To this end, we evaluate our method on several tasks that require long-term memory and planning. We first establish a proof of concept by experimenting with a simplified two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment, which we refer to as Memory Maze 2D, showing consistent improvements across different world model architectures. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL in the 3D domain, achieving new state-of-the-art results on the Memory Maze benchmark [(Pašukonis et al., 2023)]. Finally, we conduct a study to identify effective strategies for performing MBRL at test time and show that TT-MBRL maintains strong performance on non-memory benchmarks such as the DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) [(Tassa et al., 2018)] and Atari 100k [(Kaiser et al., 2020)].

4.1 Memory Maze 2D

Benchmark.

In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL, we first design a simplified and efficient two-dimensional variant of the Memory Maze environment in which the agent observes a top-down 3×3 local context centered on its current position. To enable goal identification, we augment the observation with colored borders that indicate the target color to be reached for obtaining the next reward. The observation is then flattened and normalized, forming a vector of dimension 75=5×5×3. Figure 4 illustrates a comparison between our modified setting and the original Memory Maze environment. The agent operates in the maze using a discrete action space consisting of five actions: no-op, move left, move right, move up, and move down. We consider the same four maze sizes as in the original benchmark (9×9, 11×11, 13×13, and 15×15), along with their corresponding hyperparameters. Further details on the proposed Memory Maze 2D environment are provided in Appendix A.5.

Results.

To evaluate the effectiveness of TT-MBRL, we consider three recent world model architectures: DreamerV3 [(Hafner et al., 2023)], which employs an RNN-based world model; TWISTER [(Burchi and Timofte, 2025)], which relies on a Transformer-based architecture; and R2I [(Samsami et al., 2024)], which is built on S4. Table 1 shows the results obtained after training 100M environment steps on each maze size. We also record the performance of a human player to estimate the capabilities of each method compared to human memory abilities. Oracle defines the performance obtained when following the shortest path to the target color. We find that R2I achieves the best results on all maze sizes with a score of 171.6 on Memory Maze 2D 15×15. TWISTER outperforms DreamerV3 on the 15×15 maze size due to its Transformer-based world model with self-attention. However, we find that it struggles to learn an optimal policy on smaller maze sizes. We suppose this is due to the nature of the self-attention mechanism that is not biased toward recent observations and requires accurately selecting the needed information at each time step, while DreamerV3 carries past information into a recurrent hidden state. We find that TT-MBRL improves the performance of all models when a near optimal policy is not already achieved. It allows R2I to outperform human performance on all maze sizes, except 9×9. This is due to the policy occasionally failing on a subset of episodes, despite achieving higher performance on the majority of them. We also evaluate the impact of TT-MBRL on world-model prediction accuracy using a combination of standard video prediction metrics (Table 2). We measure the world model KL divergence, Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) [(Unterthiner et al., 2018)], Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) [(Wang et al., 2004)] and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) [(Zhang et al., 2018)] over 100 unseen trajectories of 64 frames from distinct episodes. We find that TT-MBRL consistently decreases the world model prediction error in latent space. This results in more accurate predictions and better performance in video prediction metrics. Figure 6(a) shows the impact of TT-MBRL on DreamerV3 world model predictions.

4.2 Memory Maze

Benchmark.

The Memory Maze benchmark, introduced by [Pašukonis et al. (2023)], consists of a 3D domain of randomized mazes specifically designed to evaluate long-term memory in agents. In this environment, the agent must locate a target object of a specific color, indicated by the border color in the observation image. Upon reaching and interacting with the correct object, the agent receives a reward of +1, after which a new target object is randomly selected. The benchmark includes four tasks of increasing size and difficulty: Memory Maze 9×9, 11×11, 13×13, and 15×15. While the smaller maze sizes contain three objects, 15×15 mazes include six objects and a greater number of rooms, making the task more challenging while remaining solvable for human players.

Results.

We train DreamerV3, TWISTER, and R2I world models for 100M environment steps on all Memory Maze sizes. Following [Samsami et al. (2024)], we further train R2I up to 400M environment steps and include the results obtained by IMPALA [(Espeholt et al., 2018)], which serves as a strong model-free baseline for comparison. Table 3 compares the results obtained by each method. Despite the increased observation complexity of the 3D domain, where observations of the same position vary with viewing angle, unlike the fixed top-down views of Memory Maze 2D, TT-MBRL successfully identifies structural similarities between observed views to build a more accurate episode-specific world model. TT-MBRL yields consistent improvements across all world model approaches on larger maze sizes, achieving substantial gains: The performance of R2I increases from 60.1 to 63.0 on Memory Maze 13×13, and from 42.0 to 54.1 on Memory Maze 15×15, establishing new state-of-the-art results and the closest performance to the human baseline (67.7) among all proposed methods. On the smaller maze sizes, where DreamerV3 and R2I already achieve near-optimal performance, the gains are more modest, consistent with the saturation effects observed in Memory Maze 2D. We further assess the quality of world model predictions in Table 4, comparing video prediction metrics. Across all five metrics, TT-MBRL substantially reduces prediction error. Figure 5 further illustrates the dynamics of adaptation within a single episode for R2I on Memory Maze 15×15. Figure 5(a) shows the world model KL divergence over 64 predicted steps: Without TT-MBRL, prediction error accumulates rapidly beyond the first 20 steps, while the adapted model maintains substantially lower divergence. Figure 5(b) shows the episode return distribution, with TT-MBRL shifting mass toward higher scores and reducing the frequency of low-reward episodes. Figure 5(c) shows the per-step relative improvement in obtained rewards brought by TT-MBRL across the episode: The effectiveness of TT-MBRL grows steadily as more observations accumulate in the test-time replay buffer, reaching 53.7% after 4000 environment steps.

4.3 TT-MBRL Analysis

Training Data Regularization.

We conduct a set of studies to identify effective strategies for performing model-based reinforcement learning at test time. Table 5 reports the impact of different sampling schemes on mitigating overfitting. We first consider a naive approach in which the model is updated solely using trajectories collected at test time, without enforcing a minimum number of samples to prefill the test-time replay buffer before learning begins (Test Data Only, No Prefill). Although this strategy improves performance in many episodes, it also degrades performance in others, as the model overfits to limited early observations, resulting in suboptimal policies. To address this issue, we introduce a delay mechanism that postpones learning until the test-time replay buffer is populated with a sufficient number of samples (1024 Prefill). This reduces overfitting but introduces a trade-off, as it delays the benefits of adaptation. To overcome both limitations, we propose mixing trajectories collected at test time with samples from the training replay buffer (Test+Train Data, No Prefill), effectively acting as a form of regularization. This approach mitigates early overfitting while enabling immediate adaptation, leading to more stable and consistent performance improvements. To verify that the gain in performance is due to TT-MBRL rather than additional inference compute, we also perform a compute-matched evaluation. We study the impact of additional compute on performance when only training trajectories are available (Train Data Only). The comparison confirms that the performance gain is due to TT-MBRL rather than additional compute budget.

Reconstruction Loss and Parameter Freezing.

Table 6 shows the impact of freezing or updating encoder/decoder parameters using the reconstruction loss at test time. We find that the two variants achieve comparable performance across different world model architectures. These findings are as expected, given that encoder representations are independent of their temporal ordering. The episode-specific information is instead captured by the sequential and dynamics network parameters. However, unfreezing these parameters comes at a non-trivial computational cost, as gradient back-propagation must be carried through the decoder and encoder, resulting in longer evaluation times. This is especially the case for Memory Maze, where observations are 64×64 pixels images. We therefore adopt parameter freezing for encoder and decoder networks as our default setting, as it improves evaluation efficiency without sacrificing performance.

4.4 Application of TT-MBRL to Non-Memory Domains

In order to evaluate the capacity of TT-MBRL to maintain strong performance in non-memory domains, domains not designed primarily to test long-term episodic memory, we evaluate its impact on two widely adopted benchmarks that do not require long-term memory or planning: The visual DeepMind Control Suite (DMC) [(Tassa et al., 2018)], which comprises 20 continuous control tasks, and the Atari 100k benchmark [(Kaiser et al., 2020)], which includes 26 Atari games with discrete actions. Both benchmarks are largely fully observable and can be solved without extensive memory. We report aggregated mean and median scores across all 20 DMC tasks in Table 8 and human-normalized scores on Atari 100k in Table 8. Overall, we find that TT-MBRL does not degrade the performance obtained by DreamerV3. Moreover, we find that TT-MBRL consistently improves performance on Reacher Hard and Finger Turn Hard, where the agent occasionally fails to accurately reach the target sphere. TT-MBRL mitigates this issue by enabling the agent to better detect and correct such errors. Detailed results for individual tasks are provided in Appendix A.9.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we addressed the challenge of long-term memory in MBRL. While prior approaches have primarily focused on improving world model architectures to better exploit contextual information, we instead explored an orthogonal direction: encoding memory directly into model parameters. To this end, we introduced TT-MBRL, a framework that leverages gradient-based updates at test time to incorporate episode-specific information into the world model. By enabling the agent to learn a distinct set of parameters for each episode, TT-MBRL moves beyond shared representations and allows rapid adaptation to the current episode, effectively forming a form of neural memory. Through experiments on both a simplified setting and the Memory Maze benchmark, we demonstrated that TT-MBRL consistently improves performance across multiple world model architectures. Notably, our method achieves state-of-the-art results on Memory Maze. We find that the effectiveness of TT-MBRL scales proportionally to the number of environment steps collected at test-time. These results highlight the potential of parameter-based memory as a powerful complement to contextual memory in MBRL systems. More broadly, our findings suggest that test-time learning constitutes a promising direction for developing agents capable of long-term planning.

5.1 Limitations and Future Work.

The primary limitation of our approach is the reduced evaluation efficiency resulting from the use of gradient-based optimization at test time. TT-MBRL requires learning a distinct world model and behavior policy for each evaluation episode, leading to increased computational cost and longer evaluation times. While this overhead remains manageable in environments such as Memory Maze, it may become prohibitive in settings that require a large number of environment interactions. As a direction for future work, we plan to extend our approach to operate during the exploration phase. We hypothesize that integrating TT-MBRL into exploration could improve sample efficiency and overall performance by enabling the collection of more informative and diverse trajectories. Consequently, improving the computational efficiency of our approach will be crucial to making it practical for online adaptation during exploration.

（参考文献见原文。）

Appendix A Appendix

A.1 Related Works

A.1.1 Model-based Reinforcement Learning

Model-based reinforcement learning approaches use a model of the environment to simulate agent trajectories, enabling better generalization, sample efficiency, and decision-making through planning. Following the success of deep neural networks for learning function approximations [(LeCun et al., 2015)], researchers proposed to learn world models using gradient backpropagation. One of the first approaches to apply model-based reinforcement learning to high-dimensional visual observations is SimPLe [(Kaiser et al., 2020)]. The authors proposed to learn a predictive world model for Atari games directly in pixel space using a convolutional autoencoder. SimPLe’s model predicts future observations and rewards conditioned on past frames and actions, enabling the training of a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent [(Schulman et al., 2017)] using simulated rollouts.

PlaNet [(Hafner et al., 2019)] subsequently introduced Recurrent State-Space Models (RSSMs), combining deterministic recurrent dynamics implemented with Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) [(Cho et al., 2014)] and stochastic latent variables to learn compact world models in latent space. The agent learns hidden representations by encoding observations using a convolutional variational autoencoder (VAE) [(Kingma and Welling, 2014)] while predicting future latent states and rewards, enabling planning via model predictive control. Building on this framework, Dreamer [(Hafner et al., 2020)] improved performance by learning a policy and value function directly within the learned latent space. DreamerV2 [(Hafner et al., 2021)] extended this approach to Atari games by introducing categorical latent variables trained with straight-through gradients [(Bengio et al., 2013)], improving representational capacity and stability in discrete domains. More recently, DreamerV3 [(Hafner et al., 2023)] demonstrated that a single architecture with shared hyperparameters can scale across diverse domains, from continuous control to Atari. This was achieved through a set of architectural and optimization refinements, including symlog-scaled reward and value predictions to handle scale variation, layer normalization [(Ba et al., 2016)] for improved robustness, and return normalization using an exponential moving average (EMA) of return percentiles. With these changes, DreamerV3 achieved state-of-the-art performance across a wide range of benchmarks, often outperforming both specialized model-free and other model-based methods.

In parallel to the Dreamer line of work, other approaches have explored alternative world model designs. Beyond recurrent architectures, Transformer-based world models have been proposed to improve long-term memory and representation learning [(Micheli et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; Robine et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023)]. Diffusion-based world models [(Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015)] have also emerged as a compelling alternative to discrete latent variable sequence modeling, demonstrating strong performance across a range of settings [(Alonso et al., 2024; Valevski et al., 2025; Bar et al., 2025; Hafner et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026)]. Another line of work has investigated multitask world models, training a single world model jointly across multiple tasks to improve generalization and achieve stronger performance than single-task models [(Hansen et al., 2024; Hansen et al., 2026)]. Model-based reinforcement learning approaches using Monte-Carlo tree search (MCTS) [(Coulom, 2006)] have also been explored following the success of Alpha Go [(Silver et al., 2017; Silver et al., 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2020; Ye et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024)].

A.1.2 Memory in World Models

Multiple approaches have focused on improving the memory capabilities of world models. [Pašukonis et al. (2023)] proposed to augment Dreamer with Truncated Backpropagation Through Time (TBTT), conditioning training sequences on previous context representations to preserve information over time. TransDreamer [(Chen et al., 2021)] replaced Dreamer’s RSSM by a Transformer State-Space Model (TSSM) using masked self-attention to process past context more easily. The agent was evaluated on Hidden Order Discovery tasks requiring long-term memory and reasoning, demonstrating better performance. Recall To Imagine (R2I) [(Samsami et al., 2024)] proposed the Structured State-Space Model (S3M) to improve computational efficiency when handling long sequences. This allows R2I to process very long sequences and achieve strong performance on the Memory Maze benchmark. Concurrently, [Deng et al. (2023)] proposed S4WM, demonstrating that the S4 architecture outperforms Transformer-based world models in terms of long-term memory. Alternatively, EDELINE [(Lee et al., 2025)] proposed to augment the DIAMOND world model [(Alonso et al., 2024)] with a Mamba [(Gu and Dao, 2023)] SSM to enhance memory capabilities. A similar approach was concurrently proposed in [Savov et al. (2025)] where the authors use Mamba to improve model predictions on CSGO [(Pearce and Zhu, 2022)].

A.1.3 Test-Time Training

Test-Time Training (TTT) was originally proposed in [Sun et al. (2020)] for improving the performance of predictive models when training and test data come from different distributions. This work proposed to turn a single unlabeled test sample into a self-supervised learning problem, on which to update the model parameters before making a prediction. The initial TTT paper used image rotation prediction [(Gidaris et al., 2018)] as a self-supervised task to update model weights and achieve higher classification accuracy on corrupted test images. The method was later improved with TTT-MAE [(Gandelsman et al., 2022)], using MAE [(He et al., 2022)] instead of rotation prediction to reach higher performance. Test-time training was subsequently applied to multiple domains like reinforcement learning [(Hansen et al., 2021)], language modeling [(Hardt and Sun, 2023)], and video processing [(Wang et al., 2025)]. In the area of reinforcement learning, [Hansen et al. (2021)] proposed Policy Adaptation during Deployment (PAD) [(Hansen et al., 2021)], applying TTT to model-free reinforcement learning algorithms [(Haarnoja et al., 2018; Mnih et al., 2016)]. They demonstrated that PAD improves performance under distribution shifts on the DeepMind Control [(Tassa et al., 2018)] and CRLMaze [(Lomonaco et al., 2020)] benchmarks. They also showed that PAD enables more effective sim-to-real transfer for robotic manipulation tasks.

A.2 Additional Ablations

Test-Time Optimization Objective.

In order to clarify that the performance gains achieved by TT-MBRL are the results of its key differences rather than solely the product of applying test-time adaptation, we perform a comparison with PAD and study the impact of loss components. Table 9 shows the impact of test-time objectives on performance. As expected, we find that the KL objective is essential to TT-MBRL success. Removing the KL objective (w/o KL loss) causes the agent to fail because the dynamics predictor cannot adapt to moving world model representations and makes incorrect predictions. On the other hand, the agent appears robust to removing the reward and continue objectives (w/o rwd-cont loss), signaling that it is not essential to TT-MBRL success. However, given the dependency of reward and continue MLP heads on moving representations, we suppose this design choice could have a negative impact on performance in the long run. We also find that removing the actor-critic objective (w/o actor-critic) can decrease performance. The performance of the agent deteriorates along the episode, given that the actor and critic cannot adapt to moving representations. We also experiment with PAD [(Hansen et al., 2021)], which was originally proposed in the model-free context. PAD only adapts encoder parameters using a self-supervised objective and does not use training samples for regularization, leaving policy and value networks unchanged at test time. As expected, we find that PAD has a detrimental effect on performance despite relying on test-time training.

TT-MBRL Train/Test Sampling Ratio.

The default TT-MBRL setting uses a 50/50 sampling ratio for train/test trajectories. To confirm that our method is robust to this hyper-parameter choice and does not depend on a narrow setting, we study the impact of the train/test ratio by varying the ratio of training samples among the global batch. Table 10 shows the results that we obtained on Memory Maze 2D 15×15. We find that sampling only training trajectories (100/0) does not improve performance because the world model cannot learn about episode-specific patterns. Using only test trajectories (0/100) decreases performance, confirming the important role of training trajectories in regularization. Overall, we find that a sampling ratio between 25% and 75% achieves robust performance, showing the flexibility of this hyperparameter.

Test-Time Gradient Update Frequency.

We perform a study on compute–performance tradeoff by varying the number of policy steps per gradient step. Table 11 shows the impact of test-time gradient update frequency on TT-MBRL efficacy. We find that increasing the update frequency by a factor of 2 does not lead to a significant performance improvement while increasing evaluation time by the same factor. Decreasing the frequency of TT-MBRL updates slows down adaptation, which results in lower final performance. However, we find that TT-MBRL is quite robust to this hyper-parameter, achieving significant improvement with a larger factor of policy steps per gradient step while also decreasing evaluation time by the same factor. We find these results encouraging for the development of an efficient manner to apply TT-MBRL.

A.3 Actor Critic Learning

Analogously to world model predictor networks, actor and critic networks are designed as simple MLPs with parameter vectors (θ) and (ψ), respectively:

Actor: aₜ∼π_θ(aₜ|sₜ), Critic: v_ψ(sₜ)≈E_p_φ,π_θ[R^λₜ]

(7)

The critic network learns to minimize the symlog-transformed cross-entropy loss [(Hafner et al., 2023)] with discretized λ-returns obtained from imagined trajectories:

Rₜ^λ=r̂ₜ₊₁+γĉₜ₊₁((1-λ)v_ψ(sₜ₊₁)+λRₜ₊₁^λ)R_H+1^λ=v_ψ(s_H+1)
(8)

The critic also relies on its own predictions for estimating rewards beyond the prediction horizon, which requires adding a regularizing term toward the outputs of its own EMA network. Equation 9 defines the critic loss as follows:

L_critic(ψ)=1/BH∑_b=1^B∑ₜ₌₁^H[ \underbracket-\logp_ψ(Rₜ^λ | sₜ)_discrete returns regression\underbracket-\logp_ψ(v^′_ψ(sₜ) | sₜ)_critic EMA regularizer ]

(9)

The actor network is trained to select actions that maximize obtained advantages using Reinforce [(Williams, 1992)]. It also maximizes the policy entropy to ensure sufficient exploration during both data collection and imagination. The actor loss is defined as follows:

L_actor(θ)=1/BH∑_b=1^B∑ₜ₌₁^H[ \underbracket- \logπ_θ(aₜ | sₜ)sg(Aₜ^λ)_reinforce\underbracket- ηH[π_θ(aₜ | sₜ)]_entropy regularizer ]

(10)

Where Aₜ^λ=(R̂ₜ^λ-v_ψ(sₜ))/\max(1,S) defines advantages computed using normalized returns. The returns are scaled using exponentially moving average statistics of their 5ᵗʰ and 95ᵗʰ batch percentiles to ensure stable learning across environments with different return scales:

S=EMA(Per(Rₜ^λ,95)-Per(Rₜ^λ,5),momentum=0.99)

(11)

A.4 Experiments Compute Resources

We perform Memory Maze 2D and Memory Maze experiments on Nvidia L40 GPUs with 48GB of memory along with 40 CPU workers. During training, we use two GPUs for training R2I on Memory Maze experiments while a single GPU is sufficient for other experiments. For DMC and Atari 100K benchmarks, we used RTX 3090 GPUs with 24GB of memory along with 16 CPU workers. A single GPU per task was sufficient for the two benchmarks. Table 12 describes the execution time and resources required for each experiment.

A.5 Memory Maze 2D Environment

We design Memory Maze 2D to evaluate the capacity of agents to develop long-term memory by exploring a partially observable environment. Memory Maze 2D serves as a simplified and more efficient version of the Memory Maze environment, where the agent observes a top-down 3×3 local context centered on its current position. To facilitate goal identification, we augment the observation with colored borders that indicate the target color to be reached for obtaining the next reward. The observation is then flattened and normalized, forming a vector of dimension 75=5×5×3. The agent operates in the maze using a discrete action space consisting of five actions: no-op, move left, move right, move up, and move down. Following [(Pašukonis et al., 2023)], we design four maze tasks with varying sizes and difficulty: Memory Maze 2D 9×9, Memory Maze 2D 11×11, Memory Maze 2D 13×13, and Memory Maze 2D 15×15. Table 13 shows the parameters associated with each maze size and Figure 7 depicts randomly generated environment maps.
