一句话：无条件的手部先验能生成姿态，但抓握是否合理要看它和什么物体接触。

要点：

  • 观察：近期无条件生成先验在人体姿态建模上很成功，但手是「常与其他物体交互」的多关节体，无条件先验无法保证抓握的合理性
  • HaNDF 提出**物体条件化**的神经距离场，作为数据驱动先验来建模「手—物体」的合理构型
  • 它在手部关节的乘积流形上工作，把物体几何作为条件引入

为什么值得看：手部动作是 AI 生成角色动作里最容易穿帮的部分：手指与物体接触不对、抓握不合理。把物体几何作为条件，比事后做碰撞修更根本——对做交互动画、手势驱动与 VR 手部表示的团队都有用。

中文摘要：近期的无条件生成先验在人体姿态建模上取得了不错效果，但手是常与其他物体交互的多关节体，无条件先验无法保证「抓握是否合理」。HaNDF 因此提出**物体条件化的神经距离场**：把物体几何作为条件，学习手—物构型的数据驱动先验，并在手部关节构成的乘积流形上建模。相比先无条件生成再靠碰撞修正，把物体纳入条件更贴近交互的本质，也更适合手势驱动、VR 手部表示与交互动画这类场景。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

HaNDF: Object-Conditioned
Geometric Neural Hand Distance Fields

Abstract

We propose, HaNDF, object-conditional neural distance fields as data-driven priors for modeling the plausible hand–object configurations, in the product manifold of hand articulations. While recent unconditional generative priors showed success in modeling human pose, hands are versatile articulated bodies often found in interaction with other objects. This makes it crucial to develop a generative prior which can model the plausible hand poses conditioned on the object under interaction. To this end, our HaNDF proposes a geometry-aware, object-conditioned neural distance field, representing the plausible articulations in the zero-level set of a conditional field. We leverage tools from Riemannian geometry to (i) represent plausible hands in the zero level-set of an object-induced neural field, and (ii) project a given pose onto this field. Using HaNDF, we can also optimize for a plausible condition, determining the object under interaction. Our extensive evaluations demonstrate that our HaNDF provides a flexible and powerful prior for hand–object interaction, suitable for applications such as pose refinement, reconstruction under occlusion, and physically plausible manipulation synthesis.

1 Introduction

Human hands are among the most versatile articulated systems, practicing rich and diverse interactions with objects. Modeling plausible hand–object configurations is therefore fundamental to applications in robotics, AR/VR, and 3D perception. Yet, recovering or generating such interactions from often partial observations remains challenging: the space of valid configurations is highly constrained, object-dependent, and non-Euclidean, where even small pose perturbations can lead to physically implausible grasps with interpenetration or loss of contact. A central requirement is thus a strong, queryable prior that encodes which hand poses are plausible given an object.

Existing approaches fall short of this goal. Generative models based on VAEs [Rempe et al. (2021)] or diffusion [Shafir et al. (2023); Christen et al. (2024)] learn distributions over poses or interactions, but operate in Euclidean latent spaces where distances lack geometric meaning, limiting their expressivity. Neural distance field [Chibane et al. (2020)] (NDF) variants such as PoseNDF [Tiwari et al. (2022)] or NRDF [He et al. (2024)] offer an alternative by modeling the manifold of plausible articulations directly and enabling projection via gradient descent. However, current NDF-based priors are human-body specific, unconditional, capture hand articulation independent of the object, and thus fail to encode interaction-specific constraints. Conversely, object-conditioned methods [Kulkarni et al. (2024); Weng et al. (2023)] typically treat articulation in Euclidean space or rely on task-specific pipelines, sacrificing geometric consistency. As a result, no existing approach provides a unified prior that is (i) geometry-aware, (ii) conditioned on object shape, and (iii) equipped with a meaningful distance for optimization.

HaNDF addresses this gap proposing a generative, object conditioned prior of hand poses. Our key insight is to model hand articulation on its intrinsic Riemannian manifold while treating the object as a conditioning signal that modulates the manifold of plausible configurations. Concretely, we learn a conditional distance field that predicts the geodesic distance to the nearest valid hand pose given object geometry, whose zero level set defines the object-specific interaction manifold. This formulation yields a continuous, geometry-aware energy landscape where Riemannian gradients provide principled projection, refinement, and sampling directly on the articulation manifold. This perspective unifies multiple applications under a single framework without retraining: denoising, recovering physically consistent grasps from data, and generation of novel grasps. When integrated into reconstruction pipelines, HaNDF acts as a plug-and-play prior, improving robustness under occlusion without retraining task-specific models, as validated across three challenging benchmarks: HOI4D [Liu et al. (2022)], OakInk [Yang et al. (2022)], and DexYCB [Chao et al. (2021)]. In summary, our contributions are:

  • •

    We introduce HaNDF, an object-conditioned Riemannian neural distance field for hand articulation, whose zero-level set defines a family of object-dependent plausibility manifolds.

  • •

    We develop an object-specific distance-field training procedure with per-object latent fitting and nearest-pose supervision, together with a transformer architecture that jointly processes hand-joint and object tokens.

  • •

    Based upon NRDF’s RDF-Grad, we enable object-conditioned projection, denoising, completion, and generation of MANO hand poses, and introduce an inversion procedure to retrieve and refine compatible object conditions.

    • HaNDF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in challenging settings with occlusion and ambiguity. Our code is publicly available at circle-group.github.io/research/HaNDF.

    2 Related Work

    Generative priors of humans and hands

    Early efforts learned plausible-pose priors from 2D data with weak 3D supervision [Omran et al. (2018)], used GANs [Kanazawa et al. (2018)], or extended adversarial supervision to motion sequences [Kocabas et al. (2020)]. Generative priors have been built on a range of architectures. PoseD-Flow [Nadar et al. (2026)] trains a flow matching model of human pose. MotionVAE [Ling et al. (2020)], HuMoR [Rempe et al. (2021)], and PhaseMP [Shi et al. (2023)] use VAEs autoregressively for motion priors. Diffusion models [Tevet et al. (2023); Shafir et al. (2023); Ci et al. (2023)] have since become standard for pose and motion generation, with recent extensions to whole-body poses including hands [Lu et al. (2025)]. Dyn-HaMR [Yu et al. (2025)] trains an HMP prior for hand-motion infilling. For hand-object interaction, TOCH [Zhou et al. (2022)] learns an object-centric correspondence-field prior for refining tracked sequences. Object-conditional grasp generators form a parallel literature [Jiang et al. (2021); Ye et al. (2024); Cha et al. (2024); Zuo et al. (2024); Li et al. (2025)]. These methods generate diverse poses but typically lack a differentiable distance to the pose manifold. We instead learn a geodesic distance to the conditioned plausible-grasp set, whose Riemannian gradient yields an projection direction.

    Neural distance fields (NDFs)

    NDFs were introduced for implicit representation of 3D objects and scenes [Chibane et al. (2020)] and have since become a tool for learning priors over articulated forms. PoseNDF [Tiwari et al. (2022)] models body articulation as the zero-level set of an NDF. NRDF [He et al. (2024)] introduces a geometrically principled variant on the product of manifolds with better accuracy and diversity. NRMF [Yu et al. (2026)] extends NRDF to temporal motion; Gu et al.[Gu et al. (2026)] train NRDF on AMASS Retargeted-G1 [Mahmood et al. (2019)] for humanoid retargeting. We extend the conditional setting to human hands–objects, with a Riemannian distance field on the product manifold of joint quaternions and a learned object shape latent as condition.

    Hand-object interaction reconstruction

    Hand-object reconstruction systems jointly recover hand and object geometry from monocular images. Early parametric pipelines couple MANO with object pose regression [Hasson et al. (2019)]. SDF-based methods replace meshes with implicit fields: Grasping Field [Karunratanakul et al. (2020)], AlignSDF [Chen et al. (2022b)], gSDF [Chen et al. (2023)], and HOISDF [Qi et al. (2024)]. Recent approaches leverage large pretrained models: diffusion priors for object completion under occlusion [Liu et al. (2025); Fu et al. (2024); Wang et al. (2025); Aytekin et al. (2026); Ye et al. (2024)] and feed-forward transformers for direct point-cloud prediction [Chen et al. (2025)]. Our contribution is a hand prior, not a reconstruction pipeline: a differentiable distance to the conditioned plausible manifold whose gradient supports optimisation, denoising, completion, and refinement on top of any of the systems above.

    3 Background

    Since hand joints are rotations, their natural configuration space is not Euclidean but a product of rotations. Here we focus on unit-quaternion representation of rotations and review the differential / Riemannian geometry of rotations and the product-manifold structure in appendixA. Our exposition is based on NRDF [He et al. (2024)] and NRMF [Yu et al. (2026)], akin to [Birdal et al. (2018); Birdal and Simsekli (2019); Chen et al. (2022a); Boumal (2023)]. In what follows, let M be a smooth m-dimensional manifold embedded in an ambient Euclidean space X=ℝᵈ. For x∈M, the tangent spaceTₓM is the set of all velocity vectors of smooth curves passing through x.

    The rotation group as a Riemannian manifold

    The space of 3D rotations is a particular Riemannian manifold, known as the special orthogonal group:

    SO(3)={R∈ℝ^3×3 \middle| R^⊤R=I, \det(R)=1}.

    		(1)

    Inspired by [He et al. (2024)], in this work, we parameterize rotations by unit quaternions (UQ) and provide a detailed review of the group SO(3) in appendixB.

    A quaternion is an element q=(q_w,qₓ,q_y,q_z)=(w,v)∈ℝ⁴, with scalar part w∈ℝ and vector part v∈ℝ³. The conjugate is q̄=(w,-v), with the norm ∥q∥₂=√w²+∥v∥₂². The Hamilton product of q=(w_q,v_q) and r=(wᵣ,vᵣ) is

    q⊗r=(w_qwᵣ-v_q^⊤vᵣ, w_qvᵣ+wᵣv_q+v_q×vᵣ).

    		(2)

    Shown in Fig.2, the unit quaternions form the three-sphere:

    M_H=H₁={q∈ℝ⁴ \middle| ∥q∥₂=1}≃S³,

    		(3)

    and form a Lie group under Hamilton product. The inverse of a UQ is its conjugate: q⁻¹=q̄. For a rotation by angle α around unit axis u∈S², the corresponding UQ is

    q=(\cos(α/2), u\sin(α/2)).

    		(4)

    The map from H₁ to SO(3) is a two-to-one (double) covering map: q∼-q. That is, q and -q represent the same physical rotation. The tangent space at q is

    T_qH₁={η∈ℝ⁴ \middle| q^⊤η=0}.

    		(5)

    The orthogonal projection from ambient space ℝ⁴ onto T_qH₁ is

    Π_q^S³(v)=v-(q^⊤v)q=(I-qq^⊤)v.

    		(6)

    For a smooth f:H₁→ℝ, if ∇_qf is the Euclidean gradient, the spherical Riemannian gradient is

    grad_qf=(I-qq^⊤)∇_qf.

    		(7)

    Let η∈T_qH₁. In the quaternion Lie-group notation, tangent vectors are represented as pure imaginary quaternions η=(0,u) with u∈ℝ³. The exponential and logarithmic maps at q are:

    Exp_q(η)=q⊗\exp(η)=q⊗(\cosϑ, (\sinϑ)/(ϑ)u), Log_q(p)=(0, (v)/(∥v∥₂)\cos⁻¹(w)),(8)

    where η=(0,u) and ϑ=∥u∥₂, and the group exponential at the identity is

    \exp(0,u)=(\cos∥u∥₂, (\sin∥u∥₂)/(∥u∥₂)u),

    		(9)

    with the convention \sin∥u∥₂/∥u∥₂=1 when ∥u∥₂=0 and Log_q is zero when ∥v∥₂=0, as used in NRDF [He et al. (2024)]. The Riemannian (geodesic) distance between two unit quaternions q₁,q₂∈H₁ is the length of the shortest geodesic on S³, accounting for the antipodal identification q∼-q:

    d_H₁(q₁,q₂)=2\cos⁻¹(|q₁^⊤q₂|)=2\min{∥Log_q₁(q₂)∥₂, ∥Log_q₁(-q₂)∥₂}.(10)

    4 HaNDF: Geometric Object Conditioned Neural Hand Distance Fields

    Hand representation

    We instantiate the articulated hand with the MANO model [Romero et al. (2017)], which represents a hand mesh as a differentiable function of shape, pose, and global rigid motion:

    V=H(β,θ,t)∈ℝ^Nᵥ×3,

    		(11)

    where β∈ℝ^N_β denotes low-dimensional hand shape, t∈ℝ³ is global translation, and θ denotes the 3D articulated hand pose. In MANO, the pose consists of local rotations along a kinematic tree of hand joints. We exclude the global wrist rotation from the intrinsic articulation prior and parameterize the remaining K=15 local joint rotations on the power manifold of θ\vcentcolon={qᵢ∈H₁}ᵢ₌₁^K∈M_H=H₁^K. Each qᵢ parameterizes the rotation of joint i with respect to its parent in the MANO kinematic tree. This relative, local parameterization is important in coupling the configuration of all local rotations.

    Object representation

    Let O denote the space of 3D objects, represented as meshes, point clouds, or implicit fields. We assume access to an encoder E:O→ℤ, which maps an object O∈O to a latent code: z=E(O)∈ℤ. Unlike the hand pose, ℤ≡ℝ^d_z is not endowed with a special Riemannian structure. The encoder is trained jointly with a decoder D:ℤ→O in an autoencoding framework. As we will detail in Sec.4.1, while any embedding network is possible, we adopt a DeepSDF-style [Park et al. (2019)] architecture that produces a compact latent code capturing global object geometry.

    We deliberately represent the object via a latent code rather than explicit geometry (e.g., point clouds or meshes) for reasons of: (i) compactness, enabling efficient conditioning in neural fields; (ii) invariance to input resolution and representation; (iii) compatibility with generative and reconstruction pipelines, where object shape may be partially observed.

    4.1 HaNDF

    Given a hand pose θ∈M_H and an object latent z∈ℤ, our model learns a scalar distance field

    f_Φ:M_H×ℤ→ℝ_≥0,

    		(12)

    that explicitly approximates the geodesic distance to the nearest plausible hand pose conditioned on the object. The conditioned manifold of plausible hands is thus given by the zero level-set:

    S(z)={θ∈M_H \middle| f_Φ(θ>|>z)=0},

    		(13)

    such that the value of f represents the unsigned geodesic distance to the closest plausible pose on the manifold. The latent z influences the field globally, adapting the location and shape of the zero level-set S(z) according to object geometry. Intuitively, z encodes affordances such as size, curvature, and topology, which determine feasible grasp configurations.

    Projection onto HaNDF. Given an object z, an arbitrary hand pose θ⁽⁰⁾∈M_H can be projected onto the closest plausible hand pose on our object-conditioned manifold:

    Π_S(z)(θ⁽⁰⁾)=\argmin_θ∈S(z)d_M_H(θ,θ⁽⁰⁾).

    		(14)

    Since S(z) is represented implicitly by the zero level-set of f_Φ, we solve this optimization by minimizing the predicted distance field over the hand manifold, similar to [Tiwari et al. (2022); He et al. (2024)]:

    θ^⋆≈\argmin_θ∈M_Hf_Φ(θ>|>z).

    		(15)

    Since z is a condition, the optimization is performed only over θ. We then update the hand pose using an adaptive conditioned Riemannian descent step (see Fig.1 for iterations):

    θ⁽ᵗ⁺¹⁾=Exp_θ⁽ᵗ⁾(-αf_Φ(θ⁽ᵗ⁾>|>z)(grad_θf_Φ(θ⁽ᵗ⁾>|>z))/(∥grad_θf_Φ(θ⁽ᵗ⁾>|>z)∥_θ⁽ᵗ⁾+ε)),

    		(HaNDFGrad)

    where α>0 is a step-size parameter and ε>0 prevents numerical instability. By construction, Eq.HaNDFGrad respects the non-Euclidean manifold of MANO hand articulations as every update remains on M_H=H₁^K, and the multiplication by f_Φ(θ⁽ᵗ⁾>|>z) makes the step length proportional to the predicted distance, akin to the RDFGrad of NRDF [He et al. (2024)]. The projection is terminated when either the predicted distance falls below a threshold f_Φ(θ⁽ᵗ⁾>|>z)<δ or maximum iterations is reached.

    HaNDF as a conditional generative model. Beyond projection and refinement, HaNDF can be used as a conditioned generative model of plausible hand poses. For a fixed latent z, the f-induced Bolzmann density p(θ>|>z)∝\exp(-βf_φ(θ>|>z)²), approximates data distribution, understood as a product-measure over spheres, illustrated in Fig.3, analogous to [Yu et al. (2026)]. Eq.HaNDFGrad is then a maximum-aposteriori estimation.

    Our simple strategy to sample from p(·>|>z) is as follows: we (i) initialize a random hand pose θ⁽⁰⁾ by sampling each quaternion independently, qₖ⁽⁰⁾∼Unif(H₁) ∀k or sampling q̃ₖ∼ℕ(0,I₄) and normalizing qₖ⁽⁰⁾=q̃ₖ/∥q̃ₖ∥₂, (ii) project it onto HaNDF, and (iii) pass it from MANO model in Eq.11. Different initial samples can project to different connected components or basins of attraction of S(z). Hence, generation diversity is controlled by the initial distribution and by the geometry of the learned field.

    A connection to Riemannian Flow Matching [Chen and Lipman ()] has been made in [He et al. (2024)] for the unconditional NRDF. Our distance field formulation has some advantages. First, it avoids imposing a Gaussian structure on the hand-poses. Instead of predicting the step towards the manifold via a network, we obtain it via backpropagation. This allows optimization in domains where designing decoders is challenging. Also, we can utilize existing optimizers of deep learning frameworks for Lagrangian iterations by simply minimizing distance.

    HaNDF as a generative prior

    The same learned field can be used for generation, denoising, completion, and reconstruction, since all tasks reduce to minimizing or projecting through the same object-conditioned distance field. Typically, in downstream tasks, our prior is combined with task-specific data terms involving observations Y, leading to the inference problem111 In the language of diffusion or flow matching, such inference is understood as inversion or training-free guidance[Nadar et al. (2026); Ben-Hamu et al. (2024)].:

    \min_θ∈M_H,z∈ℤ L_data(θ,z>|>Y)+λₚᵣᵢₒᵣf_Φ(θ>|>z)²+λ_zℝ(z),

    		(16)

    which can be minimized for θ∈M_H (Riemannian Adam [Becigneul and Ganea (2019)]) to recover hands or for z (Euclidean) to recover objects that best fit the hand. The regularizer ℝ(z) prevents degenerate latent drift and may be given by a reconstruction loss through the object decoder. L_data is task-dependent and can ensure consistency with observed depth, silhouette, 3D measurements.

    Object encoding

    We represent the object as a single global shape code z∈ℝ^cₒ produced by a pretrained DeepSDF auto-decoder [Park et al. (2019)]. Following DeepSDF, each shape is paired with an continuous latent code z, and the decoder g_ψ(z,x) regresses the signed distance at any query point. We choose DeepSDF auto-decoder for two reasons: (i) its latent space is inherently aligned with our object condition formulation, and (ii) its decoder-only design supports geometry refinement via latent optimization at test time. Note that our object guidance only requires a permutation-invariant representation of the object and is therefore compatible with alternative encoders [Cho et al. (2025); Yang et al. (2025)].

    To recover objects at inference, we invert (auto-decode) to obtain the DeepSDF latent code K times, starting from different initializations and retrieve the nearest training latents, and keep hand-object pair with smallest error. We use PCA to reduce the dimensionality of this search. We provide the details and comparisons to other encoders in Sec.C.3.

    HaNDF architecture

    We tokenize hand and object into a shared d-dimensional space and process them with a transformer encoder. The K joint quaternions are linearly projected to hand tokens hₖ=Wₕqₖ+bₕ. We project the DeepSDF latent code to obtain one object token o=Wₒz+bₒ. A learnable [DIST] token d is prepended as an aggregator, yielding the input sequence

    X = [ d; h₁,…,h_K; o ] ∈ ℝ^(K+2)×d.

    		(17)

    After learnable positional embeddings, X is processed by L self-attention layers; the final-layer representation at the [DIST] position is mapped to the scalar prediction by a linear head with softplus function,

    f_Φ(θ>|>z) = softplus(w^⊤d^(L)+b).

    		(18)

    Self-attention lets every hand-joint token attend to the object token and vice versa, so the prediction is jointly conditioned on hand articulation and object shape. Encoding the entire shape code as a single token preserves its holistic semantics and lets each joint query the full object descriptor in one attention hop; we use L=4 layers and cₒ=64, with both choices justified in Tab.12. MLP is also an alternative to build the architecture, as shown in Sec.C.1.

    Training

    We train f_Φ using the regression loss on paired hand–object data with synthetic noise applied to the hand pose. The training distribution must place sufficient mass on near-manifold (hard-negative) samples since at inference our projection spends most of its iterations around the narrow band. Hence, we inherit the exponential sampling schedule from [He et al. (2024)] for hands. The exponential distribution assigns higher density to small magnitudes than to large ones, with non-zero density throughout the tail. We also sample the conditioning object over the epochs proportional to the plausible grasps per object provided in the dataset. We provide the full training algorithm in Alg.1.

    5 Experiments

    To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed HaNDF, we conduct experiments on generation, denoising, in-the-wild hand recovery, and hand–object recovery, using task-specific evaluation metrics. We evaluate our method on several datasets, including HOI4D [Liu et al. (2022)], OakInk [Yang et al. (2022)], and DexYCB [Chao et al. (2021)]. We also provide detailed ablation studies on the network architecture, object encoding, and field geometry, along with further analyses of runtime, robustness, and generalization.

    Datasets

    We evaluate our method on three large-scale hand–object interaction datasets. HOI4D[Liu et al. (2022)] provides egocentric RGB-D sequences with dense MANO annotations, object poses, and masks. We follow an object-level split across six rigid categories, using 219 objects (63K poses) to train and 30 unseen objects (7.5K poses) to test. We retain only contact frames. DexYCB[Chao et al. (2021)] contains 1,000 third-person grasp sequences over 21 YCB objects with full MANO and object pose annotations, from which we use the standard s0 split (582K frames). OakInk[Yang et al. (2022)] complements these with diverse hand–object interactions in multi-view RGB sequences. We use sequences from 7 object categories to build our training and test sets, with 53 objects for training and 14 unseen objects for testing. More details in appendixF.

    Baselines

    We compare against three groups of baselines. First, we adapt pose distance-field priors to the hand domain by re-implementing PoseNDF [Tiwari et al. (2022)] and NRDF [He et al. (2024)] on the 15-joint MANO manifold, denoted H-PoseNDF (Euclidean updates with quaternion normalization) and H-NRDF (Riemannian formulation on (S³)¹⁵), both of which are unconditional and serve as direct ablations of our object conditioning. Second, we compare to recent hand and hand–object generative priors, including HMP [Duran et al. (2024)] and object-conditioned models such as G-HOP [Ye et al. (2024)], LatentHOI [Li et al. (2025)], and Text2HOI [Cha et al. (2024)]. Third, for single-image hand recovery, we evaluate against EasyHOI [Liu et al. (2025)], AlignSDF [Chen et al. (2022b)], and IHoI [Ye et al. (2022)], providing ground-truth object geometry to all methods to isolate hand reconstruction, and integrating our method as an object-conditioned refinement prior within EasyHOI and AlignSDF. appendixE provides further information.

    Metrics

    We adopt a unified set of evaluation metrics across all downstream tasks, covering four complementary aspects: realism, distribution fidelity, sample diversity, and pose reconstruction accuracy. All angular metrics are computed on the product manifold (S³)¹⁵ formed by the 15 MANO finger-joint quaternions and reported in degrees; Euclidean metrics are reported in millimeters (mm) or centimeters (cm) as indicated, and F-scores are reported at distance thresholds expressed as percentages of the object’s longest bounding-box half-side. A summary of our metrics are given below and appendixG provides further details:

  • •

    Δ_q: Geodesic rotation error with GT hand across all 15 joints (degrees)

  • •

    dNN: Geodesic distance to nearest GT pose in train set under the same object catogory (degrees)

  • •

    m2m: Mean Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth 3D vertices (mm)

  • •

    MPVPE / MPJPE: Mean per-vertex / per-joint position error on MANO mesh (mm)

  • •

    I.V.: Intersection volume between hand mesh and object mesh (cm3)

  • •

    Chamfer: Chamfer distance between the reconstructed and ground-truth objects in normalized units.

  • •

    FID: Fréchet Inception Distance for pose distribution matching

  • •

    APD: Average pairwise geodesic distance measuring generation diversity (degrees)

    • Generation uses {FID, APD, dNN}; denoising {Δ_q, dNN, m2m}; completion {Δ_q, dNN, APD, FID}; recovery {MPJPE, MPVPE, I.V.}, and {obj-CD, obj-F@τ} when object geometry is optimized.

    5.1 Results on Downstream Tasks

    Grasp pose generation. Given an object instance represented by its canonical geometry O, the goal is to generate hand poses θₕ that plausibly grasp O. A successful generator should produce hand poses that are (i) plausible as natural human grasps, (ii) compatible with the conditioning object’s geometry, and (iii) diverse, covering the many ways a human would naturally grasp the same object.

    As shown in Fig.4, HaNDF lands in the bottom-left of the FID–dNN plane while maintaining a competitive bubble size, dominating both unconditional priors (H-NRDF, H-PoseNDF) and conditional generative baselines. As detailed in Tab.7, our method achieves the best dNN (4.77∘) and a highly competitive FID (0.54), indicating that our generated poses are both realistic and well-aligned with the data distribution. Although H-NRDF also reports low FID (0.77), its much higher dNN reveals limited per-sample realism. Compared to LatentHOI, HaNDF attains substantially higher diversity (APD 12.73∘ vs. 6.01∘) while also improving FID and dNN, demonstrating a better balance between fidelity and diversity. We provide more pose generation results in Sec.D.1.

    Hand pose denoising

    We evaluate our hand pose denoising on the HOI4D test split with novel objects per category. For each clean test pose, we add noise at different levels σ, producing n=3000 noisy samples per σ; identical noisy inputs are fed to all methods to ensure an fair comparison. We report three metrics (lower-is-better for Δ_q, dNN, and m2m). All distance-field methods (HaNDF, H-NRDF, H-PoseNDF) denoise by gradient descent on the learned scalar field for the same iterations with the same step size. Except our method, none of the baselines can consider the object condition. We provide further results with varying object encoders in Sec.D.4, and more hand denosing results can be found in Sec.D.2.

    As shown in Fig.5 (supplemented by Tab.8), HaNDF  achieves the best Δ_q and m2m at every noise level, with margins that widen as σ grows. Most strikingly, HaNDF’s dNN stays nearly constant across the full noise range (4.54^∘→5.20^∘). On dNN, HaNDF dominates from σ≥ 0.8 onward. At the smallest two σ, H-PoseNDF sits slightly closer to the manifold, but at the cost of much higher Δ_q and m2m. This is a mode-collapse signature, where outputs cluster near a few training centroids rather than tracking the input. Qualitative comparisons in Fig.6 and Fig.7 further validate these findings, showing that HaNDF consistently recovers plausible poses.

    Hand completion

    We now evaluate (object-conditioned) hand pose completion on the HOI4D test split under two masking protocols: Missing Fingers, where one of the 5 fingers (3 joints) is randomly masked per sample with the other 12 joints observed at GT; and Missing Finger Parts, where only the 5 finger-base joints are observed and the remaining 10 joints are masked. The masked joints are initialized with the same exponential noise, and n=3000 samples are drawn per task with identical inputs fed to all methods. Inference performs gradient descent on the learned scalar field, updating only the masked joints and keeping observed joints frozen. To isolate completion quality from the trivially-correct observed joints. All metrics are computed on the masked-joint subset including Δ_q, dNN, APD , and FID.

    As reported in Tab.1, HaNDF  achieves the best Δ_q, dNN, and FID on both completion tasks, cutting Δ_q by ∼25% and FID by 3–4× over the strongest baseline (H-NRDF), with even larger gaps against H-PoseNDF and HMP. The unconditional baselines follow a consistent ranking H-NRDF > H-PoseNDF > HMP. Notably, H-NRDF’s gap to HaNDF  widens on Missing Fingers (dNN 8.01∘ vs. 5.44∘) compared to Missing Finger Parts (4.52∘ vs. 3.57∘), highlighting that HaNDF’s object conditioning compensates when more joints anchor the pose.

    Hand-object reconstruction

    Single-image hand–object reconstruction remains a challenging task due to severe mutual occlusion, and serves as a natural downstream application of our prior. Since existing methods adopt heterogeneous object reconstruction pipelines (e.g. EasyHOI [Liu et al. (2025)] relies on LISA + InstantMesh, while AlignSDF [Chen et al. (2022b)] uses a trained implicit SDF), we provide the ground truth object geometry to all methods for a fair comparison and focus the evaluation on hand reconstruction quality. We reserve optimizing for the object (shape recovery) to Sec.5.2. We retrain and evaluate all methods on HOI4D, DexYCB, and OakInk under this unified protocol. To validate the effectiveness of our prior, we plug HaNDF into two representative baselines, EasyHOI and AlignSDF, as an object-conditioned hand prior that refines their hand results.

    As shown quantitatively in Tab.2 and qualitatively in Fig.8, integrating HaNDF consistently improves two baselines across all three datasets. In particular, HaNDF (AlignSDF-based) achieves the best MPVPE, MPJPE, and intersection volume on most benchmarks, demonstrating that our prior provides a strong and generalizable regularization for hand reconstruction under occlusion. We provide more in-the-wild hand recovery results in Sec.D.3.

    Tab.3 compares hand-object recovery on the HOI4D test set, using AlignSDF [Chen et al. (2022b)] as the baseline. Starting from AlignSDF’s predictions, applying HaNDF as a denoiser substantially improves hand reconstruction quality, reducing Δq from 14.77 to 9.60, MPJPE from 12.08 to 11.74, and MPVPE from 11.90 to 11.52. This confirms that the learned hand prior, conditioned on the predicted object, effectively refines noisy hand outputs. We further refine the object mesh by retrieving the nearest neighbor in the DeepSDF latent space (with PCA), which not only improves object reconstruction (obj-F@2% from 0.1187 to 0.1568) but also further boosts hand quality (MPJPE: 11.74 → 11.50, MPVPE: 11.52 → 11.30). With additional object recovery (as shown in Alg.2) with K=8 optimization, we observe better hand performance, with slight worse object metrics. This experiment validates that better object reconstruction directly translates into better hand reconstruction, closing the loop between the two modalities.

    5.2 Ablation Studies

    Architecture We provide ablations on model architecture, conditioning, and the geometry of the neural field. As shown in Tab.4, Riemannian geometry achieves a large performance gain, and object conditioning also improves performance for both MLPs and Transformers. With object conditioning and a Riemannian field, the MLP-based model also achieves comparable performance.

    Object Conditioning To verify that HaNDF indeed exploits the object as a meaningful condition rather than treating it as a nuisance input, we compare three variants in Tab.5. “Wrong condition” replaces the input object with a randomly sampled one from a different category, while “w/o object token” removes the object token from the model and retrains it with all other settings unchanged. Feeding a wrong object increases the joint-angle error, and removing the object token leads to an even larger drop in performance. These gaps confirm that HaNDF effectively leverages the object condition to guide hand denoising.

    5.3 Runtime Analysis

    To verify the runtime efficiency of the proposed HaNDF, we compare the time required to generate a single sample against LatentHOI [Li et al. (2025)] in Tab.6. The experiment is done a single NVIDIA L40S GPU. Our proposed HaNDF (i) given the same iterations, can generate poses with substantially better FID and dNN scores faster than LatentHOI, and (ii) can match the LatentHOI metrics quicker, enabling less iterations and hence even quicker runtime. We provide more details and analysis on the inference in Sec.D.7

    6 Conclusion

    We presented HaNDF, an object-conditioned neural distance field for hand articulation on Riemannian manifolds. Coupled with manifold-aware optimization, the learned geometric prior supports denoising, completion, generation, and reconstruction. It can consistently improve robustness and physical plausibility across challenging benchmarks. More broadly, our results suggest that HaNDF provide a promising direction for learning structured interaction priors beyond Euclidean latent representations.

    Limitations and future work

    Our method relies on reasonably accurate object geometry and is not a true grasp prior as we do not model a hand-object joint NDF. Such an extension must account for the different geometries of hand rotations and object latents, along with their different noise scales and optimization step sizes, and may also need to incorporate hand–object contact dynamics. We will also extend our hand prior to bimanual interactions, as well as investigating more efficient training strategies. Finally, our model can be extended to the dynamic setting in a similar vein to NRMF [Yu et al. (2026)]. More future work analysis are shown in appendixH.

    Appendix

    Appendix A Riemannian Geometry

    Let M be a smooth m-dimensional manifold embedded in an ambient Euclidean space X=ℝᵈ. For x∈M, the tangent spaceTₓM is the set of all velocity vectors of smooth curves passing through x:

    TₓM={γ̇(0) \middle| γ:ℝ→M, γ(0)=x, γsmooth}.

    A Riemannian metricG assigns every x∈M an inner product ⟨u,v⟩ₓ=u^⊤Gₓv for u,v∈TₓM, varying smoothly with x. The pair (M,G) is a Riemannian manifold. For a smooth f:M→ℝ, the Riemannian gradientgrad f(x)∈TₓM is defined as the unique tangent vector satisfying

    Df(x)[v]=⟨v,grad f(x)⟩ₓ, ∀v∈TₓM.

    		(19)

    For M⊆X and f implemented for example by a neural network, automatic differentiation gives the Euclidean gradient ∇f(x)∈ℝᵈ. The intrinsic gradient is obtained by projecting onto TₓM:

    grad f(x)=Πₓ(∇f(x)),

    		(20)

    where Πₓ:ℝᵈ→TₓM is the orthogonal projection. This egrad-to-rgrad[6] conversion is the key enabler of our distance field operators. A Riemannian gradient step from x along a tangent vector ξ∈TₓM is performed by mapping ξ back to the manifold, ideally via the exponential mapExpₓ:TₓM→M, yielding Riemannian gradient descent[6, 5] (RGD) of the form

    xₜ₊₁=Exp_xₜ(-τₜ grad f(xₜ)),

    		(21)

    where τₜ>0 is a step size, which can often be adaptively computed, e.g., via line search.

    Appendix B The Rotation Group SO(3)

    For the sake of being self contained, we now present the space of 3D rotations as a Riemannian manifold, the special orthogonal group:

    SO(3)={R∈ℝ^3×3 \middle| R^⊤R=I, \det(R)=1}.

    		(22)

    Its Lie algebra is the vector space of skew-symmetric matrices:

    so(3)={Ω∈ℝ^3×3 \middle| Ω^⊤=-Ω}.

    		(23)

    For Ω=(ω₁,ω₂,ω₃)^⊤∈ℝ³, define the hat operator [·]_× so that [Ω]_×x=Ω×x for all x∈ℝ³:

    [Ω]_×=\beginbmatrix0&-ω₃&ω₂ ω₃&0&-ω₁ -ω₂&ω₁&0\endbmatrix,

    		(24)

    The inverse map is denoted by vee(·): vee([Ω]_×)=Ω. The tangent space of SO(3) at R is

    T_RSO(3)={RΩ \middle| Ω∈so(3)}.

    		(25)

    Indeed, for a smooth curve R(t)∈SO(3) with R(0)=R, differentiating the constraint R(t)^⊤R(t)=I gives Ṙ(0)^⊤R+R^⊤Ṙ(0)=0. Thus R^⊤Ṙ(0) is skew-symmetric, and every tangent vector can be written as Ṙ=RΩ for some Ω∈so(3). Using the Frobenius inner product ⟨A,B⟩_F=Tr(A^⊤B), the Riemannian gradient of f:SO(3)→ℝ can be obtained from the Euclidean gradient ∇f(R) by

    grad f(R)=R \skewrm(R^⊤∇f(R)), where \skewrm (A)=1/2(A-A^⊤).

    		(26)

    This projection removes the normal component and keeps only the component tangent to SO(3). The exponential map on SO(3) is

    Exp_R(RΩ)=R\exp(Ω),

    		(27)

    where \exp(Ω) is the matrix exponential. If Ω=[Ω]_× and ϑ=∥Ω∥₂, Rodrigues’ formula gives

    \exp(Ω)=I+(\sinϑ)/(ϑ)Ω+(1-\cosϑ)/(ϑ²)Ω².

    		(28)

    The logarithmic map is the local inverse Log_R₁(R₂)=R₁\log(R₁^⊤R₂), where \log(·) is the matrix logarithm. The geodesic distance between rotations is

    d_SO(3)(R₁,R₂)=∥\log(R₁^⊤R₂)∥ₛₒ₍₃₎=\cos⁻¹((Tr(R₁^⊤R₂)-1)/(2)).

    		(29)

    These matrix expressions are useful conceptually, but for articulated hands we use unit quaternions because they provide a computationally convenient representation for gradient-based optimization.

    Appendix C Implementation Details

    C.1 Model Architecture

    Our HaNDF applies a transformer encoder that processes hand and object tokens jointly. The architecture details are:

  • 1.

    Hand token projection: Linear layer ℝ⁴→ℝ²⁵⁶ for each quaternion

  • 2.

    Object token projection: Linear layer ℝ⁶⁴→ℝ²⁵⁶ for the single object token

  • 3.

    [DIST] token: Learnable embedding ∈ℝ²⁵⁶ to aggregrate information

  • 4.

    Positional encoding: Learnable positional embeddings for all tokens

    • As illustrated in Fig. 9, HaNDF adopts a multi-head transformer as its backbone by default. The 15 hand tokens, the object token, and a learnable distance token are concatenated and jointly processed by the backbone. The output distance token is then fed into a lightweight head to predict the final distance.

    MLPs are also applicable as the backbone network for HaNDF, offering faster convergence at the cost of slightly degraded performance (as shown in Tab.4). However, this performance gap does not necessarily preclude their applicability to downstream tasks, and in some cases MLP-based HaNDF can still achieve competitive results.

    C.2 Training Algorithm

    The algorithm to train HaNDF is as follow:

    The training dataset normally stores data in the form of sequences, where we first get the object-hand pairs for interacting actions in the dataset to build the training set. Specifically, for each object Oⱼ, we first fit DeepSDF to obtain the object code zⱼ with 500 optimization steps, and we store the object code together with each hand pose under that object as a pair (θ_j,n,zⱼ,j), which serves as one training sample later. Note that for HOI4D and OakInk, we split the dataset based on objects, which means that the objects used during evaluation never appear during training. After constructing the training set, we sweep through the training samples to add perturbation noise based on an exponential distribution ℙ, and calculate the dNN between the noisy pose and all clean poses for that specific object to get the training label.

    C.3 Object Recovery

    Alg.2 summarizes the object recovery and hand refinement procedure. We first fit PCA to the mean-centred object codes in training set and retain the top-d principal directions to define the retrieval space. For each of the K candidates, we initialize an object latent code from ℕ(0,0.01²I) and optimize it using the fixed DeepSDF decoder. Specifically, we minimize the squared predicted SDF values at the input object surface points, whose target SDF values are zero. We then project the fitted code and the training codes into PCA space and retrieve the nearest training code as our retrieved object code.

    Starting from the initial hand pose, we apply T_c Riemannian updates conditioned on each retrieved object code. Our candidate selection is motivated by the intuition that a compatible object should require relatively little correction of the initial hand pose. To evaluate this, we record the predicted HaNDF distances before and after refinement. We take their logarithms and standardize the initial and final values separately across the K candidates. We then select the candidate object code with the smallest difference between its standardized initial and final distances. We finally refine hand with this selected object code. Quantitative results are shown in Tab.3.

    Appendix D Additional Results

    D.1 Quantitative hand pose generation results

    We evaluate hand pose generation on the HOI4D dataset using FID, APD, and dNN. The reults on Tab.7 corresponds to visualization in Fig.4 .

    As shown in Tab.7, HaNDF achieves the best FID (0.5466) and dNN (4.77∘) scores, indicating that our generated poses most closely match the real data distribution while maintaining high fidelity. Although HMP attains a higher APD, this comes at the cost of substantially worse FID and dNN, suggesting that its diversity stems from generating implausible poses rather than capturing the true pose manifold. Overall, HaNDF strikes the best balance between fidelity and diversity among all competing methods.

    D.2 More results on hand denoising

    Quantitative evaluation

    Tab.8 provides the per-σ breakdown underlying Fig.5. HaNDF achieves the best Δ_q and m2m at all three noise levels, with widening margins as σ grows (Δ_q: 3.67^∘/5.52^∘/8.00^∘; m2m: 4.38/6.58/10.08), while its dNN remains nearly constant (4.74^∘ → 5.20^∘) and becomes the lowest from σ ≥ 0.8. H-PoseNDF’s marginally lower d_NN at σ = 0.4 (3.81^∘) is offset by substantially worse Δ_q (5.67^∘) and m2m (6.62), evidencing mode collapse rather than better denoising. HMP trails all distance-field methods across every metric.

    In addition to the quantitative metrics presented in Tab.8, we provide extended qualitative evaluations of our pose denoising method. Due to space constraints in the main manuscript, we present the remainder of our visual results here.

    More qualitative results

    Fig.10 showcases further examples of the iterative denoising process. Starting from highly corrupted initial states, it is evident that over 1000 steps, HaNDF successfully resolves penetrations and guides the hand toward physically plausible, tight grasps across diverse object topologies.

    Furthermore, Fig.11 provides additional baseline comparisons for the denoising task. Consistent with our main findings, our method produces hand-object configurations that align more accurately with the ground truth manifold, avoiding the artifacts observed in HMP and H-NRDF.

item.title: 别只切「语义部件」：这篇专攻 3D 网格中间的「几何纹理」分割，VLM 直接问是问不出来的 ｜ Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes
item.description:
一句话：现有 3D 分割偏语义部件、VLM 又看不懂几何纹理；中间这一层长期缺位。

要点：

  • 需求侧：识别 3D 模型上的**几何纹理**（如雕花、编织、褶皱这类中尺度结构）对文物保护、模型编辑与 3D 打印都很关键
  • 现有 3D 分割方法主要识别高层语义部件，捕捉不到这类「中间层纹理」；而近期 VLM 在图像分割上强，但对 3D 几何纹理仍然吃力
  • 这篇因此直接针对几何纹理做分割，而不是把它们当作语义部件的一部分

为什么值得看：UV 与材质管线最怕的就是「同一块几何上同时有结构与纹理」。把几何纹理单独切出来，意味着可以做针对性重拓扑、法线与材质编辑——这是资产重构里长期靠手工的一步。

中文摘要：识别 3D 模型上的**几何纹理**（雕花、编织、褶皱这类中尺度结构）在文物保护、模型编辑与 3D 打印等场景都很关键。但现有 3D 模型分割方法主要面向高层语义部件，捕捉不到这类「中间层」的纹理；而近期视觉语言模型虽然在图像分割上表现很强，对 3D 几何纹理仍难胜任。这篇因此专门针对 3D 网格的几何纹理做分割，把这一层从语义部件里独立出来。对 UV 与材质管线而言，能单独切出几何纹理，就能做针对性的重拓扑与法线/材质编辑。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes

Abstract

Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.

1 Introduction

Geometric textures/patterns constitute local, repetitive geometric variations across a 3D surface, remaining independent of the global model structure [BTB∗18, PTB∗25]. High-quality 3D models featuring intricate geometric textures are typically acquired via physical scanning or manual design (see Figure 1). These assets drive critical downstream applications, ranging from digital twins and heritage preservation to immersive gaming and 3D printing [XHW∗26]. Effective recognition of geometric textures is therefore essential, facilitating cultural heritage analysis (e.g., reassembling fragmented artifacts [BTB∗18]) and enabling texture-aware 3D editing workflows. However, current practice relies heavily on manual inspection and laborious analysis by users or modelers, which is both time-consuming and inefficient.

However, existing model analysis and segmentation methods predominantly operate either at high-level semantics [HHF∗19, VPP∗23] or at low-level geometric features (e.g., curvature, normals, and noise) [WGS∗18, GKOM18], often failing to capture the intricate patterns of middle-level geometric textures. While professional tools like ZBrush facilitate interactive, local modifications, they lack the capability for holistic, global editing of regions characterized by specific texture patterns in a single pass. Consequently, despite growing research interest in recognizing and editing geometric textures on 3D surfaces [GDJ∗25], a robust and comprehensive solution remains an open challenge.

In this work, we propose a framework for geometric texture recognition on 3D surface models. Leveraging a 2D-to-3D paradigm, our method begins by rendering multi-view images from the input 3D mesh. We then employ a visual segmentation model fine-tuned on our newly constructed benchmark to identify texture regions within the rendered images. Corresponding features are extracted from these segmented patches and clustered into semantic groups. Subsequently, we introduce a weighted voting strategy to fuse these 2D predictions and lift them into a coherent 3D segmentation. Finally, we adopt a filter-based geometric editing technique and develop an interactive tool that enables users to perform holistic, one-pass editing of specific texture patterns on the 3D model based on the segmentation results. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A texture material dataset and a geometric texture segmentation benchmark. The datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/ALingll/GTSeg;

  • •

    A geometric texture segmentation method for 3D meshes, based on multi-view rendering and visual foundation models;

  • •

    An interactive, texture-oriented 3D model editing tool, supporting model segmentation and retrieval as well as geometric texture enhancement, removal, and transfer.

    • 2 Related Works

    Geometric Texture over 3D model surfaces are high-frequency, repetitive surface details distinct from global shape and random noise (excluding hollowing and winding structures). Existing research on geometric textures mainly focused on synthesis and interactive editing. Early works established procedural and example-based methods for texture synthesis [BIT04, Elb05, ZXZD24], a direction recently advanced by deep generative models [HHGCO20, YCK∗25]. Complementarily, editing tools have evolved from manual manipulation of displacement maps [LHGM] to recent texture generation based on the vision-language model [MWS∗25]. However, as the prerequisite for automated analysis and editing, the fundamental problem of geometric texture recognition and segmentation is significantly less explored. Several studies have attempted to bridge this gap. One direction is to separate texture and non-texture regions using learning-based methods [GDJ∗24, PTB24]. Tortorici et al. [TBOW21] introduced a convolution-based descriptor for recognizing user-specific textures.

    Despite these efforts, current methods still exhibit poor generalization when dealing with multiple textures, multi-scale structures, and complex topologies. To the best of our knowledge, an open-source benchmark, a robust and automated solution for geometric texture segmentation and recognition that handles diverse and complex patterns over a complicated model, is still missing in the literature [BTB∗18, PTB∗25].

    Model Segmentation is an essential task in computer graphics and vision. Early methods mainly rely on low-level geometric primitives such as curvature, surface normals, and geodesic distances to partition 3D models, including region growing [LYW∗20], graph cuts [KT03], spectral clustering, and MRF/CRF-based optimization [Sha08]. Although these methods perform stably on segmenting homogeneous low-level geometric regions (e.g., planar surfaces, smooth curved patches), they fail to capture high-frequency, repetitive geometric patterns that define geometric textures. Recent deep learning works focus on semantic or part-level segmentation. For native 3D representations, point cloud networks (e.g., PointNet [QSMG17, QYSG17], DGCNN[WSL∗19]) and mesh-based networks [HHF∗19] achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks such as ShapeNet Part[CFG∗15] and PartNet[MZC∗19]. However, these methods are limited to coarse-grained category or part labels (e.g., separating chair legs from seats) and cannot recognize fine-grained geometric textures [YLX∗24, XYQ∗25, LUX∗25]. Recent works following a 2D-to-3D pipeline, leverage pre-trained 2D foundation models (e.g., SAM [KMR∗23], CLIP [CLZ∗25]) to project multi-view 2D predictions back to 3D [ZXL∗24, TZF∗24b, TCC∗26, ZHR∗26]. While these methods enable open-vocabulary segmentation, they still focus on semantic object categories rather than geometric texture patterns.

    To the best of our knowledge, the segmentation of geometric textures on 3D models remains an open problem [PTB∗25]. Current attempts indicate that image-like local descriptors offer the most promising solution for geometric texture recognition and segmentation [BTB∗18]. Hence, we borrow the ability from the visual foundation model and employ the 2D-to-3D pipeline to address this problem.

    Image Segmentation aims to partition an image into regions that are coherent in semantics, instance identity, or visual attributes. Earlier deep segmentation methods primarily focus on dense prediction and instance mask modeling [LSD15, RFB15, HGDG17]. Recent segmentation research has increasingly shifted toward unified and promptable foundation models. MaskFormer and Mask2Former cast semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation as mask classification [CSK21, CMS∗22]. SAM3 introduces strong promptable concept segmentation, enabling the detection and segmentation of all instances matching a text or exemplar concept [CGH∗25]. SAMesh lifts multi-view SAM2 masks onto mesh surfaces for zero-shot mesh part segmentation [TZF∗24b]. These studies suggest that SAM-family models are effective front-ends for 3D model segmentation. Recently, textureSAM validates the zero-shot capability of SAM in 2D texture segmentation after fine-tuning with sufficient training data [CMT∗26].

    However, unlike the 2D textures provided by TextureSAM, the identical geometric texture can look dramatically different across viewpoints, which implies the critical role of proper training data and geometric constraints. Therefore, in this work, we do not directly treat 2D masks as the final predictions; instead, we leverage both image and geometry evidence, combining curvature re-rendering, mask-level texture-feature clustering, and multi-view 3D voting to obtain view-consistent geometric texture segmentation.

    3 Geometric Texture Segmentation Benchmark

    To begin, we construct a large-scale geometric texture segmentation benchmark, consisting of synthetic and annotated 3D models. Collecting reconstructed models through scanning is extremely expensive and labor-intensive. Instead, we choose to sculpt 3D models via texture displacement maps, see Figure 2.

    Texture Displacement Maps Dataset. We use Chord [YRWX25] to generate displacement maps based on the open-source 2D texture images dataset DTD [CMK∗14]. We construct a displacement map dataset, TDSet, consisting of 350 diverse displacement maps. The displacement maps in TDSet are employed to synthesize 3D geometric textures over 3D models.

    3D Geometric Texture Benchmark. Next, we construct a geometric texture benchmark called GTSeg, which consists of a training set and a test set. For the training set, we collect 80 synthetic models from Thingi10K [ZJ16]. We randomly select four or five displacement maps from TDSet and apply them to the surface of each model. All geometric texture instances are automatically annotated. For each model, we repeat this process ten times. The final training set consists of 800 models, each with multiple geometric texture categories and instances. Moreover, we construct a test set comprising 20 synthetic models generated following the above procedure (with no overlap with the training set) and 10 real scans from [XZZ∗14] and public domain. We manually annotate the geometric texture instances on the real scans.

    4 Geometric Texture-oriented Image Segmentation Model

    In this section, we develop a 2D image segmentation model specifically for segmenting 3D geometric textures. We first justify our choice of representation, and subsequently detail the training dataset construction pipeline and the model fine-tuning protocol.

    Although recent advancements have made significant progress in texture-aware 2D image segmentation, they cannot be directly generalized to 3D geometric texture recognition. TextureSAM [CMT∗26] mitigates the semantic bias of foundation models by fine-tuning on 2D RGB images where object regions are synthetically replaced with descriptive visual textures. In contrast, 3D geometric textures lack explicit colors and depend solely on local topographic variations. Furthermore, the 2D projection of the same 3D geometric pattern exhibits severe perspective distortions and foreshortening across different viewing angles. Consequently, without explicit adaptation to intrinsic 3D geometry and multi-view consistency, models constrained to 2D visual priors inevitably fail to achieve view-consistent segmentation of complex 3D surface patterns.

    Grayscale Curvature and Mask Rendering. Surface curvature is an intrinsic geometric property that remains strictly invariant to lighting conditions and rigid transformations. To bridge 3D geometry with 2D segmentation, we compute per-vertex mean curvature as the raw scalar sᵢ. To mitigate the impact of mesh singularities and ensure high image contrast, we clip outliers according to the 5th/95th percentiles. The curvature values are then normalized to [0,1] via min-max normalization.

    Here, we split the models in the training set of GTSeg into two sets: 76 models are used for training and 4 for validation. We rendered each model to generate curvature maps and ground-truth masks from 14 uniformly sampled viewpoints. That is to say, the training set contains 10,640 image and mask pairs, while the validation set contains 560 image and mask pairs. All rendered views and synthesized variants derived from the same source model are assigned to the same split to prevent data leakage. Finally, we generate a dataset of 11,200 pairs of view-dependent curvature maps and corresponding ground-truth masks. The training set will be employed to adapt the vision foundation model to our task later.

    Model Fine-tuning. While the pre-trained SAM3 model demonstrates strong zero-shot capabilities in general concept segmentation, it struggles to precisely delineate non-semantic, mid-level geometric textures. To efficiently bridge this domain gap without catastrophic forgetting, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [HSW∗22] to fine-tune the model on our synthesized dataset and obtain GTSAM.

    The recognition of geometric textures relies heavily on mid-level patterns rather than high-level linguistic concepts. Hence, we freeze the entire language encoder to preserve general semantic priors and reduce computational overhead. To this end, we inject trainable rank-decomposition matrices into the Vision Encoder, Geometry Encoder, and the decoding modules. This targeted injection maximizes the model’s sensitivity to high-frequency textural signals while maintaining its robust zero-shot foundation.

    5 Geometric Texture-oriented Model Segmentation

    In this section, we introduce a framework to address the problem of geometric texture segmentation, via formulating it as a task of multi-view consistency perception. The overview of our framework is visualized in Figure 3.

    Given a 3D mesh M, we first render a set of grayscale curvature maps {Cᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N from a collection of predefined camera poses {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. Subsequently, the rendered images are fed to our GTSAM to predict a set of pixel-level geometric texture masks. We introduce a feature association module based on DINOv2 to maintain semantic consistency across disparate views. This module extracts and clusters high-dimensional feature descriptors from each mask, thereby establishing label correspondences across different viewpoints in a unified latent space. Finally, multi-view masks with consistent labels are projected onto the model surface M. To resolve prediction conflicts arising from occlusions or perspective distortions, we implement a spatial-consistency weighted voting mechanism. This mechanism performs per-face arbitration to make definitive label decisions, yielding precise and smooth geometric texture segmentation results.

    5.1 Texture-oriented Image Segmentation

    We set N cameras to render the input mesh, ensuring complete coverage and sufficient overlap. In our implementation, we let N=50. The t-th camera renders a curvature image Iₜ. Next, we send the rendered curvature images to our GTSAM. For Iₜ, GTSAM predicts a set of Nₜ instance masks. Each instance mask M_t,m is paired with a confidence score c_t,m∈[0,1].

    For each predicted mask M_t,m, we perform 8-connected component analysis. Components with an area smaller than the threshold A_\min are discarded. We retain those sufficiently large connected components and treat them as independent mask instances. This prevents disconnected 2D regions from being merged into the same texture cluster.

    5.2 Feature-based Patch Clustering.

    Although GTSAM produces high-quality class-agnostic masks {M_t,m}, these masks are generated independently for each view and lack explicit semantic correspondence. To assign accurate instance labels to disparate views, we leverage DINOv2 as a robust feature extractor. It’s capable of achieving cross-view semantic consistency in the absence of per-view labels [DHM∗25].

    Region Re-rendering. After that, we project each mask component onto the mesh. The set of faces covered by the mask component Cₐ is denoted as Pₐ. We discard mask components that contain very few faces and store the remaining components as a group.

    To extract a view-normalized texture descriptor, we re-render each projected region. The region center and average normal are estimated as:

    oₐ=(1)/(|V(Pₐ)|)∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)vᵢ, nₐ=(∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)nᵢ)/(∥∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)nᵢ∥₂).

    		(1)

    An orthographic camera is then placed along nₐ and oriented toward oₐ, producing a local curvature rendering Jₐ for the mask instance.

    Next, we extract the DINOv2 patch tokens of local curvature rendering Jₐ[ODM∗24]. The visible region is cropped and resized to a fixed resolution. Each rendered view is augmented with rotations (0^∘, 90^∘, 180^∘, and 270^∘) and horizontal flip. We then generate patch tokens using DINOv2 for each augmented view. The region mask is down-sampled to the DINO patch grid, and the tokens covered by the mask are sampled to create a token pool: Tₐ={ẑ_a,1,…,ẑ_a,Kₐ}. Each token is normalized into a unit vector.

    Consistency Filtering. To eliminate masks that contain inconsistent textures, we compute a consistency score γₐ for each Jₐ. This score is defined as the median similarity between each local feature ẑ_a,i and the normalized average feature direction of the entire mask. The score is formulated as:

    γₐ=medianᵢ((ẑ_a,i^⊤∑ⱼẑ_a,j)/(∥∑ⱼẑ_a,j∥₂)).

    		(2)

    We eliminate masks with γₐ smaller than a predefined threshold τₛ. In our implementation, we let τₛ=0.65. Two masks of the Merlion example are provided in Figure 4. The mask on the left contains only one geometry texture, therefore exhibits high consistency. Meanwhile, the mask on the right is eliminated since it contains two types of texture, which deliver a consistency score smaller than the threshold.

    Feature Clustering. To merge instances representing the same geometric texture, for each pair of mask instances Jₐ and J_b, we compute a token-token similarity matrix Sᵃᵇᵢⱼ=ẑ_a,i^⊤ẑ_b,j. We utilize bidirectional top-k matching to reduce the sensitivity to boundary tokens and partial occlusions. Specifically, we first identify the maximum matching scores along both directions: uᵢ=\maxⱼSᵃᵇᵢⱼ and vⱼ=\maxᵢSᵃᵇᵢⱼ. The pairwise instance similarity is then defined as the average of the top-k mean values from both sets:

    sim(a,b)=1/2[TopKMeanₖ({uᵢ}ᵢ)+TopKMeanₖ({vⱼ}ⱼ)].

    		(3)

    To segment geometric texture instances, we not only consider the similarity of the rendered textures, but also consider their connectivity over the surface. We store the disconnected regions with the same pattern as different texture instances. We first construct a mutual-kNN graph G over all valid mask instances [YZZW24]. The nearest neighbors k of a are denoted as ℕₖ(a). We create an edge between a and b if they are mutual neighbors (b∈ℕₖ(a) and a∈ℕₖ(b)) and their similarity satisfies sim(a,b)≥τ_clu. Subsequently, the raw mask clusters {ℚᵣ} are obtained by extracting the connected components of G, formulated as {ℚᵣ}=CC(G).

    To refine the clusters, we calculate a cluster support score for each mask a∈ℚ, defined as the median similarity to its cluster peers: ρₐ=median_b∈ℚ,b≠asim(a,b). Low-support members are split into singleton clusters. Finally, the mask confidence used for 3D voting is reweighted by incorporating its internal consistency γₐ and cluster support ρₐ:

    ŝₐ=\max(s_\min,sₐγₐ^αρₐ^β).

    		(4)

    In our implementation, we let k=8 for the bidirectional top-k matching, k=5 for the mutual-kNN graph construction, and τ_clu=0.8. For the confidence reweighting, we set α=1.0, β=1, and s_\min=0.25. A visualization of the resulting mask clusters is shown in Figure 5.

    5.3 Mask Fusion by 3D Voting

    To fuse the 2D mask clusters {ℚᵣ} into the 3D mesh, we project the masks onto the mesh surface and accumulate votes on the visible faces. For a mask Cₐ∈ℚᵣ and a view tₐ, a mesh face f will receive a positive weight w₊ when its projected face center falls inside Cₐ, and will receive a negative penalty -w₋ otherwise. This vote is further scaled by the mask confidence score csₐ and an angular weight \cos(θ_a,f), where θ_a,f is the angle between the face normal and the viewing direction. The raw voting score is accumulated as:

    V_r,fʳᵃʷ=∑_a∈V_r,fcₐ\cos(θ_a,f)·W(a,f),

    		(5)

    where V_r,f⊆ℚᵣ denote the subset of masks from which face f is visible, W(a,f)=w₊ if the projected face center of f lies inside mask Cₐ, and -w₋ otherwise. To avoid bias toward frequently observed regions, the raw score is averaged by the visibility count, yielding the final score:

    V_r,f=(V_r,fʳᵃʷ)/(\max(1,|V_r,f|)).

    		(6)

    A face is assigned to cluster r if its average score V_r,f>τ_V and it accumulates at least n_\min⁺ positive hits. Face-label conflicts are resolved by weighted voting. When a face receives positive votes from multiple texture clusters, the cluster with the highest accumulated normalized score is selected.

    Finally, we refine the assignments by extracting the connected components over the 3D mesh and discarding isolated components whose area is smaller than a minimum value. Ultimately, we get a set of 3D instances {ℙᵣ} from {Qᵣ}. In our implement, we set w₊=2.0, w₋=1.0 and n_\min⁺=3.

    Finally, different initial 3D parts may correspond to the same physical region due to different perspectives. We therefore merge parts that exhibit strong spatial overlap. For any two 3D semantic parts ℙₐ and ℙ_b, we calculate their 3D Intersection-over-Union (IoU) as IoU(a,b)=|ℙₐ∩ℙ_b|/|ℙₐ∪ℙ_b|, where |·| denotes the number of mesh faces.

    If IoU(a,b)≥τᵢₒᵤ, the two parts are connected in a region-adjacency graph. We set a threshold of τᵢₒᵤ=0.8 to ensure that only highly overlapping parts are merged. The final non-overlapping 3D regions, denoted as {ℙₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, are obtained by extracting the connected components of this graph.

    The first row of Figure 8 shows the final result on the Merlion example. The resulting face regions are rendered with distinct colors. The result indicates that our method effectively recognizes all the distinct geometric textures over the model. Even the text on the base is successfully segmented.

    6 Applications

    Geometric Texture Enhancement and Removal. For model editing, normal filters are capable of removing all the high-frequency local characteristics, such as noises [ZDZ∗15, XZSJ18]. Specifically, the static/dynamic filter effectively identifies all the relief structures over the model surface, without recognizing their higher-level patterns. Based on our segmentation results, we employ the static/dynamic filter to interactively enhance or remove a specific type of geometric texture over the model (see Figure ). Our segmentation method dramatically improves editing efficiency.

    Geometric Texture Replacement. After removing the user-specific geometric texture instance, the user can select an arbitrary texture from our DTSet, and apply it to the target region to achieve replacement of geometric texture (see Figure ).

    Model Retrieval. Effective retrieval of the reconstructed model that shares similar geometric texture is critical for the projection and restoration of the heritage. The query in Figure  is the brick wall texture of Merlion. The retrieval is performed among four models. For each model, we performed segmentation and extracted the DINOv2 feature tokens of all the texture instances. Then, we measure the similarity between all the texture instances and the target (Eq. 3), returning the model that contains the texture instance with the highest similarity.

    7 Experimental Results

    7.1 Ablation Study

    Firstly, we evaluate the contribution of three key components. The LoRA-adapted SAM3 is replaced with the original zero-shot model. Next, the step of feature-based association is removed from the framework. All the masks are grouped solely according to the overlap of their projected 3D regions. Then, feature-based association is removed from the framework, and masks are grouped solely according to the overlap of their projected 3D regions. The experimental results are shown in Table 1. For all quantitative evaluations, the results are presented as percentages.

    The results indicate that replacing the fine-tuned model with zero-shot SAM3 brings the largest degradation in segmentation accuracy. Removing feature-based clustering also substantially reduces performance. Consistency filtering provides a further improvement over the unfiltered variant. The complete method consistently achieves the best performance across all metrics. Overall, the results demonstrate that all three components are necessary for accurate and reliable 3D geometric-texture instance segmentation.

    7.2 Comparisons on Image Segmentation

    We compare the results of segmentation on rendered curvature maps with zero-shot SAM3 [CGH∗25] and TextureSAM [CMT∗26]. SAM3 and our methods are given the identical prompt: “repetitive pattern”, in all experiments.

    Figure  6 qualitatively illustrates the performance of our method compared to the methods described above in wild examples. We performed quantitative evaluation on the GTSeg test set. Statistics are provided in Table 2. To comprehensively assess both semantic and instance-level quality, we adopt mIoU and Dice coefficient to measure overall spatial overlap, Precision and Recall for pixel-level exactness, and Average Precision (AP, AP₅₀, AP₇₅) for instance-level localization accuracy.

    As shown in Table 2, our fine-tuned SAM3 significantly outperforms all baseline methods on every metric. Specifically, while TextureSAM achieves a high Recall (0.913), its excessively low Precision (0.129) and mIoU (0.128) indicate severe over-segmentation and massive false positives, rendering its instance-level AP scores negligible. The SAM3 demonstrates solid foundational capability with an mIoU of 0.669; however, its performance degrades drastically under stricter boundary criteria (AP₅₀ drops to 0.124), indicating its struggle with precise boundary adherence required by the GTSeg domain. In contrast, our fine-tuned SAM3 effectively bridges this domain gap, achieving a state-of-the-art mIoU of 0.933 and a Dice score of 0.965. Most notably, our method maintains exceptional accuracy under strict intersection thresholds, boosting the Mean AP from 0.218 to 0.890 and AP₇₅ from 0.124 to 0.831. These results demonstrate that our fine-tuning strategy retains the strong recall of the foundation model while drastically improving its precision and boundary localization.

    7.3 Comparisons on Model Segmentation

    We collect 12 models reconstructed from real objects from public resources [BWHSH25] and synthetic models from SHREC’25 examples  [PTB24], with various resolutions, functions, complexities, and semantics. Their geometric textures cover diverse scales, structures, and shapes with open boundaries.

    Qualitative Evaluation. We compare our segmentation results with ShapeDiameter [SSCO08] and SAMesh [TZF∗24a]. Figure 7 shows a qualitative comparison of three unlabeled models from SHREC’25. Figure 8 and Figure 9 further compare the performance of these methods on real scans.

    ShapeDiameter relies on volumetric thickness and global shape structure, making it insensitive to fine-grained surface-level texture boundaries, particularly when textured patterns are shallow, repetitive, or confined to the same semantic part. SAMesh offers better flexibility by projecting 2D segmentation onto 3D meshes, but its behavior is dominated by object/part-level visual priors, leading to cross-view inconsistencies when texture elements share similar semantic appearance, yet differ geometrically. Our method addresses these limitations by using curvature renderings as input, directing segmentation toward intrinsic surface variation rather than color, illumination, or semantic category. Combined with mask-level clustering and multi-view voting, it produces coherent, view-consistent regions for repeated geometric patterns and resolves texture boundaries defined by subtle local surface relief. These comparisons confirm that conventional mesh segmentation and general 2D-to-3D pipelines are insufficient for geometric texture segmentation, and that curvature-based representation with texture-aware clustering provides a more suitable formulation.

    Quantitative Evaluation. We compute two metrics for all mesh vertices to assess the quality of the segmentation results: i) MUCoV, which quantifies the overall region-wise overlap between the predicted segments and the ground truth; and ii) Recall50, which measures the which measures the fraction of ground-truth instances correctly identified with an IoU threshold of 50% [RZ17, LMB∗14]. The statistics are reported in Table 3. The segmentation results of our method achieve the best MUCoV and Recall₅₀ scores. These results confirm that our target problem is challenging, and validate the effectiveness of our proposed method in segmenting geometric texture instances over 3D models.

    8 Conclusion

    Existing model segmentation methods focus predominantly on semantics or low-level geometry. In this work, we presented a method for the automatic recognition and segmentation of geometric textures on 3D surface models. We first constructed a specialized benchmark for geometric texture segmentation. Then, we proposed a geometric texture-oriented segmentation method that follows a 2D-to-3D pipeline. By leveraging a fine-tuned visual segmentation model and DINO feature-based clustering, our method effectively identifies repetitive texture patterns across multiple views. Furthermore, we designed a weighted voting fusion strategy to achieve precise 3D segmentation. Building upon this, we developed a tool that enables users to segment geometric texture instances and to edit or retrieve models based on the segmentation result. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

    Limitations and Future Works. However, our method fails in segmenting weak relief, hollow structures or heavy occlusions, as shown in Fig. 10. In the future, we plan to enrich our benchmark with more complex synthetic models and models reconstructed from real objects. Other future directions include: speeding up the segmentation process, integrating generative models for texture synthesis and transfer, and enabling interactive model segmentation [LXD∗24, ZHC∗25].

    Acknowledgements

    This work was supported in part by NSFC (62302313), ICFCRT (W2441020), GD Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2023B1515120026), Shenzhen Science and Technology Program (KQTD20210811090044003, KJZD20240903100022028), and Scientific Development Fund from Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Visual Media and Multidimensional Intelligence.

    （参考文献见原文。）
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有 3D 分割偏语义部件、VLM 又看不懂几何纹理；中间这一层长期缺位。

要点：

  • 需求侧：识别 3D 模型上的**几何纹理**（如雕花、编织、褶皱这类中尺度结构）对文物保护、模型编辑与 3D 打印都很关键
  • 现有 3D 分割方法主要识别高层语义部件，捕捉不到这类「中间层纹理」；而近期 VLM 在图像分割上强，但对 3D 几何纹理仍然吃力
  • 这篇因此直接针对几何纹理做分割，而不是把它们当作语义部件的一部分

为什么值得看：UV 与材质管线最怕的就是「同一块几何上同时有结构与纹理」。把几何纹理单独切出来，意味着可以做针对性重拓扑、法线与材质编辑——这是资产重构里长期靠手工的一步。

中文摘要：识别 3D 模型上的**几何纹理**（雕花、编织、褶皱这类中尺度结构）在文物保护、模型编辑与 3D 打印等场景都很关键。但现有 3D 模型分割方法主要面向高层语义部件，捕捉不到这类「中间层」的纹理；而近期视觉语言模型虽然在图像分割上表现很强，对 3D 几何纹理仍难胜任。这篇因此专门针对 3D 网格的几何纹理做分割，把这一层从语义部件里独立出来。对 UV 与材质管线而言，能单独切出几何纹理，就能做针对性的重拓扑与法线/材质编辑。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

Segmenting Geometric Textures of 3D Meshes

Abstract

Recognizing geometric texture patterns on 3D models is critical for applications such as heritage protection, model editing, and 3D printing. Existing 3D model segmentation methods predominantly focus on identifying high-level semantic parts, thereby failing to capture middle-level textures. While recent Vision-Language Models can perform image segmentation with appropriate text prompts, they still struggle to recognize 3D geometric textures. In this work, we present a method that segments 3D mesh models based on middle-level geometric textures. We further introduce a new geometric texture segmentation benchmark and fine-tune SAM3 accordingly. The segmented texture regions are then clustered based on DINO feature similarity and lifted from 2D to 3D. Additionally, we develop an interactive tool to enable both 3D model editing based on our segmentation results and model retrieval from the dataset based on geometric and texture similarity. Experiments demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing methods in segmenting geometric textures and can facilitate various applications.

1 Introduction

Geometric textures/patterns constitute local, repetitive geometric variations across a 3D surface, remaining independent of the global model structure [BTB∗18, PTB∗25]. High-quality 3D models featuring intricate geometric textures are typically acquired via physical scanning or manual design (see Figure 1). These assets drive critical downstream applications, ranging from digital twins and heritage preservation to immersive gaming and 3D printing [XHW∗26]. Effective recognition of geometric textures is therefore essential, facilitating cultural heritage analysis (e.g., reassembling fragmented artifacts [BTB∗18]) and enabling texture-aware 3D editing workflows. However, current practice relies heavily on manual inspection and laborious analysis by users or modelers, which is both time-consuming and inefficient.

However, existing model analysis and segmentation methods predominantly operate either at high-level semantics [HHF∗19, VPP∗23] or at low-level geometric features (e.g., curvature, normals, and noise) [WGS∗18, GKOM18], often failing to capture the intricate patterns of middle-level geometric textures. While professional tools like ZBrush facilitate interactive, local modifications, they lack the capability for holistic, global editing of regions characterized by specific texture patterns in a single pass. Consequently, despite growing research interest in recognizing and editing geometric textures on 3D surfaces [GDJ∗25], a robust and comprehensive solution remains an open challenge.

In this work, we propose a framework for geometric texture recognition on 3D surface models. Leveraging a 2D-to-3D paradigm, our method begins by rendering multi-view images from the input 3D mesh. We then employ a visual segmentation model fine-tuned on our newly constructed benchmark to identify texture regions within the rendered images. Corresponding features are extracted from these segmented patches and clustered into semantic groups. Subsequently, we introduce a weighted voting strategy to fuse these 2D predictions and lift them into a coherent 3D segmentation. Finally, we adopt a filter-based geometric editing technique and develop an interactive tool that enables users to perform holistic, one-pass editing of specific texture patterns on the 3D model based on the segmentation results. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    A texture material dataset and a geometric texture segmentation benchmark. The datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/ALingll/GTSeg;

  • •

    A geometric texture segmentation method for 3D meshes, based on multi-view rendering and visual foundation models;

  • •

    An interactive, texture-oriented 3D model editing tool, supporting model segmentation and retrieval as well as geometric texture enhancement, removal, and transfer.

    • 2 Related Works

    Geometric Texture over 3D model surfaces are high-frequency, repetitive surface details distinct from global shape and random noise (excluding hollowing and winding structures). Existing research on geometric textures mainly focused on synthesis and interactive editing. Early works established procedural and example-based methods for texture synthesis [BIT04, Elb05, ZXZD24], a direction recently advanced by deep generative models [HHGCO20, YCK∗25].
