Complementarily, editing tools have evolved from manual manipulation of displacement maps [LHGM] to recent texture generation based on the vision-language model [MWS∗25]. However, as the prerequisite for automated analysis and editing, the fundamental problem of geometric texture recognition and segmentation is significantly less explored. Several studies have attempted to bridge this gap. One direction is to separate texture and non-texture regions using learning-based methods [GDJ∗24, PTB24]. Tortorici et al. [TBOW21] introduced a convolution-based descriptor for recognizing user-specific textures.

    Despite these efforts, current methods still exhibit poor generalization when dealing with multiple textures, multi-scale structures, and complex topologies. To the best of our knowledge, an open-source benchmark, a robust and automated solution for geometric texture segmentation and recognition that handles diverse and complex patterns over a complicated model, is still missing in the literature [BTB∗18, PTB∗25].

    Model Segmentation is an essential task in computer graphics and vision. Early methods mainly rely on low-level geometric primitives such as curvature, surface normals, and geodesic distances to partition 3D models, including region growing [LYW∗20], graph cuts [KT03], spectral clustering, and MRF/CRF-based optimization [Sha08]. Although these methods perform stably on segmenting homogeneous low-level geometric regions (e.g., planar surfaces, smooth curved patches), they fail to capture high-frequency, repetitive geometric patterns that define geometric textures. Recent deep learning works focus on semantic or part-level segmentation. For native 3D representations, point cloud networks (e.g., PointNet [QSMG17, QYSG17], DGCNN[WSL∗19]) and mesh-based networks [HHF∗19] achieve state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks such as ShapeNet Part[CFG∗15] and PartNet[MZC∗19]. However, these methods are limited to coarse-grained category or part labels (e.g., separating chair legs from seats) and cannot recognize fine-grained geometric textures [YLX∗24, XYQ∗25, LUX∗25]. Recent works following a 2D-to-3D pipeline, leverage pre-trained 2D foundation models (e.g., SAM [KMR∗23], CLIP [CLZ∗25]) to project multi-view 2D predictions back to 3D [ZXL∗24, TZF∗24b, TCC∗26, ZHR∗26]. While these methods enable open-vocabulary segmentation, they still focus on semantic object categories rather than geometric texture patterns.

    To the best of our knowledge, the segmentation of geometric textures on 3D models remains an open problem [PTB∗25]. Current attempts indicate that image-like local descriptors offer the most promising solution for geometric texture recognition and segmentation [BTB∗18]. Hence, we borrow the ability from the visual foundation model and employ the 2D-to-3D pipeline to address this problem.

    Image Segmentation aims to partition an image into regions that are coherent in semantics, instance identity, or visual attributes. Earlier deep segmentation methods primarily focus on dense prediction and instance mask modeling [LSD15, RFB15, HGDG17]. Recent segmentation research has increasingly shifted toward unified and promptable foundation models. MaskFormer and Mask2Former cast semantic, instance, and panoptic segmentation as mask classification [CSK21, CMS∗22]. SAM3 introduces strong promptable concept segmentation, enabling the detection and segmentation of all instances matching a text or exemplar concept [CGH∗25]. SAMesh lifts multi-view SAM2 masks onto mesh surfaces for zero-shot mesh part segmentation [TZF∗24b]. These studies suggest that SAM-family models are effective front-ends for 3D model segmentation. Recently, textureSAM validates the zero-shot capability of SAM in 2D texture segmentation after fine-tuning with sufficient training data [CMT∗26].

    However, unlike the 2D textures provided by TextureSAM, the identical geometric texture can look dramatically different across viewpoints, which implies the critical role of proper training data and geometric constraints. Therefore, in this work, we do not directly treat 2D masks as the final predictions; instead, we leverage both image and geometry evidence, combining curvature re-rendering, mask-level texture-feature clustering, and multi-view 3D voting to obtain view-consistent geometric texture segmentation.

    3 Geometric Texture Segmentation Benchmark

    To begin, we construct a large-scale geometric texture segmentation benchmark, consisting of synthetic and annotated 3D models. Collecting reconstructed models through scanning is extremely expensive and labor-intensive. Instead, we choose to sculpt 3D models via texture displacement maps, see Figure 2.

    Texture Displacement Maps Dataset. We use Chord [YRWX25] to generate displacement maps based on the open-source 2D texture images dataset DTD [CMK∗14]. We construct a displacement map dataset, TDSet, consisting of 350 diverse displacement maps. The displacement maps in TDSet are employed to synthesize 3D geometric textures over 3D models.

    3D Geometric Texture Benchmark. Next, we construct a geometric texture benchmark called GTSeg, which consists of a training set and a test set. For the training set, we collect 80 synthetic models from Thingi10K [ZJ16]. We randomly select four or five displacement maps from TDSet and apply them to the surface of each model. All geometric texture instances are automatically annotated. For each model, we repeat this process ten times. The final training set consists of 800 models, each with multiple geometric texture categories and instances. Moreover, we construct a test set comprising 20 synthetic models generated following the above procedure (with no overlap with the training set) and 10 real scans from [XZZ∗14] and public domain. We manually annotate the geometric texture instances on the real scans.

    4 Geometric Texture-oriented Image Segmentation Model

    In this section, we develop a 2D image segmentation model specifically for segmenting 3D geometric textures. We first justify our choice of representation, and subsequently detail the training dataset construction pipeline and the model fine-tuning protocol.

    Although recent advancements have made significant progress in texture-aware 2D image segmentation, they cannot be directly generalized to 3D geometric texture recognition. TextureSAM [CMT∗26] mitigates the semantic bias of foundation models by fine-tuning on 2D RGB images where object regions are synthetically replaced with descriptive visual textures. In contrast, 3D geometric textures lack explicit colors and depend solely on local topographic variations. Furthermore, the 2D projection of the same 3D geometric pattern exhibits severe perspective distortions and foreshortening across different viewing angles. Consequently, without explicit adaptation to intrinsic 3D geometry and multi-view consistency, models constrained to 2D visual priors inevitably fail to achieve view-consistent segmentation of complex 3D surface patterns.

    Grayscale Curvature and Mask Rendering. Surface curvature is an intrinsic geometric property that remains strictly invariant to lighting conditions and rigid transformations. To bridge 3D geometry with 2D segmentation, we compute per-vertex mean curvature as the raw scalar sᵢ. To mitigate the impact of mesh singularities and ensure high image contrast, we clip outliers according to the 5th/95th percentiles. The curvature values are then normalized to [0,1] via min-max normalization.

    Here, we split the models in the training set of GTSeg into two sets: 76 models are used for training and 4 for validation. We rendered each model to generate curvature maps and ground-truth masks from 14 uniformly sampled viewpoints. That is to say, the training set contains 10,640 image and mask pairs, while the validation set contains 560 image and mask pairs. All rendered views and synthesized variants derived from the same source model are assigned to the same split to prevent data leakage. Finally, we generate a dataset of 11,200 pairs of view-dependent curvature maps and corresponding ground-truth masks. The training set will be employed to adapt the vision foundation model to our task later.

    Model Fine-tuning. While the pre-trained SAM3 model demonstrates strong zero-shot capabilities in general concept segmentation, it struggles to precisely delineate non-semantic, mid-level geometric textures. To efficiently bridge this domain gap without catastrophic forgetting, we employ Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [HSW∗22] to fine-tune the model on our synthesized dataset and obtain GTSAM.

    The recognition of geometric textures relies heavily on mid-level patterns rather than high-level linguistic concepts. Hence, we freeze the entire language encoder to preserve general semantic priors and reduce computational overhead. To this end, we inject trainable rank-decomposition matrices into the Vision Encoder, Geometry Encoder, and the decoding modules. This targeted injection maximizes the model’s sensitivity to high-frequency textural signals while maintaining its robust zero-shot foundation.

    5 Geometric Texture-oriented Model Segmentation

    In this section, we introduce a framework to address the problem of geometric texture segmentation, via formulating it as a task of multi-view consistency perception. The overview of our framework is visualized in Figure 3.

    Given a 3D mesh M, we first render a set of grayscale curvature maps {Cᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N from a collection of predefined camera poses {Pᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^N. Subsequently, the rendered images are fed to our GTSAM to predict a set of pixel-level geometric texture masks. We introduce a feature association module based on DINOv2 to maintain semantic consistency across disparate views. This module extracts and clusters high-dimensional feature descriptors from each mask, thereby establishing label correspondences across different viewpoints in a unified latent space. Finally, multi-view masks with consistent labels are projected onto the model surface M. To resolve prediction conflicts arising from occlusions or perspective distortions, we implement a spatial-consistency weighted voting mechanism. This mechanism performs per-face arbitration to make definitive label decisions, yielding precise and smooth geometric texture segmentation results.

    5.1 Texture-oriented Image Segmentation

    We set N cameras to render the input mesh, ensuring complete coverage and sufficient overlap. In our implementation, we let N=50. The t-th camera renders a curvature image Iₜ. Next, we send the rendered curvature images to our GTSAM. For Iₜ, GTSAM predicts a set of Nₜ instance masks. Each instance mask M_t,m is paired with a confidence score c_t,m∈[0,1].

    For each predicted mask M_t,m, we perform 8-connected component analysis. Components with an area smaller than the threshold A_\min are discarded. We retain those sufficiently large connected components and treat them as independent mask instances. This prevents disconnected 2D regions from being merged into the same texture cluster.

    5.2 Feature-based Patch Clustering.

    Although GTSAM produces high-quality class-agnostic masks {M_t,m}, these masks are generated independently for each view and lack explicit semantic correspondence. To assign accurate instance labels to disparate views, we leverage DINOv2 as a robust feature extractor. It’s capable of achieving cross-view semantic consistency in the absence of per-view labels [DHM∗25].

    Region Re-rendering. After that, we project each mask component onto the mesh. The set of faces covered by the mask component Cₐ is denoted as Pₐ. We discard mask components that contain very few faces and store the remaining components as a group.

    To extract a view-normalized texture descriptor, we re-render each projected region. The region center and average normal are estimated as:

    oₐ=(1)/(|V(Pₐ)|)∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)vᵢ, nₐ=(∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)nᵢ)/(∥∑_vᵢ∈V(Pₐ)nᵢ∥₂).

    		(1)

    An orthographic camera is then placed along nₐ and oriented toward oₐ, producing a local curvature rendering Jₐ for the mask instance.

    Next, we extract the DINOv2 patch tokens of local curvature rendering Jₐ[ODM∗24]. The visible region is cropped and resized to a fixed resolution. Each rendered view is augmented with rotations (0^∘, 90^∘, 180^∘, and 270^∘) and horizontal flip. We then generate patch tokens using DINOv2 for each augmented view. The region mask is down-sampled to the DINO patch grid, and the tokens covered by the mask are sampled to create a token pool: Tₐ={ẑ_a,1,…,ẑ_a,Kₐ}. Each token is normalized into a unit vector.

    Consistency Filtering. To eliminate masks that contain inconsistent textures, we compute a consistency score γₐ for each Jₐ. This score is defined as the median similarity between each local feature ẑ_a,i and the normalized average feature direction of the entire mask. The score is formulated as:

    γₐ=medianᵢ((ẑ_a,i^⊤∑ⱼẑ_a,j)/(∥∑ⱼẑ_a,j∥₂)).

    		(2)

    We eliminate masks with γₐ smaller than a predefined threshold τₛ. In our implementation, we let τₛ=0.65. Two masks of the Merlion example are provided in Figure 4. The mask on the left contains only one geometry texture, therefore exhibits high consistency. Meanwhile, the mask on the right is eliminated since it contains two types of texture, which deliver a consistency score smaller than the threshold.

    Feature Clustering. To merge instances representing the same geometric texture, for each pair of mask instances Jₐ and J_b, we compute a token-token similarity matrix Sᵃᵇᵢⱼ=ẑ_a,i^⊤ẑ_b,j. We utilize bidirectional top-k matching to reduce the sensitivity to boundary tokens and partial occlusions. Specifically, we first identify the maximum matching scores along both directions: uᵢ=\maxⱼSᵃᵇᵢⱼ and vⱼ=\maxᵢSᵃᵇᵢⱼ. The pairwise instance similarity is then defined as the average of the top-k mean values from both sets:

    sim(a,b)=1/2[TopKMeanₖ({uᵢ}ᵢ)+TopKMeanₖ({vⱼ}ⱼ)].

    		(3)

    To segment geometric texture instances, we not only consider the similarity of the rendered textures, but also consider their connectivity over the surface. We store the disconnected regions with the same pattern as different texture instances. We first construct a mutual-kNN graph G over all valid mask instances [YZZW24]. The nearest neighbors k of a are denoted as ℕₖ(a). We create an edge between a and b if they are mutual neighbors (b∈ℕₖ(a) and a∈ℕₖ(b)) and their similarity satisfies sim(a,b)≥τ_clu. Subsequently, the raw mask clusters {ℚᵣ} are obtained by extracting the connected components of G, formulated as {ℚᵣ}=CC(G).

    To refine the clusters, we calculate a cluster support score for each mask a∈ℚ, defined as the median similarity to its cluster peers: ρₐ=median_b∈ℚ,b≠asim(a,b). Low-support members are split into singleton clusters. Finally, the mask confidence used for 3D voting is reweighted by incorporating its internal consistency γₐ and cluster support ρₐ:

    ŝₐ=\max(s_\min,sₐγₐ^αρₐ^β).

    		(4)

    In our implementation, we let k=8 for the bidirectional top-k matching, k=5 for the mutual-kNN graph construction, and τ_clu=0.8. For the confidence reweighting, we set α=1.0, β=1, and s_\min=0.25. A visualization of the resulting mask clusters is shown in Figure 5.

    5.3 Mask Fusion by 3D Voting

    To fuse the 2D mask clusters {ℚᵣ} into the 3D mesh, we project the masks onto the mesh surface and accumulate votes on the visible faces. For a mask Cₐ∈ℚᵣ and a view tₐ, a mesh face f will receive a positive weight w₊ when its projected face center falls inside Cₐ, and will receive a negative penalty -w₋ otherwise. This vote is further scaled by the mask confidence score csₐ and an angular weight \cos(θ_a,f), where θ_a,f is the angle between the face normal and the viewing direction. The raw voting score is accumulated as:

    V_r,fʳᵃʷ=∑_a∈V_r,fcₐ\cos(θ_a,f)·W(a,f),

    		(5)

    where V_r,f⊆ℚᵣ denote the subset of masks from which face f is visible, W(a,f)=w₊ if the projected face center of f lies inside mask Cₐ, and -w₋ otherwise. To avoid bias toward frequently observed regions, the raw score is averaged by the visibility count, yielding the final score:

    V_r,f=(V_r,fʳᵃʷ)/(\max(1,|V_r,f|)).

    		(6)

    A face is assigned to cluster r if its average score V_r,f>τ_V and it accumulates at least n_\min⁺ positive hits. Face-label conflicts are resolved by weighted voting. When a face receives positive votes from multiple texture clusters, the cluster with the highest accumulated normalized score is selected.

    Finally, we refine the assignments by extracting the connected components over the 3D mesh and discarding isolated components whose area is smaller than a minimum value. Ultimately, we get a set of 3D instances {ℙᵣ} from {Qᵣ}. In our implement, we set w₊=2.0, w₋=1.0 and n_\min⁺=3.

    Finally, different initial 3D parts may correspond to the same physical region due to different perspectives. We therefore merge parts that exhibit strong spatial overlap. For any two 3D semantic parts ℙₐ and ℙ_b, we calculate their 3D Intersection-over-Union (IoU) as IoU(a,b)=|ℙₐ∩ℙ_b|/|ℙₐ∪ℙ_b|, where |·| denotes the number of mesh faces.

    If IoU(a,b)≥τᵢₒᵤ, the two parts are connected in a region-adjacency graph. We set a threshold of τᵢₒᵤ=0.8 to ensure that only highly overlapping parts are merged. The final non-overlapping 3D regions, denoted as {ℙₖ}ₖ₌₁^K, are obtained by extracting the connected components of this graph.

    The first row of Figure 8 shows the final result on the Merlion example. The resulting face regions are rendered with distinct colors. The result indicates that our method effectively recognizes all the distinct geometric textures over the model. Even the text on the base is successfully segmented.

    6 Applications

    Geometric Texture Enhancement and Removal. For model editing, normal filters are capable of removing all the high-frequency local characteristics, such as noises [ZDZ∗15, XZSJ18]. Specifically, the static/dynamic filter effectively identifies all the relief structures over the model surface, without recognizing their higher-level patterns. Based on our segmentation results, we employ the static/dynamic filter to interactively enhance or remove a specific type of geometric texture over the model (see Figure ). Our segmentation method dramatically improves editing efficiency.

    Geometric Texture Replacement. After removing the user-specific geometric texture instance, the user can select an arbitrary texture from our DTSet, and apply it to the target region to achieve replacement of geometric texture (see Figure ).

    Model Retrieval. Effective retrieval of the reconstructed model that shares similar geometric texture is critical for the projection and restoration of the heritage. The query in Figure  is the brick wall texture of Merlion. The retrieval is performed among four models. For each model, we performed segmentation and extracted the DINOv2 feature tokens of all the texture instances. Then, we measure the similarity between all the texture instances and the target (Eq. 3), returning the model that contains the texture instance with the highest similarity.

    7 Experimental Results

    7.1 Ablation Study

    Firstly, we evaluate the contribution of three key components. The LoRA-adapted SAM3 is replaced with the original zero-shot model. Next, the step of feature-based association is removed from the framework. All the masks are grouped solely according to the overlap of their projected 3D regions. Then, feature-based association is removed from the framework, and masks are grouped solely according to the overlap of their projected 3D regions. The experimental results are shown in Table 1. For all quantitative evaluations, the results are presented as percentages.

    The results indicate that replacing the fine-tuned model with zero-shot SAM3 brings the largest degradation in segmentation accuracy. Removing feature-based clustering also substantially reduces performance. Consistency filtering provides a further improvement over the unfiltered variant. The complete method consistently achieves the best performance across all metrics. Overall, the results demonstrate that all three components are necessary for accurate and reliable 3D geometric-texture instance segmentation.

    7.2 Comparisons on Image Segmentation

    We compare the results of segmentation on rendered curvature maps with zero-shot SAM3 [CGH∗25] and TextureSAM [CMT∗26]. SAM3 and our methods are given the identical prompt: “repetitive pattern”, in all experiments.

    Figure  6 qualitatively illustrates the performance of our method compared to the methods described above in wild examples. We performed quantitative evaluation on the GTSeg test set. Statistics are provided in Table 2. To comprehensively assess both semantic and instance-level quality, we adopt mIoU and Dice coefficient to measure overall spatial overlap, Precision and Recall for pixel-level exactness, and Average Precision (AP, AP₅₀, AP₇₅) for instance-level localization accuracy.

    As shown in Table 2, our fine-tuned SAM3 significantly outperforms all baseline methods on every metric. Specifically, while TextureSAM achieves a high Recall (0.913), its excessively low Precision (0.129) and mIoU (0.128) indicate severe over-segmentation and massive false positives, rendering its instance-level AP scores negligible. The SAM3 demonstrates solid foundational capability with an mIoU of 0.669; however, its performance degrades drastically under stricter boundary criteria (AP₅₀ drops to 0.124), indicating its struggle with precise boundary adherence required by the GTSeg domain. In contrast, our fine-tuned SAM3 effectively bridges this domain gap, achieving a state-of-the-art mIoU of 0.933 and a Dice score of 0.965. Most notably, our method maintains exceptional accuracy under strict intersection thresholds, boosting the Mean AP from 0.218 to 0.890 and AP₇₅ from 0.124 to 0.831. These results demonstrate that our fine-tuning strategy retains the strong recall of the foundation model while drastically improving its precision and boundary localization.

    7.3 Comparisons on Model Segmentation

    We collect 12 models reconstructed from real objects from public resources [BWHSH25] and synthetic models from SHREC’25 examples  [PTB24], with various resolutions, functions, complexities, and semantics. Their geometric textures cover diverse scales, structures, and shapes with open boundaries.

    Qualitative Evaluation. We compare our segmentation results with ShapeDiameter [SSCO08] and SAMesh [TZF∗24a]. Figure 7 shows a qualitative comparison of three unlabeled models from SHREC’25. Figure 8 and Figure 9 further compare the performance of these methods on real scans.

    ShapeDiameter relies on volumetric thickness and global shape structure, making it insensitive to fine-grained surface-level texture boundaries, particularly when textured patterns are shallow, repetitive, or confined to the same semantic part. SAMesh offers better flexibility by projecting 2D segmentation onto 3D meshes, but its behavior is dominated by object/part-level visual priors, leading to cross-view inconsistencies when texture elements share similar semantic appearance, yet differ geometrically. Our method addresses these limitations by using curvature renderings as input, directing segmentation toward intrinsic surface variation rather than color, illumination, or semantic category. Combined with mask-level clustering and multi-view voting, it produces coherent, view-consistent regions for repeated geometric patterns and resolves texture boundaries defined by subtle local surface relief. These comparisons confirm that conventional mesh segmentation and general 2D-to-3D pipelines are insufficient for geometric texture segmentation, and that curvature-based representation with texture-aware clustering provides a more suitable formulation.

    Quantitative Evaluation. We compute two metrics for all mesh vertices to assess the quality of the segmentation results: i) MUCoV, which quantifies the overall region-wise overlap between the predicted segments and the ground truth; and ii) Recall50, which measures the which measures the fraction of ground-truth instances correctly identified with an IoU threshold of 50% [RZ17, LMB∗14]. The statistics are reported in Table 3. The segmentation results of our method achieve the best MUCoV and Recall₅₀ scores. These results confirm that our target problem is challenging, and validate the effectiveness of our proposed method in segmenting geometric texture instances over 3D models.

    8 Conclusion

    Existing model segmentation methods focus predominantly on semantics or low-level geometry. In this work, we presented a method for the automatic recognition and segmentation of geometric textures on 3D surface models. We first constructed a specialized benchmark for geometric texture segmentation. Then, we proposed a geometric texture-oriented segmentation method that follows a 2D-to-3D pipeline. By leveraging a fine-tuned visual segmentation model and DINO feature-based clustering, our method effectively identifies repetitive texture patterns across multiple views. Furthermore, we designed a weighted voting fusion strategy to achieve precise 3D segmentation. Building upon this, we developed a tool that enables users to segment geometric texture instances and to edit or retrieve models based on the segmentation result. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.

    Limitations and Future Works. However, our method fails in segmenting weak relief, hollow structures or heavy occlusions, as shown in Fig. 10. In the future, we plan to enrich our benchmark with more complex synthetic models and models reconstructed from real objects. Other future directions include: speeding up the segmentation process, integrating generative models for texture synthesis and transfer, and enabling interactive model segmentation [LXD∗24, ZHC∗25].

    Acknowledgements

    This work was supported in part by NSFC (62302313), ICFCRT (W2441020), GD Basic and Applied Basic Research Foundation (2023B1515120026), Shenzhen Science and Technology Program (KQTD20210811090044003, KJZD20240903100022028), and Scientific Development Fund from Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Visual Media and Multidimensional Intelligence.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: coding agent 造 3D 到底行不行：Frontier3DBench 用 145 个任务统一考「物体 / 场景 / 可交互开放世界」 ｜ Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
item.description:
一句话：现有基准把评测切碎在各任务与协议里，看不出 agent 在「不同建造层级」上的能力。

要点：

  • 定位：coding agent 把图像与指令翻成可编辑程序，把重建、生成与编辑并进同一工作流，是自动化 3D 创作的一条新路径
  • 缺陷：现有基准把评测碎片化在不同任务范围与协议上，导致「agent 在不同建造层级上到底能做到什么」并不清楚
  • Frontier3DBench 提供 145 个任务的统一基准，覆盖物体、场景与可交互开放世界三个层级

为什么值得看：「AI 造 3D」的评价长期各说各话：有人考单物体、有人考场景。把三个层级放进同一套协议，才能看清 agent 的能力断点在哪里——这比再报一个 SOTA 更有用。

中文摘要：coding agent 把视觉理解与程序执行结合起来，为自动化 3D 创作提供了新路径：把图像与指令翻译成可编辑的程序，让重建、生成与编辑进入同一工作流。但现有基准把评测切碎在不同的任务范围与协议里，导致「agent 在不同建造层级上究竟能做到什么」并不清楚。Frontier3DBench 因此提出一个统一的 145 任务基准，覆盖物体、场景与可交互开放世界三个层级。对关心「AI 能不能自己把 3D 内容造出来」的团队，这种跨层级统一协议能暴露出能力的真实断点。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds

November 6, 2026

Abstract

Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model–harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

1 Introduction

Automating 3D creation has long been a central pursuit in computer vision, spanning reconstruction, generation, and editing [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Yet these tasks demand more than recognizing visual content: they require translating observations and instructions into explicit geometry and spatial structure. Coding agents offer a new route toward this goal because they combine strong visual understanding with the ability to write and execute programs that construct 3D content [8, 9]. We argue that coding agents will replace traditional, task-specific computer vision pipelines for 3D creation. The critical question is therefore: how far have coding agents come in 3D creation?

Existing benchmarks, however, fragment this evaluation across different construction tasks and application settings. For example, object and scene authoring benchmarks assess geometry, visual fidelity, construction, and editing [10, 11], whereas executable-world and game benchmarks emphasize mechanical dependencies, interactive behavior, and gameplay completion [12, 9, 13]. Because their task scopes and evaluation protocols differ, these results are difficult to combine into a consistent account of an agent’s capabilities across objects, scenes, and interactive worlds. A single aggregate score can also obscure whether an agent fails to match a reference, organize a scene, or implement the required behavior. Object fidelity, scene coherence, and world functionality impose distinct construction requirements. A unified benchmark must therefore evaluate each level through dedicated tasks and complementary visual, structural, and behavioral checks.

Our key insight is that successful 3D creation demands faithful appearance, coherent structure, and functional behavior. Accordingly, we organize evaluation around objects, scenes, and interactive open worlds, requiring executable, editable artifacts at every level. Within this hierarchy, we assess object geometry and detail, scene layout and composition, and world-level appearance and activity completion through complementary visual, structural, and behavioral checks. Rendered views measure appearance, native scene inspection measures structure, and runtime tests measure behavior.

Following these principles, we introduce Frontier3DBench, comprising 145 tasks across 9 categories: 65 object tasks, 65 scene tasks, and 15 interactive open-world tasks. The suite covers generation, reconstruction, and scene editing in Blender, together with interactive world construction in Unreal Engine. Evaluation of 11 model–harness configurations reveals three key findings. First, model strengths vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. Second, every configuration scores lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in both object and scene tasks, highlighting the difficulty of matching specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Third, local mechanisms remain far stronger than coordinated activities: across all 165 L3 submissions (11 configurations × 15 tasks), the local-mechanism component of interaction correctness averages 83.08/100, compared with 20.82 for motion clearance and 30.26 for stateful workflows. These findings point to reference fidelity and the coordination of moving parts, actions, and persistent state as the main open challenges in 3D creation.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A unified benchmark for coding agents in 3D creation. Frontier3DBench comprises 145 tasks across 9 categories, bringing object, scene, and interactive-world construction into a shared suite covering generation, reconstruction, and scene editing. Dedicated tasks at each level reveal whether an agent’s strengths extend from individual assets to complete environments.

  • •

    Joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. We assess executable Blender and Unreal Engine artifacts through visual judgments, structural measurements, and independent runtime tests, connecting content quality with action effects, state consistency, and activity completion.

  • •

    An empirical account of current capabilities and bottlenecks. Across 11 model–harness configurations, we identify strengths that vary by construction level and persistent gaps in reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion. We further analyze capability dimensions and API costs to characterize differences in performance and resource demands.

    • 2 Frontier3DBench

    2.1 Task Formulation

    Frontier3DBench formulates 3D creation as a mapping from a task specification to project files for the prescribed 3D engine (Figure 2). These files encode the requested objects (L1), scenes (L2), or open worlds (L3), together with the code and assets needed to construct or run them.

    Input.

    We represent the agent-visible input as x=(d,I,a₀), where d is a written task instruction, I is an optional set of reference images, and a₀ denotes any supplied starter code, initial scene, or reusable assets. The instruction defines the required geometry, appearance, spatial relationships, and, for open worlds, connected regions and functional behavior. Reference-conditioned tasks provide one or more images; text-conditioned tasks use I=∅. Editing tasks additionally specify the initial scene, the requested modification, and the content to preserve. For L3, the input includes an interaction contract specifying functional zones, entities, initial states, and available operations. Source assets and evaluation annotations are used only for scoring and are not provided to the agent.

    Output.

    Given x, a coding agent A produces a submission y=A(x;e) for the task’s prescribed engine e:

    e=\begincasesBlender,&L1 objects and L2 scenes, Unreal Engine,&L3 open worlds.\endcases

    		(1)

    For L1 and L2, y contains Blender project files for the resulting object or scene, executable construction or editing code, and task-required exports. For L3, y contains Unreal Engine project files for an open world that connects multiple regions into a coherent environment, including its assets and required interaction logic. Executing the submission must realize the visual and structural requirements of the input; L3 must also support the specified actions and their persistent effects within a session. An independent observer tests the required interactions and state persistence as the player moves through the generated world.

    2.2 Benchmark Construction

    2.2.1 Data Sources

    Object and scene tasks draw on publicly available 3D models (primarily .glb, with some .blend files), images from public datasets, and photographs captured by the authors. Interactive open-world tasks use game screenshots and real-world photographs, including panoramic imagery, as visual references for interactive environments. Text-conditioned tasks use text instructions without reference images.

    2.2.2 Benchmark Composition

    Overview. Frontier3DBench organizes 3D creation tasks by the unit being built and the behavior it must support. The hierarchy progresses from individual objects and assemblies, through spatially organized scenes, to connected worlds with persistent interaction states. Table 1 summarizes the inputs and requirements of the 145 tasks across 9 categories and three levels.

    Level 1 (L1): Object Level. L1 concerns the construction of a single editable 3D asset, which can be an individual object or a mechanical assembly. Task requirements address the asset’s geometry, dimensions, appearance, and relationships among constituent parts. The 65 tasks cover modeling from text (Text2Code, 15), reconstruction from multiple reference views (Img2Code, 25), and reconstruction from a single image (Img2Code-SingleView, 25).

    Level 2 (L2): Scene Level. L2 concerns the construction or modification of a complete scene composed of multiple objects and their shared surroundings. The objects must form a coherent spatial layout with consistent relative scales, while materials and lighting must support the specified appearance and camera composition. The 65 tasks comprise scene generation from text instructions (Brief2Scene, 20), reconstruction from reference images (Ref2Scene, 10), reconstruction from real photographs (Ref2Scene-RealPhoto, 25), and modification of an existing scene (SceneEdit, 10). Scene editing requires changing specified objects or scene properties while preserving the surrounding content.

    Level 3 (L3): Open-World Level. L3 concerns the construction of an explorable world that connects multiple functional regions within a shared environment. The player must be able to move between regions and interact with objects and mechanisms whose state changes persist across action sequences within a session. Complexity is defined by the required spatial organization and connected operations, allowing both dense indoor environments and larger outdoor worlds. The 15 tasks are grouped by input modality: Text2Env (5) uses a text instruction without reference images, while Img2Env (10) pairs the instruction with one or more reference images. Both categories require executable interactions that respect action prerequisites, so that changes produced by earlier actions determine which subsequent operations are available.

    2.2.3 Data Processing Pipeline

    Task instructions. We first define the creation objective and use GPT-6-astra to expand it into a task instruction. The instruction specifies what the agent should construct and how the result should satisfy the intended geometry and appearance. It also makes spatial relationships explicit so that the instruction describes a coherent asset or environment. For tasks with visual references, the text complements the images with construction requirements; text-only tasks express the target entirely through the instruction.

    Reference images. We prepare visual inputs from existing 3D assets and collected imagery. When a source 3D model or scene is available, we render it in Blender to obtain the required reference views. Photographs and game screenshots provide references for environments captured outside this rendering workflow. Where panoramic imagery is used, we project it into rectilinear views that show different directions from the same capture position. The resulting images are paired with the task instruction to define the visual reconstruction target.

    Initial scenes for editing. We construct each editing task from a complete source scene. The agent receives an initial Blender project that differs from the source scene in designated target components, a rendered reference of the target scene, and an instruction describing the requested edit. The instruction identifies the content to modify and the surrounding content to preserve. The source scene serves as the evaluation target for both the edited components and the preserved content.

    Environment and interaction specifications. We use GPT-6-astra to develop open-world instructions from the intended environment and activity. Each instruction defines how functional regions connect and what the player must be able to accomplish within them. When images are supplied, it distinguishes visible reconstruction targets from additional spaces and mechanisms that must be constructed to support the activity. An accompanying interaction contract specifies the entities and their initial states, then defines the available operations and their physical constraints. Action prerequisites and persistent state changes connect individual interactions into an activity that can be completed across the environment.

    2.3 Evaluation

    Frontier3DBench evaluates the appearance and structure of objects, the composition and editing of scenes, and the visual and functional coherence of interactive worlds. Table 2 defines the score components used across these levels. Task-specific component weights are specified in Appendix A.

    2.3.1 Object-Level Scoring

    L1 evaluates appearance fidelity, structural consistency, and detail fidelity. Text-driven generation uses visual fidelity V, requirement satisfaction R, and detail fidelity D. Reference reconstruction replaces requirement satisfaction R with image similarity I and object localization L, grounding appearance and placement in the supplied views. The evaluator combines inspection of the delivered Blender scene with rendered evidence judged by GPT-6-astra at medium reasoning effort, with generator identity hidden. Detail fidelity is measured on both the native scene and the exported asset.

    2.3.2 Scene-Level Scoring

    L2 evaluates scene appearance, spatial organization, and completion of the requested construction or edit. Brief2Scene uses the text-generation score (Eq. 3), and Ref2Scene and Ref2Scene-RealPhoto use the reference score (Eq. 4), with native scene measurements and main and alternate rendered views. Scene editing additionally assesses target modification T and preservation P, comparing the candidate with the initial scene and target reference to determine whether the requested change is achieved while protected content is retained.

    2.3.3 Open-World-Level Scoring

    L3 evaluates visual quality A, task fidelity F, spatial layout G, and interaction correctness H. The submitted Unreal Engine project is rebuilt with an independent observer that captures scene views and records geometry, action effects, character movement, and state changes. Local tests inspect individual mechanisms, while continuous workflows assess whether the environment supports the complete activity without teleportation or reset.

    2.3.4 Overall Score

    Task scores are reported on a 0–100 scale and averaged within each level, including measured zeros. The overall score combines the three level means:

    Sₒᵥₑᵣₐₗₗ=0.30S_L1+0.30S_L2+0.40S_L3.

    		(2)

    The higher weight on open worlds emphasizes the integration of visual construction, interactive mechanisms, and complete activities. Measurement procedures are detailed in Appendix A.2.

    3 Experiments

    3.1 Experimental Setting

    We evaluate 11 frontier models: GPT-6.1-sol, GPT-6-astra, GPT-6-luna, Claude Opus 5.5, Kimi-K3, Kimi-K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash, GLM-5.3-Flash, Doubao-Seed-Evolving, and Qwen3.8-Max. Each model runs in its developer’s agent harness: Codex for the GPT models, Claude Code for Claude Opus 5.5, Kimi CLI for the Kimi models, DeepSeek Harness (DSH) for DeepSeek-v4.1-Flash, and ZCode for GLM-5.3-Flash. MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Qwen3.8-Max, and Doubao-Seed-Evolving, which do not provide their own harness, run in Claude Code. Each configuration uses the same harness for all three levels. In the text, we abbreviate GPT-6.1-sol, GPT-6-astra, GPT-6-luna, and Claude Opus 5.5 as Sol, Astra, Luna, and Opus, and refer to other models by family name where unambiguous.

    All models use their highest available reasoning effort: xhigh for Qwen and max for the others. Each agent decides when its work is ready for submission. If a submission fails the public execution and delivery checks, the agent can retry with the execution errors but without score feedback, within a fixed time budget (Appendix B.1).

    3.2 Overall Performance

    The best overall configuration combines strong object and scene performance, while category leaders vary.

    GPT-6.1-sol with Codex achieves the highest overall score of 66.02, with level means of 71.21 on objects, 70.35 on scenes, and 58.89 on open worlds. Its lead over the runner-up is 2.17 points, with scene construction contributing the largest weighted advantage. Across the 9 task categories, however, the highest scores are shared by three configurations: Sol leads six, Opus leads Text2Code, and Astra leads Text2Env and Img2Env. No single configuration leads every category.

    Reference reconstruction and interactive world construction remain challenging across configurations.

    Every configuration scores higher on text-to-object generation than on either object-reconstruction category, and higher on brief-driven scene generation than on either scene-reconstruction category. Text-to-object scores range from 75.93 to 84.05, whereas even the best multi-view and single-view reconstruction scores reach only 69.61 and 66.26, respectively. Every configuration also has a lower mean on L3 than on L1 or L2, with the highest open-world mean reaching 61.28. Matching a specified reference and constructing an interactive world thus remain harder than generating plausible content.

    3.3 Model Capabilities across Tasks

    Figure 3 shows each model’s profile across the 9 task categories relative to the cross-model mean. We examine these profiles alongside Table 3 to identify strengths that the overall ranking can obscure.

    Task leaders vary across reconstruction, scenes, and worlds.

    Sol leads both object-reconstruction categories and all four scene categories, while Astra leads both open-world categories with the highest L3 mean of 61.28. Opus instead achieves the highest text-to-object score of 84.05. These complementary strengths make task-specific profiles useful for model selection.

    Text-driven generation and reference reconstruction show distinct strengths.

    Kimi-K3.1-Pro and DeepSeek rank second and third in both text-to-object and brief-driven scene generation, but trail the leading models on reference reconstruction. Qwen makes this gap especially clear: its text-to-object score of 81.98 nearly matches Sol’s 82.10, whereas its multi-view and single-view reconstruction scores fall to 43.97 and 37.34. Strong text-driven generation therefore does not imply accurate reconstruction of specified geometry and appearance.

    Scene editing reveals strengths beyond the top overall ranks.

    MiniMax ranks second in editing at 78.70 despite placing sixth overall, ahead of both Astra and Opus. Kimi-K3 and GLM also exceed the cross-model editing mean, scoring 73.22 and 72.91. Their ability to modify existing scenes stands out relative to their weaker reference-reconstruction and open-world results.

    3.4 Model Performance across Capability Dimensions

    We group the score components in Table 2 into three capability dimensions. Visual quality Sᵥᵢₛ covers V and I in L1/L2 and A in L3; structural and spatial consistency Sₛₜᵣ covers R and L in L1/L2 and G in L3; task fulfillment Sₜₐₛₖ covers D, T, and P in L1/L2 and F and H in L3. For each task, a dimension score is the weighted average of the components that the task uses, with weights given by their coefficients in Eqs. 3–6 and normalized to sum to one within the dimension. We then average each dimension within L1, L2, and L3. Figure 4 presents the resulting capability profiles on a 0–100 scale.

    Visual leadership shifts from assets to worlds.

    Sol has the highest mean visual quality on objects and scenes, at 68.68 and 69.70, respectively. Astra leads on open worlds at 57.37, followed by Sol at 55.49 and Opus at 53.80. Object and scene appearance emphasize the requested form and reference agreement, while world appearance also spans lighting, composition, and style across a larger environment.

    Structural consistency reveals a different ordering.

    Opus has the highest L1 structural score at 83.27, slightly above Sol at 82.93, despite trailing Sol in visual quality. Sol leads L2 structure at 74.57, while Astra leads L3 layout at 86.37. Across models, L1 structure averages 72.77 compared with 57.28 for visual quality and 52.15 for task fulfillment. Coarse placement and structural requirements are thus easier to satisfy than complete appearance and fine detail.

    Task fulfillment distinguishes detailed assets from usable worlds.

    Sol leads task fulfillment on objects and scenes at 68.90 and 78.72, whereas Astra leads worlds at 64.40, followed by Opus at 62.78 and Sol at 61.44. This dimension measures detail completion in L1 and L2, adds target modification and preservation for scene editing, and combines environment coverage with interaction correctness in L3. The world results show a gap between working parts and complete activities: across all 165 L3 submissions, the local-mechanism, motion-clearance, and state/workflow components of H (Appendix A.2.3) average 83.08, 20.82, and 30.26, respectively.

    3.5 Cost Efficiency Analysis

    Figure 5 compares the overall score with estimated average API cost per task across all 145 tasks. Costs cover recorded usage in each task’s final successful generation attempt and weight every task equally, while the overall score uses the 30/30/40 level weights. We use the midpoint of each exported cost range as its plotting coordinate; accounting and pricing assumptions are detailed in Appendix B.2.

    Luna, DeepSeek, and Sol define the score–cost frontier at the plotted estimates.

    Luna achieves 48.56 at approximately $0.27 per task, DeepSeek achieves 57.45 at $0.45, and Sol reaches the highest overall score of 66.02 at $1.01. Moving from DeepSeek to Sol gains 8.57 points at roughly 2.2 times the estimated cost. DeepSeek’s position reflects its low per-token prices and cache usage; because its usage records are partial, its estimated cost is a lower bound (Appendix B.2).

    Higher estimated spending does not consistently yield higher scores.

    Astra scores 63.85 at approximately $5.58 per task, while Opus scores 62.29 at $21.17. Both cost more than Sol while scoring lower. Kimi-K3.1-Pro scores 55.96 at $1.54 per task, compared with DeepSeek’s 57.45 at $0.45.

    3.6 Qualitative Comparison

    Figure 6 compares object reconstruction, scene editing, and reference-image environment creation. For the spinning wheel, Sol (71.97) and Opus (66.21) recover the main mechanical assembly, whereas Kimi-K3 (38.87) reduces it to a ring-and-rod abstraction with missing components. For the bathtub edit, Sol (91.43) and Astra (82.97) fit the tub to the retained supports, while Luna (55.42) places the shell apart from the feet and fails to accommodate the cloth. For the Minecraft village, Astra (71.89) and Sol (70.29) reconstruct the village axis and continuous terraced landscape, though both simplify building variation; Luna (46.16) produces a dense cluster on largely flat terrain. Across these cases, stronger outputs preserve component relationships and spatial context, while weaker outputs retain recognizable elements but lose important structure.

    3.7 Human–Score Agreement

    To evaluate alignment with human visual judgments, we conduct a four-candidate ranking study with eight raters over 45 items from the four reference-conditioned L1/L2 task families (Img2Code, Img2Code-SingleView, Ref2Scene, and Ref2Scene-RealPhoto), yielding 360 judgments.

    Automatic scores align with human fidelity rankings.

    Mean Kendall τ_b is 0.727, with 79.2% top-one agreement and 44.7% exact-order agreement (Table 4), indicating stronger agreement on the winner than on the complete ordering. Human raters agree with one another at a mean τ_b of 0.679 across 1260 same-item pairs, so the automatic ranking agrees with individual raters at least as closely as raters agree with each other. The 25 items spanning at least 30 score points reach mean τ_b=0.793, compared with 0.644 for the other 20 items, so agreement increases with the score gap between candidates.

    4 Related Work

    Code-based 3D creation benchmarks.

    CAD benchmarks evaluate geometry, parametric structure, and engineering constraints from text and visual specifications [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. 3DCodeBench and 3DHarnessBench assess procedural asset generation and reconstruction through Blender code [19, 20], and GeoCodeBench [21] benchmarks research-level coding for 3D geometric computer vision. BlenderGym, VIGA, and MUSE study visual reconstruction and instruction-guided authoring or editing [22, 8, 23], while VoxelCodeBench and SceneActBench probe spatial composition and scene operations [24, 25]. Code4Scene evaluates Unreal Engine scene construction and editing through artifact, static-physics, and auxiliary navigation checks [11]. BlenderWorld spans object and environment creation, reconstruction, modification, and animation, combining rendered evidence with editable-project inspection [10].

    Agents for interactive 3D creation.

    Recent systems connect object construction, scene organization, and physical interaction. NeoWorld-3 reconstructs articulated objects and compositional scenes from visual observations through executable programs and physics validation [26]. SceneCode couples room planning with part-wise object code generation to produce editable indoor scenes with articulated assets [27]. EmbodiedGen V2 integrates asset generation, multi-room environments, task-driven worlds, and agent-based editing for embodied simulation [28]. Code2Worlds-2 extends object and scene generation with physical compilation and simulator feedback, while Code2Games connects Blender world construction to UE5 gameplay through scene–gameplay correspondence and execution-guided repair [29, 9]. These systems show that coding agents can construct content across scales, which motivates evaluating each scale with dedicated tasks.

    Dynamics and world evaluation.

    Video-conditioned benchmarks assess programmatic reconstruction of appearance, camera motion, geometry, and dynamics [30, 31, 32, 33]; text-conditioned benchmarks assess generated simulations [34, 35]. ExeWorldBench progresses from individual mechanisms to composed mechanical systems and goal-driven executable worlds, organizing evaluation around mechanical and causal dependencies [12]. Video2World and ScIntBench assess reconstruction from embodied demonstrations and physical interactions in generated scenes, respectively [36, 37]. WorldClaw and VibeWorlding study open-world authoring [38, 39], and VibeWorlding’s VWE-Bench uses rubric-based verification of physical feasibility and intent fulfillment. Browser-world evaluations combine visual assessment, code inspection, or runtime behavioral checks [40, 41, 42]. Game benchmarks assess integrated assets, scenes, and mechanics [43, 44, 9, 13], and CEGame-Bench additionally checks completion and saved state across engines. CraftBench-UE and GenXR-Bench evaluate executable engine and XR features [45, 46], while WorldScore evaluates sequential world generation across 3D, 4D, and video systems [47].

    Frontier3DBench organizes coding-agent evaluation around dedicated object, scene, and interactive-open-world tasks within a shared benchmark. Its hierarchy follows the unit being constructed and the corresponding correctness requirements: object geometry and parts, scene layout and composition, and connected world regions with stateful interaction sequences. All three levels cover generation and reconstruction; L2 additionally covers editing, and L3 adds interactive activities with persistent state. This design allows comparison across levels while each level keeps its own visual, structural, and behavioral checks.

    5 Conclusion

    We introduced Frontier3DBench to measure how far coding agents have come in 3D creation. Its 145 tasks across 9 categories unify object, scene, and interactive-world construction, while evaluation of executable artifacts jointly assesses appearance, structure, and behavior. Across 11 model–harness configurations, leadership shifts from GPT-6.1-sol on objects and scenes to GPT-6-astra on interactive worlds. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks, and strong local interactions remain insufficient for completing coordinated activities. The central challenges are therefore matching specified geometry and layouts, and coordinating moving parts, actions, and persistent state. Frontier3DBench makes these gaps measurable across construction levels, supporting progress toward coding agents that create faithful, coherent, and functional 3D content.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix A Scoring Details

    This appendix specifies the numerical weights and measurement procedures for the evaluation components defined in Section 2.3 and Table 2. All components lie in [0,1], and the task score is s=100Q.

    A.1 Task-Specific Quality Scores

    Text-driven object and scene generation.

    For Text2Code and Brief2Scene, visual fidelity V, requirement satisfaction R, and detail fidelity D give

    Qₜₑₓₜ=0.60V+0.30R+0.10D.

    		(3)

    V measures fidelity to the instruction and aesthetics, R measures task-specific geometric and spatial requirements, and D measures the coverage and accuracy of fine details.

    Reference-based object and scene reconstruction.

    For Img2Code, Img2Code-SingleView, Ref2Scene, and Ref2Scene-RealPhoto, the score is

    Q_ref=0.20V+0.50I+0.20L+0.10D.

    		(4)

    Here V measures visual fidelity to the input reference, I measures image similarity, L measures projected object placement and count, and D measures reference-detail fidelity.

    Scene editing.

    For SceneEdit, the score is

    Q_edit=0.20V+0.20R+0.10D+0.30T+0.20P.

    		(5)

    The additional terms T and P measure achievement of the requested target modification and preservation of protected content, respectively.

    Interactive open worlds.

    Both image- and text-conditioned L3 tasks use

    Q_world=0.60A+0.20F+0.05G+0.15H.

    		(6)

    A measures visual quality, F task fidelity, G spatial layout, and H interaction correctness.

    A.2 Component Measurements

    Task-specific checks validate execution, delivery, and artifact integrity. Confirmed failures receive zero; valid artifacts receive component-wise quality scores.

    A.2.1 Blender and Image Measurements

    The evaluator executes each submitted program in Blender 5.2.1 for a baseline and three seed reruns, checking required files, scene loading, editable geometry, and dependencies. Measurements combine native scene data with rendered evidence. R measures task-specific dimensions, parts, geometry, and spatial relations against declared tolerances; for Brief2Scene, these requirements are specified as an evidence checklist. For editing, T measures the requested change and P measures preservation of protected content.

    Reference similarity combines SSIM [48], color, tone, and edges:

    I_global=0.45I_SSIM+0.25I_color+0.15Iₜₒₙₑ+0.15I_edge.

    		(7)

    SSIM averages the original and two blurred scales; color and tone use a 4×4 grid, and edges use symmetric distance. Region-level similarity combines SSIM, edge F1, and color with weights 0.50, 0.30, and 0.20, respectively, attenuated by edge-density and contrast agreement. I combines region-level and global similarity with weights 0.90 and 0.10; tasks with static reference regions use the region term alone. Localization L matches fixed reference boxes to visually grounded candidate boxes using overlap, center proximity, and size with weights 0.50, 0.30, and 0.20, respectively, penalizing missing and extra instances. It measures projected placement and count.

    A.2.2 Visual Judgments and Detail

    GPT-6-astra with medium reasoning effort judges predefined criteria from the task instruction and rendered evidence views, together with the input references or, for SceneEdit, the initial and target views. Generator identity is hidden from the judge at all levels. Visual fidelity is V=∑ⱼaⱼgⱼ/4, where ∑ⱼaⱼ=1 and gⱼ∈{0,1,2,3,4} denotes absent, weak, partial, mostly correct, or fully demonstrated fulfillment. Grades require evidence-linked observations. Each submission is scored with its first valid judgment.

    For feature coverage cⱼᵥ∈[0,1], implementation deviation eⱼᵥ∈[0,1], and measured variant set V, detail fidelity is

    D=\min_v∈V∑ⱼbⱼcⱼᵥ(1-eⱼᵥ), ∑ⱼbⱼ=1.

    		(8)

    We set eⱼᵥ=0 whenever cⱼᵥ=0. The variant set V contains eight L1 variants (the baseline and three seed runs, each as a native scene and a GLB export) or four native L2 variants.

    A.2.3 Open-World Measurements

    The evaluator rebuilds the submitted Unreal Engine project with an independent observer in a separate workspace and measures rendered appearance, geometry, motion, character trajectories, and inventory changes. Both image- and text-conditioned tasks are scored with Eq. 6. The visual judge receives the instruction, references, the task’s fixed reference-feature list, and independently rendered views, with generator identity hidden. A averages six criteria: shape and construction, materials, lighting, composition, detail, and style. F averages scene coverage and the visible identity of functional areas and mechanisms. These criteria are scored directly with evidence anchors whose upper bounds are 0, 0.34, 0.64, 0.84, and 1 for absent through exceptional realizations.

    G combines support connectivity, static penetration, traversability, and layout semantics with weights 0.25, 0.25, 0.30, and 0.20, respectively. Support measures geometric connectivity to inferred ground; traversability uses actual character movement. H combines local mechanisms, motion clearance, and state/workflow checks with weights 0.40, 0.25, and 0.35, respectively. Local tests weight entity presence, observable action effects, and invalid-reach rejection by 0.20, 0.50, and 0.30, respectively, averaging within and across mechanism roles. The Minecraft task uses task-specific probes with the same weights. Motion-clearance checks test sampled moving parts for intersections. State/workflow equally weights satisfied end-state predicates and complete-route success. Local probes can place test fixtures, whereas continuous workflows prohibit teleportation and resets.

    Appendix B Experimental Protocols

    B.1 Tasks and Runtime Configurations

    We evaluate 145 tasks: 65 object tasks (L1), 65 scene tasks (L2), and 15 interactive-world tasks (L3). Each of the 11 model–harness configurations completes the full suite, and all 1,595 task scores are fully measured. Models use their highest available reasoning effort, as listed in Section 3.1. Agents receive the English task instruction and public task assets; evaluator files and scores are not accessible during generation. At all levels, general network access is disabled during generation and evaluation, and model requests use a restricted host gateway. L1/L2 generation allows at most six attempts within a 32-hour budget per task; a new attempt starts after a timeout, a transport error, or a failed public execution or delivery check, and receives the execution errors without score feedback. L3 agents work under a 24-hour time limit. The released code uses longer identifiers for some task families and harnesses (e.g., Image2Code, Reference2Scene, Image2Environment, and kimi-codecli), which correspond one-to-one to the names used here.

    Object and scene tasks.

    Generation runs in isolated Docker containers with two CPU cores and 4 GiB of memory. Submitted source bundles are executed in headless Blender 5.2.1. L1 deliverables include an editable native scene and a GLB export; L2 deliverables include a native scene and main and alternate renders. Rendering settings follow each task’s specification. Visual judgments use GPT-6-astra with medium reasoning effort under the scoring protocol in Appendix A.2.

    Interactive-world tasks.

    Agents develop Unreal Engine 5.8.3 projects in persistent Docker workspaces with eight CPU cores, 64 GiB of memory, and an assigned GPU. Public inputs include the instruction, applicable reference images, the interaction contract, integration interfaces, and read-only task-appropriate asset libraries. The visual judge is GPT-6-astra with medium reasoning effort.

    B.2 Cost Accounting and Uncertainty

    Figure 5 reports the estimated average cost of each task’s final successful generation attempt. For each task, recorded ordinary input, cache-read input, cache-write input, and output tokens are priced separately, then costs are averaged equally across the 145 tasks. Cached tokens are included in input counts and are assigned their respective rates without double counting; reasoning tokens are included in output. Prices follow the providers’ Standard API pricing as of October 30, 2026. CNY prices are converted at 6.6684 CNY per USD using the November 5, 2026 exchange rate; USD quotes require no conversion. Qwen’s cache-read price is set to 10% of its ordinary input price.

    Cost ranges reflect variation in cache-write lifetime, peak and off-peak pricing, and long-context tiers. For aggregated input counts above a context threshold, the long-context multiplier is applied to the upper bound. The figure plots range midpoints for model positions and the Pareto line and omits horizontal ranges. Usage records are partial for DeepSeek, both Kimi configurations, and GLM, so their estimates are lower bounds. The estimates cover generation API usage; judging, tool use, infrastructure, cache storage, and taxes are not included.

    The vertical bars show 95% task-bootstrap intervals for the overall score. We jointly resample task identities across all 11 configurations within each level, drawing 65 L1, 65 L2, and 15 L3 tasks with replacement and retaining the 0.30/0.30/0.40 weights. The intervals use 100,000 resamples with seed 20261105 to estimate task-sampling variation for the evaluated submissions.

    B.3 Human-Evaluation Protocol

    The 45 items comprise 14 multi-view objects, 16 single-view objects, eight rendered-reference scenes, and seven photographic-reference scenes. Each item contains the highest- and lowest-scoring valid runs and the two nearest the score interval’s trisection points, with adjacent options at least four points apart. Eight raters rank every item by reference fidelity, producing 360 complete rankings.

    Raters view the reference and four equally sized candidate images labelled A–D, with model identities and scores hidden. Candidate labels are permuted independently for each rater and item. Kendall’s τ_b, top-one agreement, and exact-order agreement compare human and score rankings of the same candidates; rater-to-rater agreement uses all 45\binom82=1260 same-item pairs.

    Appendix C More Visual Results
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有基准把评测切碎在各任务与协议里，看不出 agent 在「不同建造层级」上的能力。

要点：

  • 定位：coding agent 把图像与指令翻成可编辑程序，把重建、生成与编辑并进同一工作流，是自动化 3D 创作的一条新路径
  • 缺陷：现有基准把评测碎片化在不同任务范围与协议上，导致「agent 在不同建造层级上到底能做到什么」并不清楚
  • Frontier3DBench 提供 145 个任务的统一基准，覆盖物体、场景与可交互开放世界三个层级

为什么值得看：「AI 造 3D」的评价长期各说各话：有人考单物体、有人考场景。把三个层级放进同一套协议，才能看清 agent 的能力断点在哪里——这比再报一个 SOTA 更有用。

中文摘要：coding agent 把视觉理解与程序执行结合起来，为自动化 3D 创作提供了新路径：把图像与指令翻译成可编辑的程序，让重建、生成与编辑进入同一工作流。但现有基准把评测切碎在不同的任务范围与协议里，导致「agent 在不同建造层级上究竟能做到什么」并不清楚。Frontier3DBench 因此提出一个统一的 145 任务基准，覆盖物体、场景与可交互开放世界三个层级。对关心「AI 能不能自己把 3D 内容造出来」的团队，这种跨层级统一协议能暴露出能力的真实断点。

主题：图形学

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-09

本期推送：2026-11-10

Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds

November 6, 2026

Abstract

Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model–harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

1 Introduction

Automating 3D creation has long been a central pursuit in computer vision, spanning reconstruction, generation, and editing [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]. Yet these tasks demand more than recognizing visual content: they require translating observations and instructions into explicit geometry and spatial structure. Coding agents offer a new route toward this goal because they combine strong visual understanding with the ability to write and execute programs that construct 3D content [8, 9]. We argue that coding agents will replace traditional, task-specific computer vision pipelines for 3D creation. The critical question is therefore: how far have coding agents come in 3D creation?

Existing benchmarks, however, fragment this evaluation across different construction tasks and application settings. For example, object and scene authoring benchmarks assess geometry, visual fidelity, construction, and editing [10, 11], whereas executable-world and game benchmarks emphasize mechanical dependencies, interactive behavior, and gameplay completion [12, 9, 13]. Because their task scopes and evaluation protocols differ, these results are difficult to combine into a consistent account of an agent’s capabilities across objects, scenes, and interactive worlds. A single aggregate score can also obscure whether an agent fails to match a reference, organize a scene, or implement the required behavior. Object fidelity, scene coherence, and world functionality impose distinct construction requirements. A unified benchmark must therefore evaluate each level through dedicated tasks and complementary visual, structural, and behavioral checks.

Our key insight is that successful 3D creation demands faithful appearance, coherent structure, and functional behavior. Accordingly, we organize evaluation around objects, scenes, and interactive open worlds, requiring executable, editable artifacts at every level. Within this hierarchy, we assess object geometry and detail, scene layout and composition, and world-level appearance and activity completion through complementary visual, structural, and behavioral checks. Rendered views measure appearance, native scene inspection measures structure, and runtime tests measure behavior.

Following these principles, we introduce Frontier3DBench, comprising 145 tasks across 9 categories: 65 object tasks, 65 scene tasks, and 15 interactive open-world tasks. The suite covers generation, reconstruction, and scene editing in Blender, together with interactive world construction in Unreal Engine. Evaluation of 11 model–harness configurations reveals three key findings. First, model strengths vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. Second, every configuration scores lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in both object and scene tasks, highlighting the difficulty of matching specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Third, local mechanisms remain far stronger than coordinated activities: across all 165 L3 submissions (11 configurations × 15 tasks), the local-mechanism component of interaction correctness averages 83.08/100, compared with 20.82 for motion clearance and 30.26 for stateful workflows. These findings point to reference fidelity and the coordination of moving parts, actions, and persistent state as the main open challenges in 3D creation.

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    A unified benchmark for coding agents in 3D creation. Frontier3DBench comprises 145 tasks across 9 categories, bringing object, scene, and interactive-world construction into a shared suite covering generation, reconstruction, and scene editing. Dedicated tasks at each level reveal whether an agent’s strengths extend from individual assets to complete environments.

  • •

    Joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. We assess executable Blender and Unreal Engine artifacts through visual judgments, structural measurements, and independent runtime tests, connecting content quality with action effects, state consistency, and activity completion.

  • •

    An empirical account of current capabilities and bottlenecks. Across 11 model–harness configurations, we identify strengths that vary by construction level and persistent gaps in reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion. We further analyze capability dimensions and API costs to characterize differences in performance and resource demands.

    • 2 Frontier3DBench

    2.1 Task Formulation

    Frontier3DBench formulates 3D creation as a mapping from a task specification to project files for the prescribed 3D engine (Figure 2). These files encode the requested objects (L1), scenes (L2), or open worlds (L3), together with the code and assets needed to construct or run them.

    Input.

    We represent the agent-visible input as x=(d,I,a₀), where d is a written task instruction, I is an optional set of reference images, and a₀ denotes any supplied starter code, initial scene, or reusable assets. The instruction defines the required geometry, appearance, spatial relationships, and, for open worlds, connected regions and functional behavior. Reference-conditioned tasks provide one or more images; text-conditioned tasks use I=∅. Editing tasks additionally specify the initial scene, the requested modification, and the content to preserve. For L3, the input includes an interaction contract specifying functional zones, entities, initial states, and available operations. Source assets and evaluation annotations are used only for scoring and are not provided to the agent.

    Output.

    Given x, a coding agent A produces a submission y=A(x;e) for the task’s prescribed engine e:

    e=\begincasesBlender,&L1 objects and L2 scenes, Unreal Engine,&L3 open worlds.\endcases

    		(1)

    For L1 and L2, y contains Blender project files for the resulting object or scene, executable construction or editing code, and task-required exports. For L3, y contains Unreal Engine project files for an open world that connects multiple regions into a coherent environment, including its assets and required interaction logic. Executing the submission must realize the visual and structural requirements of the input; L3 must also support the specified actions and their persistent effects within a session. An independent observer tests the required interactions and state persistence as the player moves through the generated world.

    2.2 Benchmark Construction

    2.2.1 Data Sources

    Object and scene tasks draw on publicly available 3D models (primarily .glb, with some .blend files), images from public datasets, and photographs captured by the authors. Interactive open-world tasks use game screenshots and real-world photographs, including panoramic imagery, as visual references for interactive environments. Text-conditioned tasks use text instructions without reference images.

    2.2.2 Benchmark Composition

    Overview. Frontier3DBench organizes 3D creation tasks by the unit being built and the behavior it must support. The hierarchy progresses from individual objects and assemblies, through spatially organized scenes, to connected worlds with persistent interaction states. Table 1 summarizes the inputs and requirements of the 145 tasks across 9 categories and three levels.

    Level 1 (L1): Object Level. L1 concerns the construction of a single editable 3D asset, which can be an individual object or a mechanical assembly. Task requirements address the asset’s geometry, dimensions, appearance, and relationships among constituent parts. The 65 tasks cover modeling from text (Text2Code, 15), reconstruction from multiple reference views (Img2Code, 25), and reconstruction from a single image (Img2Code-SingleView, 25).

    Level 2 (L2): Scene Level. L2 concerns the construction or modification of a complete scene composed of multiple objects and their shared surroundings. The objects must form a coherent spatial layout with consistent relative scales, while materials and lighting must support the specified appearance and camera composition. The 65 tasks comprise scene generation from text instructions (Brief2Scene, 20), reconstruction from reference images (Ref2Scene, 10), reconstruction from real photographs (Ref2Scene-RealPhoto, 25), and modification of an existing scene (SceneEdit, 10). Scene editing requires changing specified objects or scene properties while preserving the surrounding content.

    Level 3 (L3): Open-World Level. L3 concerns the construction of an explorable world that connects multiple functional regions within a shared environment. The player must be able to move between regions and interact with objects and mechanisms whose state changes persist across action sequences within a session. Complexity is defined by the required spatial organization and connected operations, allowing both dense indoor environments and larger outdoor worlds. The 15 tasks are grouped by input modality: Text2Env (5) uses a text instruction without reference images, while Img2Env (10) pairs the instruction with one or more reference images. Both categories require executable interactions that respect action prerequisites, so that changes produced by earlier actions determine which subsequent operations are available.

    2.2.3 Data Processing Pipeline

    Task instructions. We first define the creation objective and use GPT-6-astra to expand it into a task instruction. The instruction specifies what the agent should construct and how the result should satisfy the intended geometry and appearance. It also makes spatial relationships explicit so that the instruction describes a coherent asset or environment. For tasks with visual references, the text complements the images with construction requirements; text-only tasks express the target entirely through the instruction.

    Reference images. We prepare visual inputs from existing 3D assets and collected imagery. When a source 3D model or scene is available, we render it in Blender to obtain the required reference views.
